profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-09T11:23:26.966+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: In the fifth year of Chénghé.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, at noon.
The first and fourth ships,
carrying the various envoys,
were becalmed without a favorable wind.
They lay at anchor for three days.
On the seventeenth day, at midnight,
a strong wind arose, so they hoisted sails and rowed with oars.
At the hour of Sì, they arrived at the east sea of Zhìgā Island.
As there was no fair wind,
they anchored there for five days.
On the twenty-second day, at the hour of Mǎo,
a northeast wind enabled them to set forth.
They no longer sought shelter in coves
and sailed through the dark night.
On the twenty-third day, at the hour of Sì,
they arrived at Yǒujiù Island.
A northeast wind blew,
forcing them to stay and make adjustments.
Around the hour of Yǒu,
they hoisted sails and crossed the sea.
A northeast wind blew,
and they sailed through the dark night.
The fire signals between the two ships were communicating.
On the twenty-fourth day, they sighted the fourth ship going ahead.
It was about
thirty *lǐ* away from the first ship,
sailing far to the west.
The ambassador began to draw Guānyīn Púsà.
He asked the *yìliúfǎshī* and others
to read scriptures together and make vows and prayers.
At the hour of Hài, the fire signals communicated.
Their appearance was like stars.
By dawn, they were no longer visible.
Although there were changes in thegèn-xùn winds,
there was no fear of being driven adrift.
Large bamboo roots, squid, shells, etc.,
floated with the waves.
They lowered hooks to retrieve and examine them.
Some were fresh, others withered.
The sea color was light green.
Everyone said that they were nearing land.
At the hour of Shēn, a large fish swam alongside the ship.
On the twenty-seventh day, the iron plating was completely detached by the impact of the waves.
Weary, they couldn't leave their anchorage.
Sometimes two or three flew west,
then returned to their previous spot.
This happened several times.
The sea color was white-green.
Throughout the night, people were sent to climb the mast.
They claimed not to see any mountains or islands.
On the twenty-eighth day, early in the morning,
herons flew northwest in pairs.
The wind remained unchanged.
They set the sail sideways, pointing southwest (kūn).
At the hour of Sì, they reached Báishuǐ.
Its color was like yellow mud.
The crowd all said,
"If this is the outflow of the Dàjiāng River near Yángzhōu,
we should send someone to climb the mast to see."
It flowed straight south from the intersection of Wù and Hài.
Its width was over twenty *lǐ*.
Looking ahead, the water returned to a light green.
After a short journey,
it was as reported.
The ambassador was deeply surprised that the sea color had turned light green again.
Jīn Zhèngnán, the interpreter from Xīnlúo, reported,
"I heard that the canal (Jué Gǎng) at Yángzhōu is difficult to pass.
Now that we have passed Báishuǐ,
I suspect we might have passed Jué Gǎng."
At the hour of Wèi, the seawater was also white.
Everyone was alarmed and surprised.
They sent someone up the mast.
To see land and islands.
But still, he claimed not to see any.
The wind blew without changing.
The sea was shallow and the waves were high,
crashing like thunder.
They tied an iron weight to a rope and sank it.
It barely reached five *zhàng*.
After a short while, they lowered the iron to test the depth of the sea.
It was only five *xún*.
The envoys were afraid.
Some said,
"We should drop anchor and stop.
We can only proceed tomorrow."
Others said,
"We must half-lower the sail and dispatch a small boat
to ascertain the depth of the path ahead,
then proceed gradually."
The argument for stopping
seemed inappropriate.
While they were debating and deciding,
it was already between Yǒu and Xū.
Then the east wind violently fanned them,
and the waves rose fiercely.
The ship suddenly rushed onto a sandbank.
In a panic, they dropped the sails.
The rudder blade broke twice.
Waves from east and west crashed, tilting the ship.
The rudder blade scraped the seabed,
and the ship's stern was about to break.
So they cut down the mast and abandoned the rudder.
The ship then drifted with the waves.
When eastern waves came, the ship tilted west.
When western waves came, it tilted east,
washing over the ship.
Countless times.
Everyone on board entrusted themselves to Buddha and the gods.
All made vows and prayers.
Everyone lost their wits.
From the head envoy down to the sailors,
stripped naked and tightly tied their loincloths, as the ship was about to break in the middle.
They ran from the stern to the prow,
each seeking a safe spot.
At the junction of the structure,
the impact of the waves caused everything to loosen and come apart.
At the ends of the left and right railings,
they tied ropes to hold on,
struggling for a way to survive as water filled the ship.
The ship sank into the sand.
Official and private belongings floated and sank with the water.
On the twenty-ninth day, the tide receded at dawn.
The water also drained,
allowing them to see the bottom.
The bottom was completely cracked.
Sand buried the main mast and rudder.
The crowd made a plan.
"Now the ship is already cracked.
If we encounter another rising tide,
we fear it might be further damaged and scattered."
So they inverted the mast,
cut off the left and right gangways, and erected oars on all four sides of the ship.
They tied ropes to the main mast and rudder.
At the hour of Hài, they sighted
a distant firelight to the west.
Everyone
was overjoyed at the sight.
They watched it all night.
No mountains or islands were visible;
only the firelight could be seen.
On the second day, in the early morning, the tide rose.
We pursued for several hundred *chō* (町).
To the west, we saw an island whose appearance was like two ships moored together.
In a moment, we moved closer.
We then realized it was land.
Not long after we started sailing,
we encountered two swirling currents.
The cross current flowed for over fifty *chō*.
The ship sank and became stuck in the mud.
It could neither advance nor retreat.
Then, the strong current surged quickly,
digging out the silt around the ship.
The mud immediately boiled in reverse.
The ship eventually overturned,
almost getting buried and submerged.
Everyone was frightened,
clinging to the side of the ship.
Each person wore their loincloths,
and ropes were tied everywhere,
waiting to die.
Not long after,
the ship overturned to the left again.
The people shifted to the right accordingly.
The ship overturned and shifted
several times.
Moreover, the second timber at the bottom of the ship
broke off and floated away.
Everyone was disheartened,
weeping and making vows.
Towards the *xū-hài* (戌亥) corner (northwest),
we distantly saw something floating with the waves.
Everyone said,
"Is that a ship coming to meet us?"
While in doubt and discussing,
a headwind brought it closer.
Finally, we knew it was a boat.
We saw a small boat with one *cāng* (倉) carrying people.
Among them were the previously dispatched
archer Mibu no Kaiyama (壬生開山),
and six Great Táng (大唐) people.
They hastened to the front of our ship.
The *rokuji* (錄事) and others
first asked where the *Daishi* (大使) was.
They replied,
"We do not know where he is."
Upon hearing this, we were immediately shocked and saddened,
unable to hold back our tears.
Immediately, we transferred the national offerings to that boat.
One *rokuji*,
two *chin-senji* (知乘船事),
the student monk Enzai (圓載) and twenty-seven others
transferred to and boarded it.
Pointing towards land, they departed.
At noon, they arrived at the river mouth.
At *wèi* (未) hour, they arrived at Dōngliángfēng (東梁豐) Village, Sāngtián (桑田) Township, Báicháo (白潮) Town, Hǎilíng (海陵) County, Yángzhōu (揚州).
It was the second day of the seventh month of Jingō (承和) 5 in Japan,
which was the second day of the seventh month of Kāichéng (開成) 3 in Great Táng.
Although the era names differed,
the month and day were the same.
The student monks and others stayed overnight at Jì Bīn's (季賓) residence in the garrison.
We heard that the *Daishi* had left the ship
at *wèi* hour on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month.
During the subsequent drifting,
the wind was strong and the waves fierce.
Fearing the ship would sink,
they abandoned the anchor and threw things overboard,
calling upon Guānyīn (觀音) and Myōken (妙見),
seeking a way to survive.
The strong wind occasionally stopped.
At *zǐ* (子) hour, they drifted ashore near the reeds on the south side of the great river mouth.
On the first day of the seventh month, at dawn,
the tide receded, preventing further progress.
They sent someone to climb the masthead to look for towns and villages.
To the south, there were three distant mountains,
whose names were unknown.
The countryside was remote,
and there was no one to tell them.
If they waited for the tide to rise,
they feared it would take too long and become dark,
making it impossible to rescue those on the ship.
Therefore, they tied ropes to the ship
and dragged it towards the seashore.
The number of people was very small,
making it impossible to move it.
The *hangan* (判官) and others
took the cables and pulled it.
At *wèi* hour, they boarded a small boat
and proceeded along the seashore,
gradually searching for the river mouth.
Finally, they reached the great river mouth.
The current flowed swiftly against them,
making it impossible to proceed.
The river was somewhat shallow.
The sailors and others dragged the boat forward.
It was difficult to find people.
By chance, they met a person selling reeds,
and immediately asked about the county and village.
He replied,
"This is Dàjiāngkǒu (大江口), Huáinán (淮南) Town, Hǎilíng (海陵) County, Yángzhōu (揚州), Great Táng."
Immediately, they summoned two of these merchants
to board the ship and go towards Huáinán (淮南) Town.
They went by waterway halfway,
but those two people did not know the town residences.
They pointed back towards the river mouth and returned.
At nightfall, they stayed overnight at the river mouth.
On the second day, in the evening, those two people returned.
Nearby was a salt official.
Immediately, they dispatched the *hangan* Chōmine no Sukune Takanari (長岑宿禰高名) and the *junrokuji* (准錄事) Takaoka no Sukune Hyakkō (高丘宿禰百興)
to go to the town residences.
At the same time, the salt official's *hangan*, Yuán Xíngcún (元行存),
came in a small boat to offer condolences.
The envoys wrote about the customs of their country.
The *Daishi* presented local products and went again towards Huáinán (淮南) Town.
From the river mouth, they traveled north for about fifteen *lǐ* (里).
Upon reaching the town residences, the town garrison and others reported,
"You should return to Juégǎng (掘港)."
Immediately, they brought two town garrison soldiers back to the river mouth.
Just as they arrived at the river mouth,
the *hangan* Yuán Xíngcún
said from the side of the waterway,
"Today is already late.
Let's stop and stay overnight."
Following his words, they stayed.
The expressions of sympathy were very deep,
and they also provided a guide.
On the third day, at *chǒu* (丑) hour, the tide rose.
The boat that knew the way led the way,
proceeding to Juégǎng (掘港).
At *sì* (巳) hour, they arrived at Báihúkǒu (白湖口).
The adverse current was extremely swift.
Three Great Táng people
and sailors from their own country
dragged the boat across the current.
Upon reaching the bank, they tied the cables
and waited for the tide to rise for a moment.
Here, they heard that the fourth ship had drifted ashore in the North Sea.
At noon, they finally arrived at Zhōngcūn (中村), a garrison within the jurisdiction of Báicháo (白潮) Town, Hǎilíng (海陵) County.
There, the *rokuji* Yamashiro no Ujiari (山代氏益) and over thirty others, who had previously separated at sea, came out to greet them.
They met again, and sorrow and joy mingled.
Tears flowed as they expressed their feelings.
Then, everyone stayed together.
Here, they hired small boats and other vessels
to transport the national offerings
and to wash and dry the water-damaged public and private items.
Although several days passed,
no county or prefecture had offered condolences.
Everyone sought convenient lodging,
and their hardships were considerable.
The Buddhist priest Shōeki (請益)
stayed together with the student monks.
Eighteen *lǐ* (里) from Dōngliángfēng (東梁豐) Village,
there was Yánhǎi (延海) Village.
In the village, there was a temple
called Guóqīng (國清) Temple.
The *Daishi* and others, to rest from the ordeal of drifting,
stayed there.
On the ninth day, at *sì* (巳) hour,
Liú Miǎn (劉勉), the *Daishi* of Hǎilíng (海陵) Town, came to offer condolences to the envoys.
He presented wine and cakes
and also arranged for music.
He was accompanied by eight government officials and personal attendants.
Liú Miǎn wore a purple court robe.
The village headman
also wore purple clothing.
After inspecting the area,
he returned to the county office.
On the twelfth day, they took the waterway from Dōngliángfēng (東梁豐) Village to transport their personal belongings.
After placing them in the temple,
on the same day, at noon,
to urge the arrival of the welcoming boat,
they dispatched the interpreter Ōyake no Toshiwo (大宅年雄)
and the archer Ōyake no Miyatsugu (大宅宮繼)
to go to the county office by waterway.
At *shēn* (申) hour, there was thunder.
The student monks and others stayed in Dōngfēng (東豐) Village
and had not yet arrived here.
On the thirteenth day, it was very hot.
At *wèi* (未) hour, there was thunder.
Since they first drifted ashore,
there had been many mosquitoes and gnats.
They were as large as flies
and bothered people at night.
The hardship was endless.
At *shēn* (申) hour, the student monks arrived
and stayed together in the temple.
They suffered from dysentery.
On the fourteenth day, at *chén* (辰) hour,
because the welcoming boat from the county and prefecture did not arrive,
the *Daishi* (one person), *hangan* (two people), *rokuji* (one person), *chin-senji* (one person), *shishō* (one person), archers, and sailors, a total of thirty people,
went to the county office by waterway.
At that time, the monk Yuán Yù (元昱) from Kāiyuán (開元) Temple came.
He communicated their feelings in writing
and was quite knowledgeable in literature.
He asked about the customs of their country
and also presented local products.
The monk presented peaches and other fruits.
He had his residence near the temple.
After a brief conversation, he returned.
Towards evening, there was thunder and heavy rain,
causing even greater alarm and distress.
On the 17th day, at noon, the archer Dàzhái-gōng, along with more than ten officials like the yāguān and others.
Set off from Rúgāo-zhèn's residence.
Bringing over thirty grass boats.
Immediately heard that the ambassador had arrived at the zhèn's residence yesterday.
At shēn-shi, Chūn Zhī and others, including the chéngshānlùshì.
Came with the archers from Dōngliángfēng-cūn.
And lodged in the temple.
On the morning of the 18th day.
Public and private goods were transported by boat.
At sì-shi, the lùshì and below, and the sailors and above, went towards the zhōu by waterway.
Two water buffalo were tied to the remaining boats.
Some tied three boats together to form one vessel.
Some tied two boats together to form one vessel.
And connected them with ropes.
It was difficult to hear about the progress of the front and back.
They called out loudly.
The journey was rather swift.
A ditch, more than two zhàng wide, was dug.
Flowing straight without bends.
This was dug by Suí Yángdì.
It was hard work in the rain.
They traveled over thirty lǐ.
At shēn-shi, they arrived at Guōbǔ-cūn and stopped for the night.
Many mosquitoes came out at night.
Stinging like needles.
It was extremely arduous.
Drums were beaten all night.
It was the custom of that country.
To have guards.
Who beat drums all night to protect official property.
On the 19th day, at yín-shi.
The water buffalo were led forward, and they set off.
Dark clouds, but no rain.
At mǎo-shi, they heard the crowing of roosters.
They began to see Wú Zhúlín and young millet, small cowpeas, and so on.
At sì-shi, the ambassador's official document arrived.
It arrived.
The document stated:
"As for the damaged ship,
it should be inspected as convenient by the relevant authorities.
The shǒuzhuōsī should, according to the numbers, order the sailors guarding the ship to proceed.
No one is to be released or detained."
Immediately, the designated boat masters Yěhóusīwán and others.
Were sent back to the place where the ship was moored.
At noon, they arrived at Línhécāngpù.
They traveled through the night.
On the 20th day, at the end of mǎo-shi, they arrived at Chì'àn-cūn.
They asked the local people.
They replied:
"From here, travel one hundred and twenty lǐ.
There is Rúgāo-zhèn."
After a short journey, there was a weir.
They dug open the solid weir and departed.
Past the weir was Rúgāo-yuàn.
The identity of the dedicated official was unknown.
The boats were moving too slowly.
So they stopped the water buffalo.
And again tied three boats together to make one unit.
Each unit was assigned seven sailors.
To pull the boats along.
The people became tired after a short journey.
They again tied the buffalo with a long rope to pull them along.
They were at a loss on both sides.
Exhaustion upon exhaustion.
Too many people to pull.
The buffalo pulled swiftly.
Everyone said:
"The strength of one buffalo is equal to a hundred men."
Around noon.
On the north bank of the waterway.
Willows were connected one after another.
At wèi-shi, they arrived at Rúgāo-diàn and stopped temporarily.
On the north bank of the dug ditch.
Houses were connected one after another.
The archer Zhàngbùzhēn-míng and others.
Came from the ambassador and said:
"Travel half a lǐ from here.
To the west end, there is the zhèn's residence.
The ambassador, the pànguān, and others reside here.
They have not yet gone to the xiàn's residence."
The ambassador and pànguān, upon hearing that tribute items were arriving, would go to the zhōu again.
They ordered the boats to be prepared.
They also said:
"Today, the zhōu envoy will arrive.
Only then will raw provisions be supplied."
The envoy of the Sīlluó-guó was the vanguard.
And was placed together with the home country's (envoy).
But this year, the tribute envoy was called the Sīlluó-guó envoy.
And the greetings were sparse and cursory.
Now the ambassadors and others.
Have come to the zhèn's residence first.
It has been decided that our country and Sīlluó are far apart.
Once the xiàn and zhōu have been informed and the report completed.
Upon hearing this, they were suddenly delighted.
And much relieved of their fatigue.
At shēn-shi, the zhèn's ambassador Liú Miǎnjià, on horseback.
Came to the place where the boats were moored.
Seven or eight followers and grooms.
After inspecting the matters, he left.
The lùshì and others disembarked.
And paid their respects to the ambassador.
As it was late, they did not travel.
They stopped here for the night.
On the 21st day, at mǎo-shi.
The ambassador and those below him departed together.
Rich and noble houses lined both sides of the waterway.
Without any obstruction.
After a short journey, not long after.
The houses gradually became sparse.
This was where the zhèn's residence turned back.
The ambassador accompanied them for about three or four lǐ.
And returned to his own zhèn.
From the zhèn's residence to the xiàn was two hundred and twenty lǐ.
At sì-shi, they released the water buffalo.
Each took a boat.
And proceeded with oars.
There were absolutely no houses.
At the end of shēn-shi, they arrived at Yánhǎixiāng Yánhǎicūn.
And stopped for the night.
There were many mosquitoes and gnats.
The hardship was extreme.
They departed in the middle of the night.
Salt officials' boats loaded with salt.
Some with three or four boats.
Some with four or five boats.
Tied in pairs and connected in series.
For tens of lǐ without interruption.
Traveling together.
It was difficult to keep track of them when first seen.
It was truly extraordinary.
On the 22nd day, at dawn.
All the boats were tied to water buffalo and pulled along.
Many white geese and white ducks were seen here and there.
There were continuous human dwellings.
After sì-shi.
After traveling thirty lǐ.
There were only three or four houses.
Their presence was inconsistent.
They traveled in the dark of night.
At zǐ-shi, they arrived at a village.
Its name was unknown.
All the boats lodged there.
On the 23rd day, at mǎo-shi, they departed.
The local people reported:
"From here to the xiàn is twenty lǐ."
After a short journey.
By the side of the waterway.
Someone was raising water birds.
Gathering them in one place.
Not letting them scatter.
In one place, over two thousand were raised.
Such kinds of things.
Existed in the bends of rivers.
Bamboo forests were everywhere.
Bamboos grew up to about four zhàng tall.
They traveled north.
Since the first day of boarding the boat.
They mostly traveled west.
Sometimes north.
Sometimes northeast.
Or northwest.
Before chén-shi, a pagoda was seen ahead.
They immediately asked the local people.
They replied:
"This is Xīchí-sì.
The pagoda is an earthen pagoda.
It has nine stories.
It is one of the seven official temples."
After traveling a short distance.
They arrived at the eastern end of Hǎilíng-xiàn.
The officials in the xiàn.
One zhǎngguān.
One pànguān.
And seven bīngmǎshǐ, etc., in total.
Their ranks were unknown.
After a short journey, they arrived at the southern river of the xiàn.
The xiànlìng and others welcomed them in front of the southern river bridge of Xīchí-sì.
The ambassador, pànguān, lùshì, and others.
Disembarked and went ashore.
They lodged in the temple.
The xiàn officials offered money.
But the Yìliúxuésēng (additional student monks).
Were still on the boat.
Everyone in the xiàn gathered eagerly to see them.
The Yìliúxuésēng felt unwell.
On the 24th day, at Chen-shi (7-9 AM).
At Xīchí Sì (西池寺), a lecture was given on the *Dàshéng Qǐxìn Lùn* (大乘起信論).
The principal lecturer, Qiān (謙), along with the *sāngāng* (三綱) and others, both before and after, came aboard the ship.
They expressed their regards to the two monks who had traveled from afar.
They communicated their sentiments in writing.
The monks stayed briefly and then departed.
By Sì-shi (9-11 AM).
The Ambassador and those below him.
Left the temple and boarded the ships.
They set off together.
The officials from the county.
As they had no well-wishes or condolences.
Ordered the military to send off the group.
At Shēn-shi (3-5 PM), they arrived at Yílín Guǎn (宜陵館).
This was a place for officials and guests who traveled back and forth and were served provisions.
In accordance with the situation, Judge Fúyuán Zhēnmǐn (藤原貞敏) suddenly suffered from diarrhea.
All the ships moored in front of this inn for the night.
The two monks disembarked to check.
And inquire about the sick person.
Immediately, they returned to the ship and heard that the Judge of the fourth vessel could not tolerate hot water.
He disembarked and stayed at the residence of Bái Shuǐláng (白水郎).
Before the national tribute ships were fully loaded, they were all damaged.
However, there was no unusual damage to either public or private goods.
Due to the lack of welcoming boats, they could not be transported ashore.
On the 25th day, at Yín-shi (3-5 AM), they set off.
Everyone suffered from diarrhea.
The ships did not proceed uniformly.
The ships that went ahead.
Were held back for the later turn.
Those who were behind.
Advanced to the front.
From Hǎilíng Xiàn (海陵縣).
To Yílín Guǎn (宜陵館) was over fifty *lǐ*.
To the prefecture was sixty-five *lǐ*.
At Sì-shi (9-11 AM), they arrived at Xiāngōng Guān (仙宮觀).
They continued straight without rest.
At Wèi-shi (1-3 PM), they stopped on the east side of Chánzhì Qiáo (禪智橋).
At the north end of the bridge was Chánzhì Sì (禪智寺).
During the Enryaku (延曆) era, the matter of the Vice-Ambassador's death anniversary.
Was observed at this temple.
Three *lǐ* west from the bridge.
Was Yángzhōu Fǔ (揚州府).
The Ambassador, to communicate national affairs.
Dispatched the *yāguān* (押官) and others to the prefecture, who arrived late.
At Shēn-shi (3-5 PM), they departed.
The river was filled with large ferry boats.
Reed-laden boats.
And small boats.
Innumerable.
After Shēn-shi (3-5 PM), they passed through the Dōngguō Shuǐmén (東郭水門).
At Yǒu-shi (5-7 PM), they stopped at the river north of the city.
The Ambassador and others disembarked and stayed ashore.
They had not yet met the prefectural officials.
The monks seeking further instruction and the student monks.
Had not yet left the ship.
As night fell, it rained.
The hardship was extremely severe.
On the 26th day, at Bū-shi (3-5 PM).
They disembarked and stayed at the official inn south of the river.
The two monks each occupied a separate room.

Early in the morning, the Grand Councilor entered the temple to perform obeisance to the Buddha.
Then returned.
On the third day, the images of the two great masters, Nán-Yuè and Tiān-Tái, were begun, two sets, each with three copies.
Formerly, during the Liáng dynasty, there was Hán Gàn.
This person, during the Liáng court,
was the foremost painter.
When painting images of birds and beasts,
as soon as their eyes were drawn,
they could fly and run.
The portrait of Grand Master Nán-Yuè was sought and painted at Lóng-Xīng-Sì in Yáng-Zhōu.
An imperial edict commanded that it be placed on the south corridor wall of the liú-lí hall in the Fǎ-Huā Dào-Chǎng, and ordered the ambassador's attendant, Lì-Tián Jiā-Jì, to copy it.
There was not a single flaw or error.
Subsequently, at Kāi-Yuán-Sì,
Jiā-Jì was instructed to depict the countenance, clothing, and physique on silk.
It was entirely in the style of Hán Gàn.
Also, on the wall of the same corridor in that monastery, images of monks chanting the Fǎ-Huā Jīng were painted.
This evoked an unusual sensation.
The number of monks depicted was about twenty.
They could not all be fully described.
To the east of the Liú-Lí Hall,
there is the Pǔ-Xián Huí-Fēng-Zhī-Táng.
Once, a fire broke out
and completely burned that monastery.
The fire reached the Fǎ-Huā Yuàn.
There was a sūtra-chanting master, Líng-Yòu,
who, within this Pǔ-Xián Hall,
was chanting the Fǎ-Huā Jīng.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
blowing from within the monastery,
and repelled the fire,
preventing that hall from burning.
At that time, people therefore called it the Pǔ-Xián Huí-Fēng-Zhī-Táng.
Also, in the Dōng-Tǎ Yuàn,
the plain portrait of Monastic Jiàn-Zhēn was placed.
The inscription on the pavilion said:
"Plain Portrait of the Monk Who Crossed the Sea."
Furthermore, inside the central gate, at the eastern end,
a stele commemorating the Monk Who Crossed the Sea was erected.
Its preface
recorded the events of Monastic Jiàn-Zhēn
crossing the sea
for the sake of Buddhist dharma.
It states:
"The Monk, crossing the sea, encountered fierce winds.
First, he arrived at the Shé Hǎi (Snake Sea),
which was several tens of *zhàng* long.
Traveling for one day, it was completely traversed.
Next, they reached the Hēi Hǎi (Black Sea),
the color of the sea being like ink," and so forth.
Also heard:
"An imperial edict arrived at the prefecture."
The edict stated:
"According to the memorial of the tribute envoy,
for the envoy of the country of Rì-Běn,
an order was issued in Chǔ-Zhōu
to hire a ship,
so that in the third month
they could cross the sea."
The meaning of this is not yet clear.
On the sixth day, Lord Shěn Biàn, accompanying the army, came and said:
"The Lord conveys a message:
'From the fifth day of this month, for the sake of the nation and also obtaining money to repair the Zhān-Tán Ruì-Xiàng-Gé of Kāi-Yuán-Sì,
it is entrusted to Xiào-Gǎn-Sì
to expound sūtras and raise funds.
Invite the monks of our country to specifically attend the lectures.
Also urge the various officials of our country
to form karmic connections and donate money.'"
On the seventh day, Shěn Biàn came
and conveyed the Lord's words:
"The various officials of the prefecture and government
intend to gather tomorrow
at Xiào-Gǎn-Sì
to invite the monks from our country to come and lecture."
There was also a fund-raising appeal written by Dharma Master Fán, who was lecturing on sūtras.
According to his statement, it said:
"To repair the Ruì-Xiàng-Gé,
the Jīn-Gāng Jīng will be lectured.
The money requested is fifty *guàn*."
"The appeal, encountering the Lord's generous summons,
for a shared cause and shared karma,
is entrusted to Xiào-Gǎn-Sì
to lecture sūtras and await donations."
The appeal is as separately attached.
Shěn Biàn reported:
"The Lord donated one thousand *guàn*.
This lecture series is set for two months.
Many people attend to listen to the dharma daily.
It is estimated that ten thousand *guàn* are needed
to repair this pavilion.
During that period,
the country provided one thousand *guàn* of money,
and people from the Pú-Guó (婆國, possibly an error for other name) donated two hundred *guàn*.
Currently, the number of people from this country is small,
so fifty *guàn* are being solicited.
The urging for contributions is causing less response."
On the eighth day, a Sīn-Luó (신라) man, Wáng Qǐng, came to visit.
He was one of the Tang people, Zhāng Jué-Jì and others, who, in the tenth year of the Hóng-Rén era of this country,
drifted and landed in Chū-Zhōu-Guó, on the same ship.
When asked about the reason for drifting,
he reported that for trading various goods,
they left here and crossed the sea.
Suddenly, they encountered fierce winds,
drifted south for three months,
and landed in Chū-Zhōu-Guó.
Zhāng Jué-Jì and his brother,
just as they were about to depart,
collectively escaped and remained in Chū-Zhōu.
From northern Chū-Zhōu,
they departed towards the North Sea.
With good winds for fifteen days,
they drifted and landed in Cháng-Mén-Guó.
They somewhat understood the language of this country.
On the ninth day, the portraits of Nán-Yuè and Tiān-Tái were finished.
On the fourteenth day was Lì-Chūn.
People in the market made and sold orioles (paper birds).
People bought and played with them.
On the fifteenth night,
in the east and west streets,
people's houses lit lanterns.
It was no different from the last night of the year in our country.
Inside the monasteries, lanterns were lit to offer to the Buddha,
and also offerings were made to the images of masters.
Lay people also did the same.
In front of the Buddha hall of the monastery, a lantern tower was erected.
In the courtyard below the steps,
and beside the corridors, oil was burned everywhere.
The number of lamp dishes could not be counted.
Men and women in the streets,
not fearing the deep night,
entered the monasteries to observe the events.
Before the lantern offerings,
they donated money according to their means.
After touring and observing,
they would go to other monasteries to observe, bow, and donate money.
In the halls of all monasteries and all courtyards,
everyone competed in lighting lanterns.
Those who came to attend
would certainly donate money before leaving.
Wú-Liàng-Yì-Sì
set up spoon lamps and bamboo lamps.
Counting these, there were a thousand lamps.
These spoon and bamboo lamps
were constructed as trees.
Their appearance was like a pagoda.
The intricate weaving pattern
was extremely exquisite.
Their height was about seven or eight *chǐ*.
This period, from this night
until the night of the seventeenth,
was set for three nights.
On the seventeenth day, Shěn Biàn came to assist in the sorrow, delaying the departure.
He then asked about the official dispatch from Xiànggōng Mèng Chén.
Could I go to Táizhōu?
Shěn Biàn wrote in reply,
"I, Biàn, consulted Xiànggōng
three or four times.
I mentioned that a monk from our country
wishes to go to Táizhōu.
I propose an official dispatch; I wonder if it is permissible?"
Xiànggōng said,
"An official dispatch issued in Yángzhōu,
upon reaching the Zhéxī Dào
and the Zhédōng Dào,
will not accomplish anything.
It must be reported to the emperor.
Only after an imperial edict is issued will it be permissible.
Otherwise, it will not be.
Furthermore, for the eight prefectures under Xiànggōng's jurisdiction,
with Xiànggōng's dispatch,
one can travel to and fro.
However, for Rùnzhōu
and Táizhōu,
there are other Xiànggōngs,
each with their own administration.
They each guard their posts and do not interfere with one another.
I fear that without an imperial edict,
there will be no way to proceed smoothly."
After the fast,
in front of the hall of this temple,
treasures and rarities were displayed,
and two scroll-mounted images of sages and saints were arranged.
The exotic and precious silks
were too numerous to remember.
The countenances of the sages and saints
either had their eyes closed in contemplation,
or looked up gazing into the distance,
or turned to the side as if conversing,
or were bowed down looking at the ground.
The forty-two images
each had forty-two different countenances
and variations in their seated postures.
Some sat in the full lotus position,
others in the half lotus position.
The methods of sitting differed.
Beyond the forty-two sages and saints,
separate images of Pǔxián and Wénshū Bodhisattvas, as well as the Jìngmìngniǎo and Jiālíngpínqié Niao birds, were placed.
At dusk, lamps were lit to make offerings to the images of the saints.
As night fell, chanting and bowing to the Buddha commenced,
along with chanting and praising in Sanskrit.
Eight Sanskrit masters came at once,
some holding golden lotuses and jade banners,
seated in rows before the saints,
praising in Sanskrit in unison.
This continued sleeplessly throughout the night.
Before each saint, a bowl lamp was lit.
On the morning of the eighteenth day,
medicinal porridge was offered.
During the fast, meals were provided.
A hundred varieties of delicious food were served.
Men and women, young and old,
regardless of day or night,
gathered in large numbers.
Additionally, in the head monk's hall,
a fast was held and offerings made to the monks.
As night fell, lamps were again lit for offerings,
accompanied by Sanskrit praises.
This continued for two days and two nights.
Furthermore, among the great imperial army and the monks in the temples,
all of them today
are sifting rice.
Without a set number of days,
rice is transported from the prefecture
and distributed to the various temples.
The number of hu is not fixed,
sometimes ten hu, sometimes twenty hu.
The temple treasury receives it
and then distributes it to the monks,
some receiving one dòu,
some one dòu and five shēng.
When the monks receive it,
they sort out the good from the bad.
Broken grains are considered bad,
unbroken ones good.
If one receives one dòu of rice,
it is divided into two portions.
The good portion is barely six shēng.
The good and bad are put into different bags
and returned to the officials.
All other temples follow the same procedure,
each sorting the good from the bad,
and all returning them to the officials.
Two types are received back:
the good ones are respectfully presented to the emperor
for his imperial meals,
the bad ones are kept
and stored by the officials.
However, they are only distributed among the soldiers and monks,
not to the common people.
It is even more difficult to sort the millet selected by the prefecture.
The rice selected in Yángzhōu,
the color of the rice is extremely black.
After removing the paddy grains and broken grains,
only the sound and good ones are taken.
The other prefectures
are not like this.
I heard that Xiànggōng sorts five shí,
the commander of the army's gate does the same.
The Lángzhōng sorts two shí,
the Lángguān one shí.
The military masters and monks sort one dòu and five shēng
or one dòu.
Furthermore, Xiànggōng recently invited the Vinaya Grand Master Guāngyì from Hèlínsì Temple in Dòngzhōu
to temporarily reside at Huìzhàosì Temple.
Xiànggōng intends to appoint this monk
as the Saṅgha Commissioner of this prefecture
and has ordered him to reside at Kāiyuánsì Temple.
The Saṅgha Commissioner
oversees the affairs of the various temples and monks under the jurisdiction of the Yángzhōu Dūdū Fǔ.
In the entire Táng country,
there are three types of positions: Saṅghalord (Sēnglù), Saṅgha Commissioner (Sēngzhèng), and Temple Overseer (Jiānsì).
The Sēnglù governs all temples nationwide
and manages Buddhist law.
The Sēngzhèng is only within the jurisdiction of one Dūdū Fǔ.
The Jiānsì is limited to one temple.
Beyond these, in other regions, there are the Saṅgha Directors (Sāngāng) and the Treasury Office (Kùsī).
Toward dusk, the Saṅgha Commissioner resided at this temple.
On the twentieth day, at dusk, the Saṅgha Commissioner came to visit and offer condolences.
On the twenty-first day, after the fast,
the envoy and others
brought a letter dated the sixth day of the twelfth month of last year.
According to its contents,
they arrived safely at the capital on the third day of the twelfth month
and were settled in the Lǐbīnyuàn in Dōngjīng.
The details are as specified separately.
The Assistant Judge Cóng Cūnqīng's letter, dated the same month and day, stated:
At chénshí on the third day of this month,
they arrived at Chánglè Yì.
An imperial envoy came to greet them
and conveyed imperial inquiries.
The envoy arrived at Lǐbīnyuàn and also paid respects at court.
The extraordinary events were briefly understood.
On the twenty-fifth day, three scrolls of the Fǎhuā Yuánjìng were obtained from the monk Huìwēi at Yángguāngsì Temple.
On the third day of the intercalary first month,
this temple celebrated the Saṅgha Commissioner's entry into the temple.
Elder monks from various temples were invited
to the treasury for an elaborate meal.
A hundred kinds were amply provided,
and music was also performed.
On the fourth day, as per Jīn Zhèngnán's request,
to repair the purchased boat,
thirty-six people, including master carpenters, artisans, boat builders, and blacksmiths,
were sent to Chǔzhōu.
Also, at this temple,
monks were invited to pray for rain.
Seven people formed a group
to recite scriptures.
On the fifth day, as night fell, there was thunder, lightning, and heavy rain,
like the thunderstorms of summer.
After that, rain fell for seven days
until the full moon when it finally cleared.
Xiànggōng, for the repair of the Ruìxiàng Gé at Kāiyuánsì Temple,
arranged for a lecture to solicit donations.
Starting from the first day of the first month
until the eighth day of this month, the lectures concluded.
Five hundred guàn were used to purchase wood,
which was dragged and placed in the temple courtyard.
For now, it is being managed and ordered to be planed.
Over sixty sailors and archers from the first tribute ship of our country
are all lying ill and suffering.
On the nineteenth day, the monk Jìngwén (敬文) from Tiāntái Shān Chánlín (天台山禪林) came to see me.
The letter said:
Jìngwén (敬文) resides at Tiāntái Shān Chánlín Sì (天台山禪林寺).
He has been with his master in these mountains.
It has been twenty-one years since he became a monk.
He studied the Nánshān Chāo (南山鈔) of the Sìfēnlǜ (四分律).
He studied the Fǎhuā Jīng Zhǐguān (法花經止觀) of the Tiāntái (天台) school.
On the third day of the tenth month last year,
he left the monastery and went to Zhè (浙).
He reached Xīsūzhōu (西蘇州).
He learned that the Japanese nation had envoys presenting tribute,
and that a great Heshang (和尚) was accompanying them.
Therefore, he came here seeking them.
Jìngwén (敬文) also, in his youth,
accompanied Heshang Xíngmǎn (行滿),
and saw Zuìchéng Shélí (㝡澄闍梨) arrive
to obtain the Tiāntái (天台) teachings.
Since then, it has been thirty years,
and he has not received any news.
He has just heard
that Dàdé Chéng (澄大德) has undergone spiritual transformation (passed away),
and the Buddhist community is in sorrow.
What should be done?
Previously,
Heshang Mǎn (滿和尚) was expected to return to Tiāntái Shān (天台山).
Heshang Mǎn (滿和尚) has already passed away,
sixteen years ago.
Jìngwén (敬文) suddenly heard that the two Dàdé (大德) were present,
and therefore came searching.
He received a letter from the monk seeking instruction.
It stated that Yuánrén (圓仁) is a disciple of the former Heshang Chéng (澄和尚) who entered Táng (唐),
and has come here to seek the遗迹 (relics/traces) of Tiāntái (天台).
As the imperial edict has not yet been issued,
he is temporarily residing in this monastery
and cannot proceed.
Please take note of this.
Jìngwén (敬文)'s letter said:
Heshang Zuìchéng (㝡澄和尚),
in the twenty-first year of Zhēnyuán (貞元),
entered Tiāntái (天台).
Afterwards, he returned to his home country.
I am deeply pleased that he was able to reach it.
How many people in that land were receptive to the Tiāntái (天台) teachings he brought?
It was said that the Crown Prince of that country at the time was an incarnation of Nányuè (南岳).
I am not familiar with matters from then onwards.
Now that you are a disciple of Heshang Chéng (澄和尚),
before the imperial edict comes down,
why not go and wait in Tiāntái (天台)?
If you suddenly stay here for a long time and the edict arrives,
the envoy will immediately return to his home country.
How then could you leisurely proceed?
The monk seeking instruction asked:
I do not know how many monks and how many Zhǔ (座主) there are at Guóqīng Sì (國清寺) in your Tiāntái (天台) country.
Jìngwén (敬文) replied:
Guóqīng Sì (國清寺) usually has one hundred and fifty monks residing permanently.
During the summer season, there are over three hundred people staying there.
Chánlín Sì (禪林寺) usually has forty people residing.
During the summer season, over seventy people.
Guóqīng Sì (國清寺) has the Zhǔ (座主) Wéijuān (維蠲),
who frequently lectures on Zhǐguān (止觀).
The Zhǔ (座主) Guǎngxiū (廣修) has many disciples.
Chánlín Sì (禪林寺) is where Zhǔ (座主) Guǎngxiū (廣修) regularly lectures on the Fǎhuā Jīng Zhǐguān Xuányì (法花經止觀玄義).
He does not miss lectures in winter or summer.
There are also several junior Zhǔ (座主).
We had many conversations.
Currently, he is permitted to reside at Huìzhào Sì Chánlín Yuàn (惠照寺禪林院) in this prefecture.
He returned in the evening.
On the twenty-first day, Jìngwén (敬文) also came again.
We communicated through writing.
Afterwards, he continued to come and speak.
At Sōngshān Yuàn (嵩山院), Heshang Quányǎ (全雅), who recites mantras,
borrowed several tens of scrolls, including the Vajradhātu (金剛界) deities' rituals.
This Heshang Quán (全和尚)
currently possesses both the Garbhadhātu (胎藏) and Vajradhātu (金剛) mandalas,
and also understands the methods for constructing altars.
On the fifth day of the second month,
Heshang Quányǎ (全雅) came to the room
and constructed a Cintāmaṇicakra (如意輪) altar.
On the sixth day, the prefectural official, by imperial edict, granted stipends.
According to the Observer's (觀察使) dispatch,
it stated:
By imperial edict of the second day of the intercalary first month,
the envoy's attendants going to the capital are granted two hundred and seventy bolts of silk.
Each person receives five bolts.
Totaling one thousand three hundred and fifty bolts.
By imperial edict of the sixth day of the second month of the twenty-first year of Zhēnyuán (貞元),
each person is granted five bolts of silk.
There was no previous precedent for granting stipends to monks.
This time, when granting stipends, it is done equally for monks.
However, they are not to enter the capital for lodging.
From one judge downwards, and from sailors upwards,
each person is granted five bolts.
There is no distinction of more or less.
On the eighth day, a letter from Chief Judge Zhǎng (長判官) dated the thirteenth day of the intercalary first month stated:
On the day of meeting the Son of Heaven,
he was given special consideration for a personal audience,
but permission was not granted.
He remains deeply worried and disappointed.
One archer from the fourth ship
and two sailors,
because they forcibly violated local Táng (唐) people, were previously seized, bound, and placed in cangues in the prefecture and have not yet been released.
In the wèishí (未時) hour, they exited the eastern corridor water gate.
Not long after,
the fourth ship's Supervisor of National Trust (監國信)
and the interpreter,
because they purchased prohibited items,
were called by the local officials.
They followed the envoy into the prefecture.
All ships stopped on the east side of Chánzhì Sì (禪智寺).
They then entered the temple to make rounds.
At dawn,
the interpreter and others from the fourth ship, having been released, rushed over.
The Chief Officer's (長官) attendants, Bái Niǎo (白鳥),
Qīngcén (清岑),
Zhǎngcén (長岑),
and the four exchange students,
went ashore to the market to buy incense, medicine, etc.
They were pursued and investigated by local officials, and two hundred-plus strings of cash were confiscated, so they fled.
Only three people came back.
On the twenty-first day, they departed early in the morning.
The Grand Envoy's (大使) attendant, Sùtián Jiājì (粟田家繼), had gone to the market to buy goods previously.
He went ashore to the market.
He was seized by local officials
and detained in the prefecture.
Today, he was released and came back.
Also, an archer from the fourth ship was released and returned.
They arrived at Jiāngyáng Xiàn Huíchuán Yàn (江陽縣㢠船堰) and stayed for the night.
On the twenty-second day, they departed at chénshí (辰時).
The archer Shēnrén Bù Zhēnjìng (身人部貞淨)
was buying goods in the market.
He was previously caught and detained in the prefecture.
Today, he was released and came back.
His goods were also not lost.
Not long after,
two archers and sailors from the fourth ship were released and returned.
The historian Yuèzhì Zhēnyuán (越智貞原) had previously gone to the market to buy goods.
The local officials reported it to the prefecture for a decision.
Today, he rushed back.
They traveled briefly and stopped at Chángbái Yàn Chángbái Qiáo (常白堰常白橋).
They departed in the evening.
They traveled in the dark night.
At hàishí (亥時),
they arrived and stayed at Lùjīn Yì (路巾驛).
On the twenty-third day, they departed early in the morning.
At chénshí (辰時),
they briefly stopped at Gāoyóu Xiàn (高郵縣).
It is fifty-five lǐ (里) north to the border of Chǔzhōu (楚州) Báoyìng Xiàn (寶應縣).
It is thirty-three lǐ (里) south to the border of Jiāngyáng Xiàn (江陽縣).
They exited the eastern corridor water gate of Yángzhōu (揚州), passed east of Chánzhì Sì (禪智寺),
and traveled north.
At xūshí (戌時),
they passed Hánghè Qiáo (行賀橋) within Báoyìng Xiàn (寶應縣) jurisdiction.
They traveled briefly and then stopped.
At chǒushí (丑時), they resumed traveling.
On the 24th day, at `mǎo` hour.
Arrived at Bái Tián Shì in Bǎo Yīng Xiàn.
To the south of the market bridge was Fǎ Huā Yuàn.
At `chén` hour, arrived at Bǎo Yīng Xiàn and stopped.
Nearby was Ān Lè Guǎn.
South to Yáng Zhōu Gāo Yóu Xiàn is 120 `lǐ`.
North to the `zhōu` is 80 `lǐ`.
At `wǔ` hour.
Arrived at Shān Yáng Xiàn.
It is 65 `lǐ` from the `zhōu`.
After `shēn` hour.
Arrived at Chǔ Zhōu Chéng.
The `pàn guān`, `lù shì`, and others
disembarked and entered the `yì guǎn`.
Paid respects to the Ambassador.
Requested permission for the `yì liú xué sēng` (requesting-benefits student monk) and others
to enter the `guǎn` in the evening.
Met the Ambassador, `pàn guān`, and others.
The Ambassador declared,
"On the day of arrival in the capital,
I will immediately memorialize regarding the `yì liú xué sēng`
and the matter of going to Tái Zhōu.
Hire nine boats
and let them be repaired."
The `Lǐ Bīn Shǐ` (Minister of Rites and Guests) said,
"Before the audience,
no matters may be memorialized."
Repeatedly urged him to memorialize.
Only permission to hire boats and repair them was granted.
Permission to send to Tái Zhōu was not granted.
An imperial edict was received, stating,
"The day for the envoys and others to return to their country is approaching.
From Yáng Zhōu to Tái Zhōu,
the journey is long.
If the monk arrives there and then seeks a return date,
it is estimated that they will not meet.
On the day the envoys and others set sail,
how can they return to their homeland?
Therefore, going to Tái Zhōu is not permitted."
However, for one `liú xué sēng` (student monk),
permission was granted to go to Tái Zhōu for five years.
It was deemed appropriate to provide provisions for the entire period.
On the day of the audience, the matter was memorialized again.
The edict completely denied it.
Afterwards, it was memorialized again.
Ultimately, it was not permitted.
This was a source of shame and regret.
After the conversation,
entered Kāi Yuán Sì.
Resided in the west pavilion of the kitchen-storehouse.
On the 25th, met with the `Zhēn Yán Qǐ Yì Yuán Xíng Fǎ Shī` (true words requesting-benefits master Yuán Xíng).
He said,
"The Ambassador, while in the capital,
memorialized repeatedly,
requesting that the `qǐ yì sēng` (requesting-benefits monk) be allowed to stay in the temple.
The edict again denied it.
Later, he memorialized again.
Finally, an imperial edict was granted,
permitting him to stay in Qīng Lóng Sì.
He received the `Tāi Zàng` (Garbhadhātu) Dharma from `Yì Zhēn Zuò Zhǔ` for fifteen days
and provided for a hundred monks, but did not receive the `Jīn Gāng Jiè` (Vajradhātu) Dharma."
On the 26th, early morning, Quán Yǎ arrived.
Since the `zǒng guān` (overall official) did not allow them to stay in the temple,
they moved to Lóng Xīng Sì.
It was five `lǐ` away.
From Yáng Zhōu, there was a dispatch.

Arranged personal belongings.

The 14th,
15th,

For these three days,

On the 17th

He said,
He said,

To the north of this Chǔzhōu (楚州)

Throughout the night, the favorable wind remained unchanged.
On the 26th, early morning court.

Drums were beaten, and we set off.

At Zǐ-shí (11 PM - 1 AM).

On the 27th, at Mǎo-shí (5-7 AM).

At Sì-shí (9-11 AM), we sailed.
At Wǔ-shí (11 AM - 1 PM), the northeast wind blew.

On the 28th, the sky was clear.
At Sì-shí (9-11 AM).

In the afternoon, the wind shifted to the southeast.
At night, the wind shifted to the southwest.

On April 1st.

After the officials completed the sacrifices,

"If we go north from here for one day,
These were to be transferred to the student monk Chángcēn Sùnèi (Nagasamine Sukune) upon his return to Japan.
there is Dàzhū Shān.

At night, the wind blew,

On the 4th, at Mǎo-shí (5-7 AM).
The *Yìsēng* (benefactor monks),

On the fifth day, at dawn.

The first ship's dispatch stated:

The monks, in this desolate ravine,

They gave all their personal belongings,

The stone cliffs were steep and dangerous.

They did not know if the people's intentions were good or bad.
