you claimed to be Silla people.
But looking at your speech,
it is not Silla speech,
nor is it Dàtáng speech.
I heard that the Japanese tribute envoy ships
are anchored at Shāndōng, waiting for wind.
I fear that you, Venerables, are official guests
who have escaped from your country's ship
and come to this village.
I dare not let official guests stay.
Please tell the truth.
Do not speak falsely.
Currently, this village has a provincial dispatch
and also three or four people
from the Yāyá envoy
who are here to investigate.
I am even more afraid that if they see you, Venerables,
they will seize you and take you to the province.
At the time of this deliberation,
Zhāng Liàng and Zhāng Mào, three people from the Hǎizhōu Sì Xiàn Dū Yóu Jiàng's sub-patrol army,
came with bows and arrows and asked,
“Where are you from?”
The monks intended to answer truthfully,
but feared being accused of a crime and seized.
So they immediately made a plan
and wrote a reply.
“We monks are indeed from our country's ship.
Because of illness, we temporarily disembarked.
We stayed overnight and did not realize the ship had departed.
We hired someone to come here.
Please send an official to take us away.”
Thereupon, the army officers
clearly understood the situation.
They took the monks
to the village head Wáng Liáng's house.
They asked the army officers to record the reasons for their stay and present them to the Yāyá.
The monks then wrote a statement to report.
The statement read:
“Nine ships of the Japanese tribute envoy
are anchored in Shāndōng Dǎo in the East Sea, waiting for wind.
This monk, due to abdominal illness and beriberi,
disembarked on the third day of this month.
Two accompanying monks
and one layman
disembarked with him.
They sought water and climbed into the mountains.
Day and night they tended to their ailments, but they had not yet recovered.
The tribute envoy's ship,
because of the favorable wind,
arrived at the anchorage early yesterday morning.
We searched for it but could not find it.
While left on the desolate shore, feeling despondent,
a charcoal ship arrived.
There were ten people on it.
They fully questioned the situation
and then directed us to the village.
The monks forcibly hired one person
to come from the mountains
to Sùchéng Cūn.
Their personal belongings, clothes, alms bowl, iron bowl, documents, and washing bottle,
as well as over seven hundred cash,
and hats, etc.,
are now all lost.
We now intend to go to our country's ships
and sail back to our country.
Please send an official to take us.”
Thereupon, the sub-patrol army officers
sent another separate report
to the Yāyá Dū Yóuyì Office.
As night fell, from Hàishí (9-11 PM), there was thunder and heavy rain.
A strong wind blew fiercely.
The sound of thunder and lightning
was unbearable.
The torrential rain and fierce wind
were beyond endurance.
By the time of Chǒushí (1-3 AM),
the thunder and rain ceased.
The wind direction had changed.
In the early morning, upon asking,
many said it was a north wind.
On the sixth day, the weather was clear.
The xiànjiā (county office) dōushǐ (prefect) came to request a memorial.
I drafted the memorial according to yesterday's pattern.
And gave it to him.
Zǐxúnjiāng (commander of patrols) and others,
dispatched two laborers,
and sent them to the mooring place,
ordering them to see if those boats had departed yet.
However, because the envoy arrived late,
they could not be dispatched.
Zǐxúnjiāng Zhāng Liàng said,
“Today, dispatch one laborer,
to take the monk’s personal clothing
to the second ship.
Upon reaching Shānnán, find a donkey to carry them.
There is nowhere to borrow or rent a donkey or horse here.”
In the evening,
the xiàn dōushǐ (county prefect) came and said,
“I will depart this morning.
Tomorrow, I will be in Shānnán,
making húntun (wontons)
and hiring donkeys,
awaiting the monk’s arrival.
You must come early tomorrow morning.
Just eat porridge and come early.
Before zāi shí (mealtime),
arrive there for an empty meal.”
Having spoken, he departed.
A short while later,
Yāyá (chief of staff) dispatched Zhōusī Yáguān (provincial magistrate) Lǐ Shùn, who came running with a memorial.
The memorial stated,
“Have those nine ships departed?
Go specifically to that island
to determine the truth,
and send someone to report back day and night.”
Zǐxún Zhāng Liàng,
based on what the ship-watching envoy said,
then made a report stating that the ships had already departed,
and none were seen.
He dispatched someone to report this to the Yāyá’s office.
On the seventh day, at mǎo shí (5-7 AM),
Zǐxúnjūn zhōng Zhāng Liàng and another person
hired a laborer to carry their personal belongings,
and took the monks and others to depart.
The sky was dark with clouds.
They traveled through the mountains,
crossing two layers of rocky mountains,
and traversing a salt-collection area.
The mud was deep and the road long.
At sì shí (9-11 AM),
they arrived at the residence of the xiànjiā dōushǐ (county prefect) for a meal.
After the meal,
they rode one donkey,
while attendants and others all walked.
A short while later, a person from the army came to greet them and said,
“The Yāyá (chief of staff) is concerned that the monks and others are late,
so he specifically sent someone to urge you to come.”
At wèi shí (1-3 PM),
they arrived at Xīngguó Sì (Xingguo Temple).
The temple staff said,
“The Yāyá (chief of staff) is here.
You must not be late.
Depart immediately.”
The temple master brewed tea.
They then hired three donkeys
and rode them away.
One donkey traveled 20 lǐ (miles),
costing 50 wén.
Three donkeys totaled 150 wén.
After traveling 20 lǐ (miles),
they arrived at Xīnjìng Sì (Xinjing Temple).
This was a nunnery.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) was here.
They immediately entered the temple to meet him.
They fully explained the circumstances.
The Yāyá’s (chief of staff) official title and name were:

Hǎizhōu Yāyá (Chief of Staff of Haizhou)兼 Zuǒ Èr Jiāng Shí Jiāng Sì Xiàn Dōuyóuyì Shǐ (concurrently General of the Left Second Division, Commander of the Ten Divisions, and Inspector-General of Four Counties),
gōudàng Fānkè Cháoyìláng Shì Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi Zhāng Shí (Manager of Foreign Guests, Chao Yilang, Provisional Left Jinwu Guard, Zhāng Shí).
After drinking tea,
they then went towards the county office.
They hired one more donkey.
From the nunnery to the county was 20 lǐ (miles).
In the evening, they arrived at the county.
They stayed at the house of Yāsī Lùshì Wáng Àn (Secretary Wang An of the Censorate).
The donkey fare was 20 wén.
One person traveling 100 lǐ (miles) cost 120 wén.
On the eighth day, in the early morning,
after eating porridge,
the Yāyá (chief of staff) entered the county office.
A short while later, he returned.
Xiànlìng Tōngzhíláng Shǒulì Lǐ Yífǔ (County Magistrate Li Yifu, Tongzhilang, acting Magistrate),
Xiàn Bìng Dēngshìláng Qián Shì Tàicháng Sì Fènglǐláng Shè Bìng Cuī Jūn Yuán (County Official Cuī Jūn Yuán, Dengshilang, former provisional Tai Chang Si Fengli Lang),
Zhǔbù Jiāngshìláng Shǒuzhǔbù Lǐ Dēng (Registrar Li Deng, Jiangshilang, acting Registrar),
Xiànwèi Wénlínláng Wèi Huā Dá (County Commandant Hua Da, Wenlinlang, Commandant),
Bǔzéiguān Wénlínláng Wèi Lù Liáo (Police Chief Lu Liao, Wenlinlang, Commandant) and others accompanied him.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) came to see them
and conversed with the monks and others.
The host and the county magistrate and others
offered wine and food. After eating, they returned.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) and the monks and others,
after the meal, left Secretary Wáng’s residence
and went towards the mooring place.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) and eight army personnel
arranged a small boat,
and steered it to depart together.
Xiànlìng Lǐ Yífǔ (County Magistrate Li Yifu)
sent two dòu (bushels) of new flour with Yāyá Zhāng (Chief of Staff Zhang) to offer to the Zhōucìshǐ (Prefect of the Prefecture).
The second ship
was in a small sea ahead.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) said,
“This county is on the east bank.
The prefecture is on the west bank.
Liáng Pànguān (Judge Liang) came to board the ship due to illness.
From this small sea, on the west bank, there is a Hǎilóngwáng Miào (Dragon King Temple).
Liáng Pànguān (Judge Liang) is currently residing in this temple.
Now I intend to go to Liáng Pànguān’s (Judge Liang) place,
to see him.”
They hoisted the sail and went straight.
They passed directly by the ship.
The monks and others wanted to board the ship for a while,
but the Yāyá (chief of staff) refused.
At wèi shí (1-3 PM),
they arrived at the Hǎilóngwáng Miào (Dragon King Temple).
They met Liáng Cén Pànguān (Judge Liang Cen),
Sù Lùshì (Secretary Su),
Jì Tōngshì (Interpreter Ji),
Shén Cānjūn (Staff Officer Shen), and others.
They fully explained the reasons for being left behind
and also spoke of their hardships.
The Pànguān (Judge) and others, hearing this,
were either sad
or happy.
Here, Hē Lùshì (Secretary He)
was ill on the ship.
Fǎxiàng (Master Faxiang) asked for further instruction from Jiè Míng Fǎshī (Master Jieming),
and also the Sīnxīluó Yìyǔ Dàoxuán (Silla translator Daoxuan) and others,
who were all on the ship.
They were able to meet briefly.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) said,
“The three monks will enter the prefecture
to briefly see the Dàfū (official).
Then it will be appropriate.”
The three monks accompanied
the Yāyá (chief of staff) to enter the prefecture.
They went west from the temple for about three lǐ (miles).
They arrived in front of the prefecture gate.
The Yāyá (chief of staff) and the generals and others
entered first to report.
A short while later, the monks and others were called,
and entered before the Cìshǐ (Prefect).
Chairs were placed for them to sit.
He asked the reason for being abandoned.
He ordered the Yāyá (chief of staff) to report.
The Cìshǐ’s (Prefect) surname was Yán, and given name was Cuò.
He had a rough understanding of Buddhism.
He spoke to the monks himself.
After the conversation,
they returned to the temple.
Cìshǐ Yán Dàfū (Prefect Yan)
dispatched an army general
to escort the three monks and their attendants
to temporarily stay at the Hǎilóngwáng Miào (Dragon King Temple).
From Dōnghǎi Shān Sùchéng Cūn (Sucheng Village in Donghai Mountain)
to Dōnghǎi Xiàn (Donghai County),
it was over 100 lǐ (miles).
The entire journey was mountainous.
They either rode or walked.
They arrived in one day.
Starting from the sixth day,
the northeast wind blew.
It had not changed for several days.
I feared that those nine ships,
after encountering thunderstorms and strong winds, might not have been able to cross the sea.
Anxious and distressed,
the monks, seeking Buddhist dharma,
made plans several times,
but could not fulfill this intention.
When it was time to return to their country,
they painstakingly devised plans to stay, but the search also could not be fulfilled.
All on the left and right discussed it,
but they could not stay.
The government strictly inspected,
and not even one could escape.
Therefore, they planned to return to their home country on the second ship.
Previously, in Yángzhōu and Chǔzhōu,
they had found dharma teachings and various supplies,
which were left on the eighth ship.
When leaving behind the personal belongings they carried,
Hú Hóngdǎo (Hu Hongdao) and the others, upon arriving at the prefecture,
gave everything to others.
They sailed empty-handed,
only increasing their sighs.
All this was because their search for dharma was unfulfilled.
On the ninth day,
the wind was still from the northeast.
In the evening, the wind shifted to the west.
The tenth day.
Also set out westward.
At *wèi* (申) hour.
Ryōshin hangan
came out of the temple and boarded the ship.
Monks and others followed,
boarding the ship to visit the Dharma Master Kaimei and Ācārya Dōgen, etc.
Soku-rokuji
and Ki-tsūji
had urgent business,
so they had not yet boarded the ship.
The eleventh day.
At *mao* (卯) hour, Soku-rokuji and others
set sail and departed.
They hoisted the sail and proceeded straight.
A southwest wind blew.
They intended to reach west of Hǎixiàn,
but were driven by the wind,
running directly onto a shallow sandbar.
They lowered the sail and rowed with oars.
They managed to move to a shallower spot.
They dropped anchors and used poles to push.
They toiled all day,
barely reaching the county.
The tide receded, leaving the ship stuck in the mud,
unable to move.
They stopped for the night.
Someone on the ship said,
"Today, from Sùchéngcūn,
a report came stating
that among the nine ships of our country,
the third ship
drifted to Dàzhūshān in Mìzhōu."
At *shen* (申) hour,
the Yashō and the Xiànlìng, two persons,
came to Sùchéngcūn
to seek their original high priest,
then returned to the ship.
"However, one ship
drifted to the border of Láizhōu,
letting it drift to Dàzhūshān in Mìzhōu.
The other eight ships
were lost at sea,
their whereabouts unknown."
At *hai* (亥) hour,
they tried to pull the anchor to depart,
but the ship could not float away.
The twelfth day, at dawn.
The wind was unstable, blowing east and west.
The ship had not yet floated away.
Again, a report came from the county
to Ryōshin hangan and others, stating,
"The third ship among the tribute ships
drifted to the border of this county."
"Those who departed earlier
have not yet seen a clear report."
The wind was changing and unstable.
The thirteenth day, early morning.
The tide rose, and they planned to depart.
However, due to the unstable wind,
they faced many difficulties in advancing or retreating.
After noon, the wind rose,
shifting from southwest to west.
At *wèi* (申) hour,
the tide rose.
The ship floated by itself, moving eastward.
They hoisted the sail and set off.
From in front of Dōnghǎixiàn,
they headed eastward.
They boarded a small boat for a purification ritual
and also paid respects to the Sumiyoshi Ōkami.
Only then did they cross the sea.
The wind blew rather fiercely.
Not long after entering the sea,
one sailor,
who had been sick,
died at the end of the *shen* (申) hour.
He was wrapped in a mat
and thrown into the sea,
drifting away with the waves.
The sea color was somewhat clear.
At night, the wind was fierce.
They sailed straight on.
The fourteenth day, at dawn.
The sea was again murky white.
The wind direction did not change.
They looked in all directions,
but no mountains or islands were visible.
By noon, the wind stopped.
The sea color was light green.
At *wèi* (申) hour,
a south wind blew.
They tacked the sail towards *chǒu* (丑).
At *xu* (戌) hour,
as they had a favorable wind,
they offered the five grains according to the Guàndǐng Jīng,
sacrificed to the Five Directional Dragon Kings,
and recited sutras and dhāraṇīs.
The wind shifted to southwest.
At midnight,
the wind shifted to due west.
They adjusted the helm with the wind.
The fifteenth day.
At dawn.
The seawater was dark blue.
The wind rose from due west.
They sailed towards the sunrise.
At *si* (巳) hour, the wind stopped.
At *wèi* (申) hour,
a southeast wind blew.
They tacked the sail northward.
One sailor
died of illness and suffering.
He was dropped into the sea.
At *shen* (申) hour,
they ordered the Divination Department to divine the wind.
It was not very favorable.
However, the divination for the path ahead
said that although it was the Sīnlúo border,
there should be no alarm or strangeness.
The officials on the ship,
to stop the headwind,
jointly made vows
and prayed for a favorable wind.
They saw the sunset directly amidst the large oars at the stern.
As night fell, they offered the five grains,
recited the Bōrě Guàndǐng and other sutras,
prayed to the gods and bowed to the Buddha,
begging for a favorable wind.
At *zi* (子) hour,
the wind shifted to southwest.
Soon it changed to due west.
They saw the moon setting
behind the stern and rudder compartment.
The sixteenth day.
At dawn.
There were clouds, fog, and rain.
Nothing was visible in all directions.
There was disagreement about the wind.
Some said it was a west wind,
some said it was a southwest wind,
and some said it was a south wind.
They saw the morning sun
at the small oar's armpit-door at the stern.
They then knew they were heading northeast.
They tacked the sail and proceeded.
Some wondered if it was a south wind.
Although the sky above was clear,
the sea in all directions
was filled with dense fog,
preventing clear visibility.
Today, the Water Steward began
to distribute water from the water storage
to the people on the ship.
From officials downwards,
each person received two *shēng* per day.
From attendants downwards
to sailors upwards,
each person received one and a half *shēng* per day.
After *wu* (午) and *wei* (申) hours,
they saw the color of the wind
was mostly from the southeast.
They sailed towards *zi* (子).
The fog cleared, revealing clouds in the sky.
Towards *gèn* (艮), *kǎn* (坎), and *kūn* (坤),
there were dense, stagnant clouds.
The *qingyi* monk was unwell and not doing well.
He did not eat rice porridge.
As night fell, there was heavy rain.
The hardship was endless.
On the seventeenth, the morning rain stopped.
The clouds and fog were thick.
It was said they did not know which way to go.
The color of the sea was light green.
The white sun was not visible.
They lost their way, confused about the directions.
Some said to go northwest.
Some said to go due north.
Some said they would see an island ahead.
After proceeding for several *kè*,
the sea waves seemed shallow.
They lowered a rope to measure it.
There were only eight *xún*.
They wanted to drop anchor and stop.
But they did not know how far they were from the land.
Someone said,
"Now that we see the sea is shallow,
it would be better to sink stones and stop temporarily.
Let us wait for the fog to clear,
then we can decide whether to advance or stop."
Everyone agreed.
They dropped anchor and moored.
They could barely see white waves breaking under the fog.
They also saw a dark object.
Then they knew it was an island.
It was still indistinct.
Soon, the fog slightly cleared.
The island's shape became clear.
Not knowing which country's territory it was,
they immediately lowered a small boat.
They dispatched two archers
and five sailors,
sending them to search for land
and ask its name.
The fog began to clear somewhat.
To the north, mountains and islands were connected.
Starting from the southeast
to the southwest,
they stretched continuously.
Some said,
"This is the southern border of the Kingdom of Xīnlúo."
They ordered a *bǔbù* to divine.
He said it was the country of Dàtáng.
Later, he said Xīnlúo.
The matter was in two parts,
and they could not determine it.
While they were in doubt,
the dispatched sailors and archers
brought two Táng people.
They immediately said it was the south side of Tángyáng Táo Village, Mùpíng County, Dēngzhōu.
It was 160 *lǐ* from the county
and 300 *lǐ* from the prefecture.
From here to the east was the Kingdom of Xīnlúo.
If they got a good wind,
they could reach it in two or three days.
The officials on the ship
were given wine and cotton.
Then a letter was written to report to the prefecture and county.
Because the sky had not cleared yet,
the mountain peaks could not be seen clearly.
An east wind blew.
At dusk, the fog grew darker.
On the eighteenth,
they changed the food ration.
Each person received one *shēng* of dried rations
and one *shēng* of water daily.
The east wind did not change.
Also, this prefecture only had millet;
its polished rice was most expensive.
They requested additional monks
to arrive at their home country early,
thereby fulfilling all the vows made in recent years.
They ordered the *bǔbù* to pray to the gods.
One fire pearl
was offered to the great god Zhùjí.
One string of crystal prayer beads
was offered to the Dragon King of the Sea.
One razor
was offered to the god of the ship
to pray for a safe return to their home country.
At dawn on the nineteenth,
the sky was clear.
A north wind blew.
They raised the anchor and headed south.
At *wèi* time, the wind stopped.
They rowed, pointing southwest.
At *shēn* time,
they arrived at Shàocūn Pǔ and dropped anchor to moor.
It was to the southwest of Táo Village.
They intended to enter the bay.
The adverse current flowed swiftly, making it impossible to proceed.
On the morning of the twentieth,
Xīnlúo people came in a small boat.
Then they heard that Zhāng Bǎoliàng
and the Xīnlúo prince
had united to punish the Kingdom of Xīnlúo, and then made its prince the Xīnlúo prince.
The south wind intensified slightly.
Due to the swift adverse tide, they could not stay put.
They swayed back and forth, east and west,
shaking violently.
On the twenty-first, there was cloud and fog.
In the afternoon, a strong south wind blew.
On the twenty-second, there was cloud and rain.
At *shēn* time,
one of the scribes died.
He was carried by boat and placed on the island.
On the twenty-third,
there was cloud and south wind.
On the twenty-fourth, there was fog and rain.
At this anchoring spot, the cables were tied.
The cables broke.
The wind blew high waves.
Recently, eight cables had been lowered.
Three of these cables and anchors had all broken off.
The remaining cables were very few.
If they encountered a storm,
they would not be able to stay moored.
Their fear was boundless.
On the twenty-fourth,
a west wind blew.
At dusk, a horseman came to the north bank.
From the ship, Xīnlúo interpreter Dàoxuán was dispatched
to welcome him.
Dàoxuán returned, saying,
"The visitor is the *pànguān* of the *yāyá*.
He heard in this county
that our country's envoy ship
had been anchored here for many days,
so he came to meet us.
Because it was night, he returned,
and we could not meet.
He will come specifically to the ship tomorrow."
They further ordered the Xīnlúo people
to remain on shore
and convey a message to Dàoxuán,
asking him to relay their circumstances to the official.
Then they heard that our country's tribute envoy,
aboard five Xīnlúo ships,
had drifted to the side of Láimíng Lúshān.
The other four ships
were nowhere to be found.
Although they heard this news,
it was unclear which ship it was.
They also heard that the Son of Heaven of Dàtáng
had bestowed the royal title upon the Xīnlúo prince.
He dispatched envoys to arrange the Xīnlúo ships,
and also bestowed emoluments.
On the twenty-fifth,
the wind blew erratically.
The fog had not cleared.
At noon,
the *pànguān* of the *yāyá* who had returned from the shore yesterday, sent a message from Wáng Jiàoyán,
presenting wine, fish, etc., to the officials.
Wáng Jiàoyán
also personally brought wine, cakes, etc.
The officials bestowed cotton, etc.
This ship had many hidden reefs.
Each time, when waves caused it to drift, cables broke.
They had sunk anchors five or six times already.
Later,
they rowed towards Rǔshān.
They exited Shàocūn Pǔ
and traveled by sea.
Before reaching halfway,
dark fog suddenly rose.
All four directions were dim.
They did not know which way the wind was blowing.
They did not know which way to go.
They dropped anchor and stopped.
Wind and waves competed,
causing severe rocking and discomfort.
It continued all night without cessation.
The 26th day.
In the early morning, the clouds and mist slightly cleared.
We saw Rǔshān.
It was close by, to the west.
The wind rose from the northeast.
We hoisted sail and proceeded.
At *sìshí* (9-11 a.m.).
We arrived at the western inlet of Rǔshān.
We moored the ship and stopped.
Mountains and islands guarded it,
like a surrounding wall.
The body of Rǔshān
had steep peaks and high summits.
Its top was like a sharp point.
The mountain base extended from below the ridge, pointing in six directions.
On the western side of the inlet,
there was also a rocky mountain.
Its craggy peaks and ridges stood side by side,
towering halfway to the sky.
To the east and north,
although there were connecting mountains,
they were merely sloping.
At *wèishí* (1-3 p.m.).
Over thirty people from Xīnluó
came on horseback and donkeys, saying:
"The *Yāyá*
plans to come and meet you when the tide recedes.
Therefore, we have come first to await and greet you."
Among them, a commoner said:
"Yesterday, I came from Lúshān
and saw nine tribute ships from our country all arrive at Lúshān.
No people or goods were lost.
Their officials and others
all landed on shore
and set up temporary shelters.
They are calmly waiting for favorable winds."
Not long after,
the *Yāyá* arrived in a Xīnluó ship.
He disembarked and went ashore.
Many women were present.
The envoy for the tribute mission, the *Pànguān*,
dispatched the Xīnluó interpreter Dàoxuán,
sending him to convey the message.
Afterwards,
Recorder Sù disembarked
and went to meet the *Yāyá*.
He also presented a document requesting provisions.
"We were previously in Dōnghǎi Xiàn.
However, the provisions for crossing the sea
on this ship, after crossing the sea,
returned due to contrary winds
and drifted here.
It is absolutely necessary not to consume the sea-crossing provisions here.
Therefore, we request fresh supplies."
The *Yāyá* took the document and said:
"I will report to the prefecture
and await instructions."
In the evening, he returned home.
The northeast wind blew all day.
The 27th day.
Overcast and rainy with a north wind.
The 28th day was clear.
The *Yāyá* came to meet the officials.
The 29th day.
The north wind blew.
We ordered the Xīnluó interpreter Dàoxuán to plan
whether staying here
would be safe and convenient.
Dàoxuán and the Xīnluó people
discussed the matter.
He then returned and said:
"Staying here
would be safe and convenient."
The 1st day of the 5th month.
We sent someone to buy provisions for crossing the sea from Wáng Xùn, the village head.
We also inquired about staying in this village.
Wáng Xùn and others said:
"If you wish to stay, I will personally handle it.
The *Héshang* (Buddhist monk) need not return to his homeland."
This did not conform to the circumstances.
We could not make up our minds.
The west wind blew all day.
The 2nd day.
The west wind blew.
We untied the ropes and left the inlet.
As the wind was very strong,
we sailed close to the reefs
and could not exit immediately.
At *yǒushí* (5-7 p.m.) the wind stopped.
We let the current carry us to the mouth of the sea and stopped there.
We sent men to draw water.
At sunset,
on board the ship,
we offered sacrifices to the heavenly deities and earth spirits.
Also, official and private silks,
brocades, mirrors, etc.,
were offered to the Sumiyoshi大神 (Great God) on board the ship.
At *chǒushí* (1-3 a.m.).
A sailor,
who had been ill for some time,
was about to die.
Before he died,
we wrapped his body
and carried him by boat to abandon him near the mountain.
The people who sent him returned and said:
"He was abandoned on the shore.
The sick person was not yet dead.
He begged for food and water, saying:
'If my illness recovers,
I will seek out a village to go to.'"
All the people on the ship
were filled with sorrow.
The 3rd day.
The wind blew without change.
From the southwest sea mouth of Rǔshān,
we hoisted sail and set off.
The windy path was somewhat calm.
At noon, the wind stopped.
Soon after, an east wind blew.
We turned the sails and returned.
We arrived at the anchorage of Rǔshān and stayed there for the night.
The 4th day.
At *chénshí* (7-9 a.m.), we sailed about four or five *lǐ* southwest from the anchorage.
We moored at the northern side of Sāng Dǎo, in the eastern inlet of Wànghǎi Cūn.
The 5th day, we disembarked and went ashore.
We celebrated the Fifth Month Festival.
We also bathed and washed clothes.
In the evening, a document was brought from the ship.
The document stated:
"Favorable winds are hard to come by,
and our crossing has not been smooth.
The head *Pànguān* and the assembly have decided
that the entire ship should observe a fast.
Starting tomorrow,
for three days, we respectfully invite the various *Héshang*
to chant sūtras and recite the Buddha's name,
praying for favorable winds.
We hope you will graciously grant your presence for this observance."
As it was already night, we did not immediately go.
We stayed on land for the night.
The 6th day.
In the early morning, we went to the ship.
We observed the fast on the ship.
The Xīnluó interpreter Dàoxuán
went to the *Yāyá*'s residence.
After the fast,
we again went ashore.
We set up tents and arranged the ritual preparations.
In the evening, we sacrificed to the Dragon Kings of the Five Directions.
Master Jièmíng
was in charge of this matter.
The 7th day, it rained.
The 9th day, the sūtra chanting in the early morning concluded.
The 11th day.
We sacrificed to the heavenly deities and earth spirits of Dà Táng.
From this day until the 13th day,
the weather was either cloudy or clear.
The wind blew erratically.
The 14th day.
The prefectural *Yāyá* came to the ship and inquired about the number of people on board.
He then returned to the village.
Wáng Xùn and others, the village heads of Shào Cūn, came to meet us.
We then heard that the nine ships of our country's *Xiànggōng* and others
had previously crossed the sea from Lúshān,
encountered contrary winds,
and drifted back to Lúshān.
Since our arrival at the anchorage,
at night there was thunder and heavy rain.
The morning of the 15th day.
The clouds were turbulent,
and the rain became heavier.
The prefectural *Yāyá* came to the ship
and asked for the number of people on board.
The officials recorded the number
and reported it to the prefecture.
In the evening, the *Yāyá* returned.
The tribute envoy awarded him silk floss and other items.
The 16th day was dark.
The *Yāyá*'s envoy came
and requested the tribute envoy's report to the county.
He asked the *Yìsēng* (monk from a foreign country) to write a statement requesting to stay.
He entrusted it to the merchant Sūn Qīng
to deliver to Ambassador Lín's residence.
The officials on the ship
dispatched two archers
and two sailors
to go with the prefectural *Yāyá* to request provisions.
The *Yāyá* stated that there were no local products to present to the prefecture or county
and therefore did not go.
The aforementioned people
returned from land.
The 17th and 18th days.
The wind was either strong
or weak.
People's opinions varied.
The 19th day.
That night, it was between the hour of Bǐ and the hour of Chǒu.
Thunder roared and lightning flashed.
Torrential rain and violent winds
were insurmountable.
All the bow and stern cables snapped.
The ship immediately drifted out.
Startled, we dropped anchor,
and it quickly stopped.
The stern's divine shrine,
its roofing planks,
were blown away by the great wind,
their whereabouts unknown.
Everyone trembled in fear,
unable to control themselves.
The 20th day.
A west wind blew.
We planned to cross the sea.
Canvas sails were laid out.
People were ferried to shore.
At noon,
the wind shifted to the southwest.
We calculated we couldn't leave the anchorage,
so we didn't set off.
As night fell, the thunderstorms worsened.
The 21st day.
At the hour of Sì, a west wind blew.
We untied the cables and set forth.
The wind died down and wouldn't blow.
We temporarily stopped to wait for wind.
A gentle south wind blew,
but not strong enough to hoist the sails.
We returned to anchor and tied the cables. On board, Bǔbù
had been sick for a long time.
In the evening, he disembarked.
The 22nd day.
In the morning, we heard that Bǔbù had died on shore.
All day, a dark rain and east wind blew.
The 23rd day.
The cloudy sky cleared slightly.
As night fell, wind and rain became fiercely competitive.
The 24th day.
A strong west wind blew.
The rainy weather hadn't cleared.
We still didn't set off.
In the evening, the officials discussed.
The wind direction hadn't changed all day, so we would depart tomorrow morning.
The 25th day.
In the morning, we untied the cables.
The wind died down, and we couldn't proceed.
At the hour of Shēn,
a Sīnlüo ship with a white sail
passed out of the sea mouth.
Not long after,
it turned around and came back in.
Towards evening, it drifted towards Rǔshān to anchor.
Everyone was suspicious.
"If it's a tribute envoy,
did it come from Lúshān?"
We dispatched a fast boat to inquire.
The Sīnlüo ship sped away.
Due to the night, our boat returned without news.
The 26th day.
We planned to depart.
The wind was even more unfavorable.
In the evening,
in both the northwest
and west, lightning flashed brightly.
The clouds turned dark and turbulent.
As night fell, the ship suddenly shook and drifted.
The alarm and strangeness were boundless.
At the hour of Xū,
on the northwest shore where we were anchored,
a fox cried out, its sound echoing far
and not ceasing for a long time.
Not long after,
thunder and lightning clashed and roared.
Hearing it, our ears were deafened.
The flashes of lightning
were unbearable to look at.
The heavy rain poured like a deluge.
It greatly frightened and distressed everyone on the ship.
They couldn't move in or out.
The 27th day.
At dawn,
a lightning bolt struck,
splitting and breaking the mast towards the bow, skewing and breaking it.
The part that broke off
was more than four *cun* thick,
about six *cun* wide,
and over three *zhàng* long.
Five pieces were broken off from the outside.
Some were four *xún*,
some five *chǐ* or less.
The pieces were scattered everywhere.
We collected them in one place,
tying them to the ship's corner.
We also vowed that on the day we returned to our home country,
we would specifically build a shrine
for perpetual offerings.
We burned turtle shells to divine the cause of the calamity.
The Bǔbù gentlemen on the ship were buried before the local deity.
This calamity was caused by the deity's anger.
If we could resolve it,
we would be safe.
So, we performed an exorcism at Sāngdǎo.
Also, on the ship,
we made offerings to the local deity.
As for the broken mast,
some said, "Since it's broken and weakened,
we should make a replacement."
Others said, "The material for a mast
is hard to come by suddenly here.
If we make a replacement,
we won't be able to cross the sea this year.
We must instead bind and wrap the broken part,
so we can depart early."
Everyone agreed with the latter statement,
and decided to proceed.
A northwest wind arose,
causing the ship to move slightly.
The wind blew and then stopped.
People's minds were conflicted.
There was no unity above and below.
A gentle mountain wind blew.
We untied the cables and forced a departure.
There was no favorable wind.
We temporarily proceeded and then dropped anchor.
As night fell, a gentle mountain wind blew.
We hoisted the sails and slowly proceeded.
Just at the island mouth, the wind died, and we couldn't proceed.
We dropped anchor and tied the ship.
The 28th day.
At the hour of Chén, clouds and mist were dark.
Shíshén rumbled.
We raised anchor and returned.
The rain made it difficult.
We rowed into the small sea southeast of Sāngdǎo.
There was an island there, where we anchored the ship.
The 30th day, the sky cleared.
A northwest wind arose,
shifting restlessly.
From earlier until today,
the matter of staying in this village was reported and requested.
The officials did not permit it.
Today, we requested again, but it was not granted.
The 1st day of the 6th month.
The sky cleared slightly.
Regarding the matter of staying.
We temporarily requested a pleasure boat.
It was not refused.
We disembarked.
The 2nd day, the sky cleared.
Although there was no favorable wind,
everyone desperately wanted to return home.
We dropped anchor and forcefully proceeded.
All day, we struggled to get out.
Towards evening, as we hoisted the sail and turned the ship,
it suddenly drifted away.
Coming upon a reef, we dropped anchor with all our might.
We barely managed to get back to safety.
The 3rd day.
A gentle west wind blew,
sometimes blowing, sometimes not.
We hoisted sails and lowered sails
three or four times.
Sometimes with sails, sometimes with oars,
we steered towards Chìshān in the distance.
From Shàocūnpǔ,
we rode the tide.
As we reached the mouth of the bay, the tide ran sideways.
The ship suddenly hit a reef.
We dropped poles and spread sails,
but couldn't control it.
There were submerged rocks below.
We collided with them.
The shore reef and submerged rocks clashed and struck.
The ship was about to break apart.
Everyone combined their strength to push with poles,
dropping anchor, and together we managed to pull it out.
We drifted out with the current
and stayed in the middle of the sea.
Towards dusk, a strong wind and torrential rain.
Thunder and lightning
were unbearable to see or hear.
Everyone on the ship,
waving spears, shouting with great swords, screamed "Chuān!"
to ward off the lightning.
The 4th day, in the morning, we hoisted sails and proceeded.
We traveled a short distance, then the wind died.
We dropped anchor and secured the ship.
On the fifth day, at dawn.
We hoisted sail and proceeded.
In the afternoon, we arrived at the west side of Chìshān.
As the tide was against us, we temporarily stopped.
After a short while, we set off again.
Gradually entering the south side of the mountain, a gathering of clouds suddenly appeared.
A headwind blew fiercely.
The hoisted sail immediately changed.
Just as we were lowering the sail,
a black bird flew over.
It circled the ship three times,
then returned to perch on the island.
Everyone was surprised and amazed.
They all said it was a divine spirit
forbidding us from entering the anchorage.
We turned the ship around and sailed out.
Going a little further from the mountain,
we anchored in the middle of the sea.
To the north, there was thunder,
with lightning flashing through the clouds.
The officials on board the ship were extremely frightened,
still suspecting it was a sign of disharmony with the underworld gods.
Together, they made vows
and performed a ritual for averting disaster.
They prayed and made offerings to the Pīlìshén on the ship, and also sacrificed to the Sumiyoshi Dàshén on the ship.
They also made offerings for the Hachiman and other great gods of our own country,
as well as the sea dragon kings,
and the gods of various mountains and islands in Dēngzhōu.
Each made their vows.
The thunder gradually stopped.
The wind shifted east and west.
We cast anchor and remained there.
This ship had been away from land for a long time,
unable to cross the sea,
nor could it enter a harbor.
After many days and nights,
drifting in the sea,
unable to withstand the rocking,
our hearts and bodies were exhausted.
On the sixth day, a strong wind blew fiercely.
We intended to enter the Chìshān anchorage.
The wind became favorable.
So we raised the anchor stone
and arranged the sailcloth. The wind stopped and the waves became violent.
We cast the anchor stone again.
We could not determine if we could enter.
The wind and waves were erratic,
and the journey was not as we wished.
The hardship was extreme;
nothing could surpass this.
On the seventh day,
at noon, a strong wind blew.
We hoisted sail and proceeded.
Between Wèi (1-3 pm) and Shēn (3-5 pm),
we arrived at the east side of Chìshān and moored the ship.
The strong wind was fierce.
That Chìshān was purely a place of towering, rugged rocks.
It was the Chìshāncūn of Qīngníng Xiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn.
Inside the mountain was a temple
called Chìshān Fǎhuāyuàn.
It was originally built by Zhāng Bǎogāo.
It had extensive manor lands to provide rice porridge.
From these manor lands, five hundred *shí* of rice were obtained annually.
Lectures were given in winter and summer.
In winter, the *Fǎhuā Jīng* was lectured.
In summer, the eight-volume *Jīn Guāngmíng Jīng* was lectured.
These were lectured year-round.
To the north and south were rocky peaks.
Water flowed through the temple courtyard,
from west to east.
To the east, the sea stretched far and wide.
To the south, west, and north,
connected peaks formed a wall,
only the southwest corner sloped downwards.
Currently, the Sīllá *tōngshì yāgōng* Zhāng Yǒng,
and Lín Tàishǐ Wáng Xùn, etc., were solely in charge.
On the eighth day,
towards evening,
Yì Fǎshī,
along with Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo, etc., ascended to the temple.
They happened to meet the temple residents.
There were over thirty monks.
They conversed and drank tea.
That night, they lodged in a quiet room.
On the ninth day,
before the meal, Fǎxiàng, Yì Jièmíng Fǎshī,
and their accompanying monks
came to visit.
They all had a meal together in the refectory.
After the meal, Sùtián Lùshì,
and Sīllá *tōngshì* Dàoxuán, etc.,
came up together.
They also stayed one night.
On the tenth day, after the meal, Sù Lùshì
returned to the ship.
Seven monks from our country
remained in the mountain temple.
For more than seven days, a fierce southwest wind blew
without a moment's rest.
On the twenty-second day,
there was a great wind and violent rain,
which did not stop all night.
On the twenty-third day,
early in the morning, inspecting the mountain temple,
trees were uprooted and branches broken,
rocks collapsed and stone walls fell. From the ship's anchorage,
sailors ran up saying,
“The ship has struck a rough reef
and is completely damaged.
A pair of small boats
are also all broken apart.”
Hearing this, the surprise was immeasurable.
A special envoy was immediately dispatched
to the ship's anchorage
to ascertain the truth.
The ship had been blown by the strong wind
and had struck a rough reef.
The rudder board was broken off.
The pair of small boats
were both shattered.
The ship struck the reef three or four times.
Huge waves were like mountains.
The cables and anchor could not hold.
It drifted out with the waves.
From the west bank, it reached the east bank, as the wind blew ever more fiercely.
The pitching and rolling became even more severe.
A heavy anchor was cast.
As soon as the anchor and cable sank,
it was secured close to the shore.
Everyone on the ship
was disoriented and could not eat,
as if half-dead.
Two days later,
they returned to the old anchorage.
The small boats were patched up.
On the twenty-sixth day,
they split up to retrieve anchors
and search for timber for the rudder.
Since the beginning of the fourth month,
clouds and mist had obscured everything,
and the wind and rain had not stopped.
One or two days of clear weather,
then clouds would obscure again.
On the twenty-seventh day,
it was heard that Zhāng Dàshǐ
had two relief ships
arrive at Rìshānpǔ.
On the twenty-eighth day,
the Dàtáng emperor
dispatched an envoy to Sīllá to offer condolences to the newly enthroned king.
Qīngzhōu Bīngmǎshǐ Wú Zǐchén,
Vice Envoy Cuī,
Judge Wáng, etc.,
over thirty people, came up.
They met in the temple.
That night, Zhāng Shígāo sent the Dàtáng trade envoy Cuī Bīngmǎsī
to
the temple to offer condolences.
On the twenty-ninth day,
at dawn,
together with Dàoxuán Jiālī,
they entered the guest room
to discuss the matter of staying.
Then they returned to the ship.
Southeast of Chìshānpǔ,
crossing a small stretch of sea, there was an island
connected to the east bank.
This was where Wú Gànjiàng forged swords.
People at that time called it Mòyé Dǎo.
Mòyé was the name of the island,
while Gànjiàng was the name of the blacksmith.
On the tenth
and eleventh of July,
there was no wind in the sea,
but the waves surged violently,
boiling from the bottom.
The sound of the waves was like thunder.
The ships swayed and vibrated.
The astonishment was considerable.
On the fourteenth day,
at chénshi (7-9 am), they took leave of the mountain temple
and arrived at the ship's anchorage.
On the shore,
they bid farewell to Jièmíng Fǎshī, Sù Lùshì, and Hé Lùshì.
They went to Tiānményuàn in Zhēnzhuāngcūn
to visit Fǎkōng Jiālī.
This master had once visited our country,
and had returned twenty years ago.
That night, they lodged in his temple.
On the fifteenth day,
they had a meal at the mountain temple,
then ate newly harvested millet rice.
On the sixteenth day, morning court.
Descending from Chìshān Yuàn.
On the way, heard people say
that the tribute ships had departed yesterday.
Arrived at the anchorage.
Sought the ships but did not see them.
Temporarily stayed on the shore.
The monks of Chìshān Yuàn
all came to comfort and inquire.
We all went up to Chìshān Yuàn to eat.
Then saw four provincial envoys
who had arrived at the temple earlier,
transporting seventy dàn of rice, provisions for the Japanese tribute envoys.
Now, in this village,
because the tribute envoys had already departed,
they could not be received.
So they reported to the county office.
The old and young in the temple
were deeply surprised at being left behind.
Their comfort and inquiries were earnest.
On the twenty-first day,
at shēn hour (3-5 PM),
nine ships, including the minister (xiànggōng) from our country, arrived.
They anchored in this Chìshān Pǔ.
I immediately sent Wéizhèng
to pay respects to the minister
and inquire with the various judicial officers (pànguān), scribes (lùshì), etc.
The minister dispatched Sùtián Jiājì (粟田家繼), the Provisional Professor (Quán Bóshì) from Ōmi (近江),
and Zhàngbù Zhēnmíng (丈部貞名), the Sakon'e no Jō (左近衛丈部) of the Yate (射手) clan, etc.,
to comfort the monk seeking the Dharma and ask about his welfare.
They also ordered him to inquire about the incident where the second ship encountered danger.
On the twenty-second day,
did not depart.
On the twenty-third day,
in the early morning,
from the mountaintop, looked at the anchorage.
The nine ships were nowhere to be seen.
Then knew they had all departed during the night.
The northwest wind blew.
About a hundred *lǐ* across the sea northeast of Chìshān,
a mountain was faintly visible.
It was called Qīngshān.
Three peaks were connected.
From afar, it was not clearly distinct.
This was the place where Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) built a bridge over the sea.
Shǐhuáng also, from this mountain,
looked east and saw Pénglái Shān (蓬萊山),
Yíng Shān (瀛山),
and Hú Shān (胡山).
Then he died here.
At that time, his hemp sandals are still said to be present.
I heard the old people say this,
and thus I knew it.
The three monks, intending to go to Tiāntái (天台),
forgot their desire to return home.
They remained in Chìshān Yuàn.
Every time they asked about travel arrangements,
the road south was extremely distant.
They heard that pilgrimage to the north
included Wǔtái Shān (五臺山),
about two thousand *lǐ* from here.
South was far, north was near.
Also heard there was a Tiāntái宗 (Tiāntái zōng) monk
whose Dharma name was Zhìyuǎn (志遠).
He was a disciple of Wénjiàn (文鑒) *zuòzhǔ* and Tiāntái Xuánsù (天台玄素) *zuòzhǔ*.
He is now on Wǔtái Shān,
cultivating the Fǎhuā Sānmèi (法花三昧).
The Tiāntái teachings are transmitted at the North Terrace (Běi Tái) in Sònggǔ Lánruò (宋谷蘭若).
Previously, a monk cultivating Fǎhuā Sānmèi attained enlightenment there.
In recent times, there was Master Jìn (進 Chánshī),
a monk from Lóngxīng Sì (龍興寺) in Chǔzhōu (楚州).
He carried one thousand volumes of the *Nièpán Jīng* (涅槃經)
to Master Zhìyuǎn (志遠 Chánshī) on Tái Shān,
received the Fǎhuā Sānmèi,
entered the *dàochǎng* to seek Pǔxián (普賢),
and walked the path in the temple.
He attained sight of the Great Sage.
This was twenty years ago.
Recorded according to the oral account of the Sīllá (新羅) monk, Master Shènglín (聖林 Héshang).
This monk entered Wǔtái and Cháng'ān (長安),
traveling for twenty years.
While conversing at this mountain temple,
I often heard that the sacred sites of Tái Shān were remarkably wondrous.
I was deeply pleased that the sacred realm was near, temporarily setting aside the idea of going to Tiāntái.
Instead, I conceived the idea of entering Wǔtái.
Thus, I changed my initial plan and intended to spend the winter at the mountain temple, then in spring, travel and pilgrimage to Tái Shān.
On the twenty-eighth day,
at shēn hour,
the county envoys Dòu Wénzhì (竇文至) and another person
brought a county dispatch (xiàn tiē).
Its content stated:
County Dispatch: Qīngníng Xiāng (青寧鄉)
received a report from *bǎntóu* Dòu Wénzhì, stating:
"Three persons from the Japanese ship were abandoned."
In response, having examined the report from the aforementioned *bǎntóu*,
the ship departed on the fifteenth of this month.
Three persons were abandoned
and are currently in the Sīllá temple (Sīllá Sì Yuàn) on Chìshān.
The report is as previously stated.
According to the examination of the aforementioned persons,
since they were abandoned from the ship,
the village *bǎo* *bǎntóu* should have reported it on the same day.
How is it that fifteen days have passed
and only now is it reported?
Furthermore, the names of the abandoned persons are not seen, nor what luggage or clothing they possess.
Also, investigate the *gāngwéi* and *zhīshì* monks of Chìshān Sìyuàn.
If there are foreigners present,
why were they not reported at all?
It is necessary to dispatch a veteran (zhuānlǎorén) of the *xiāng*
to investigate the matter.
The deadline is the day the dispatch arrives.
A detailed report must be submitted.
If any discrepancy is found in the investigation,
or if there is any false refusal or concealment,
they will be pursued and held accountable.
If the deadline is missed, or if the investigation is not thorough, the original investigator
will certainly be severely punished.
Kāichéng (開成) 4th year, 7th month, 24th day. Commander Wáng Zuǒ's (王佐) Dispatch.
Master of Records (Zhǔbù) and Vice-Protector (Fùwèi) Hú Jūnzhí (胡君直).
Acting Magistrate (Shè Lìng) Qī Xuānyuán (戚宣員).
The Dharma-seeking monks and others immediately drafted a report stating the reason for their retention.
The report is as follows:
"One Japanese monk,
with two junior disciples (xiǎoshī),
and one *xíngzhě* (practitioner),
remained in the mountain temple."
"Reason: The aforementioned monks
traveled across the sea from afar to seek Buddhist Dharma.
Although they reached Táng (唐) territory,
their cherished wish has not yet been fulfilled.
Their original intention in leaving their homeland
was to pilgrimage the sacred country,
seek teachers, and learn the Dharma.
Because the tribute envoys returned early,
they could not accompany them back to their country.
Therefore, they reside in this mountain temple.
Afterwards, they intend to pilgrimage famous mountains
and seek the Way for cultivation.
As for their personal belongings,
there is one iron bowl (tiěbō),
two bronze cymbals (tóngnáo),
one bronze vase (tóngpíng),
more than twenty scrolls of documents,
and winter clothing, etc.
There are no other items.
Now, having been inquired about by the county office,
the details are as stated above."
This report is submitted as follows:
Sincerely reported.
Kāichéng 4th year, 7th month, 20th day.
Report of the Japanese monk Yuánrén (圓仁).
Disciples: Wéizhèng (惟正),
Wéixiǎo (惟曉).
Practitioner: Dīng Xióngwàn (丁雄萬). Submitted the dispatch.
Report from Chìshān Yuàn of Qīngníng Xiāng, submitted for investigation regarding the Japanese monks who did not return on the ship.
The Japanese monk Yuánrén,
junior disciples Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
and the *xíngzhě*,
a total of four people,
stated verbally:
"Having heard from afar that the flourishing spread of Buddhism is revered,
we therefore came to study the sacred teachings, intending to seek out famous mountains and sacred sites,
and pilgrimage to various places.

The ritual for lecturing scriptures at Chìshān Yuàn:
At *chén* hour,
the lecture bell was struck.
The bell for gathering the assembly was struck.
After the bells ceased,
and after a good while,
the great assembly ascended to the hall.
As the *dìngzhòng* bell rang, the lecturer ascended the hall.
While ascending the high seat,
the great assembly, in unison,
praised the Buddha's name.
The melody entirely followed Sīnlúo
and was not like Táng melody.
After the lecturer ascended the seat,
the chanting of the Buddha's name stopped.
At that time, a junior monk chanted a Sanskrit verse,
entirely following Táng style.
Immediately, he recited the verse "Why in this scripture..." and so on.
Up to "I pray to the Buddha to reveal the subtle and secret phrases,"
the great assembly chanted in unison, "Incense of precepts, incense of *samādhi*, incense of liberation..." and so on.
After chanting the Sanskrit hymn,
the lecturer chanted
the scripture's title.
Then, he began to explain the title,
dividing it into three aspects.
After explaining the title,
the *wéinà* master came out
in front of the high seat,
presenting the reasons for the assembly and the names of the individual benefactors.
After presenting the donated items,
he then passed the petition
to the lecturer.
The lecturer held the fly whisk
and individually recited the names of the benefactors,
making a solitary vow.
After the vow,
the debaters initiated the debate by posing questions.
When questions were posed,
the lecturer raised the fly whisk
upon hearing the debater's words.
After the question was posed,
he then lowered the fly whisk
and immediately raised it again
to acknowledge the question before answering.
The questions and answers were presented in written form.
This was similar to our country.
However, the debate
ritual was slightly different.
After tilting the hand three times,
before presenting the explanation,
one would suddenly point and present the debate.
The sound was like a person in great anger, shouting with full voice to dispute.
The lecturer's role in the debate
was only to answer, not to argue back.
After the debate,
they proceeded to discuss the text of the scripture.
After the lecture,
the great assembly, in unison, praised with a prolonged chant.
Within the words of praise,
there were verses of transference of merit.
As the lecturer descended the seat,
one monk chanted the verse "The world is like empty space...",
the sound and momentum of which were quite similar to our country.
The lecturer ascended the prostration mat.
One monk chanted "Three prostrations finished."
The lecturer and the great assembly, in unison,
exited the hall and returned to their rooms.
There was also a "review lecturer,"
positioned south of the high seat.
Upon descending from his seat, he would discuss the text lectured by the principal lecturer yesterday,
up to the sentence that required explaining the meaning.
The principal lecturer would then refer to the text to explain its meaning.
The review lecturer would also read.
After reading all the text lectured yesterday,
the principal lecturer would then read the next passage.
It was like this every day.
Sīnluó one-day lecture ritual. At Chénshí, the bell is struck.
The prolonged striking is finished.
The lecturer (Jiǎngshī) and the supervising lecturer (Dūjiǎng), two people, enter the hall.
The assembly enters first and sits in rows.
The lecturer reads the assembly for the master’s entry into the hall.
The assembly, in unison,
praises the Buddha’s name with a long drawn-out sound.
Then the lecturer ascends the north seat,
and the supervising lecturer ascends the south seat.
The praise of the Buddha then ceases.
At this time, a monk from the lower seat performs a chant,
saying, "Why in this Sūtra, etc." a stanza of one line.
After the chant is finished,
the south seat chants the Sūtra title.
This is called the long drawn-out chanting of the Sūtra.
The sound has many twists and turns during the chanting of the Sūtra.
The assembly scatters flowers three times.
Each time flowers are scattered,
each has something to recite.
After the Sūtra is chanted,
the title is chanted again in a short tone.
The lecturer opens the Sūtra outline,
dividing it into three sections,
and explains the general meaning of the Sūtra.
After the explanation of the Sūtra title is completed,
there is a Vinaya master (Wéinàshī)
who reads out the statement of the reason for the request.
In that document,
the principle of impermanence,
the merits of the deceased,
and the number of days since the passing are fully recorded.
It is known that the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dēngzhōu has the surname Wū and the given name Jiǎo.
People at the time called him Master Wū (Wū Shǐjūn).
He has three taboo characters:
Míng, Qǐ, and Gěi.
Tomorrow means the coming day.
The Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ) of Qīngzhōu has the surname Shòu.
People at the time called him Minister Shòu (Shòu Shàngshū).
He has no taboo characters.
The Sīnluó Sūtra recitation ritual
is called 'chanting Sūtras' (Niànjīng) in Dàtáng.
After the bell is struck and the assembly is settled,
a monk from the lower seat
rises, strikes a clapper, and chants, "All reverently bow to the permanently residing Three Jewels."
Next, a monk performs a chant,
saying, "The Tathāgata’s wondrous physical body," a two-line stanza.
The rhythm is the same as in Táng.
During the chant,
one person holds an incense cup
and walks past the seats of the assembly.
After a quick walk, he stops.
The assembly, in unison,
recites the title of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā many tens of times.
There is a master
who states the reason for the Sūtra recitation.
The assembly, in unison, recites the Sūtra.
Sometimes Sūtra texts are distributed,
sometimes not.
After the Sūtra recitation,
the guide (Dǎoshī) alone chants, "I take refuge in the Buddha,
I take refuge in the Dharma,
I take refuge in the Saṅgha."
Next, the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are invoked.
The guide chants, saying,
"Námó Twelve Great Vows."
The assembly says,
"Yàoshī Liúlíguāng Fó."
The guide says, "Námó Yàoshī."
The assembly, in unison, says,
"Liúlíguāng Fó."
The guide says, "Námó Great Compassion."
The assembly, in unison, says,
"Guānshìyīn Púsà."
All others are like this.
After bowing to the Buddha,
the guide alone makes a vow and dedicates merit.
The dedication is somewhat long.
After the dedication,
the guide says,
"Arouse the Bodhi-mind."
The assembly, in unison, also says,
"Arouse the Bodhi-mind."
Next, the guide chants, "The vow is completed."
They prostrate before the Three Jewels.
Next, the donor holds the offering and sits.
The guide gives a blessing, and then they disperse.
