I regret that due to prior arrangements I could not express
my feelings, so how can I express my heartfelt joy?
Yúanrén, admiring the teachings of Śākyamuni, has lingered in the Táng realm.
Now I wish to travel to various regions
to seek out sacred sites.
I humbly look up to your great benevolence.
I fortunately request your grace and protection.
I respectfully send my disciple, the monk Wéizhèng,
to present this letter on my behalf.
Without further ado, respectfully submitted.
Kāichéng 5th year, first month, twentieth day.
Letter from the Japanese monk Yúanrén, who seeks the Dharma, presented to
Yāyá Zhāng.
The twenty-first day.
Received a report from the yáyá, stating:
"Tomorrow, an envoy will be dispatched
to Wéndēng Xiàn to obtain a post-report.
A special envoy will hurry with the report to Chìshān Yuàn.
Those who should pay attention and wait
are the monks in the monastery,
and the yáyá, as well as the villagers, all said:
'From Qīngzhōu onwards, in various places,
for the past three or four years,
there has been a locust plague.
It devoured the grain and rice.
Because people are hungry and poor,
there are many bandits.
They kill and rob not a few.
Furthermore, travelers beg for food,
but no one gives alms.
At present, for four people to travel together,
it is expected to be extremely difficult.
For now, stay in this monastery,
pass the summer and wait for autumn.
Once the grain is ripe, then depart.
This will be safe and convenient. If you wish
to travel, head towards the border of Yáng Chǔzhōu.
There, the grain is ripe,
and food is easy to obtain.
If you wish to fulfill your original vow,
it is also possible to go directly north from Chǔzhōu and Hǎizhōu via the main road.'
People’s opinions differed,
causing indecision in my mind.
The magistrate of Wéndēng Xiàn is named Dòng,
and the shǎofǔ is named Píng.
On the evening of the twenty-seventh, I received a report from the yáyá, stating:
'Yesterday, I already submitted your esteemed request.
The current county magistrate
recently reported, saying:
It is necessary to wait for ten-odd days for the matter to be reported to the prefecture.
Only when the prefectural office has made a decision
will it be possible to travel east or west.'
On the first day of the second month,
I drafted another petition
to urge the yáyá. The petition is as follows:
'Mid-spring is gradually warming.
I humbly presume
that Your Excellency the yáyá's revered body
is always in excellent health.
I, Yuánrén, having received grace,
suddenly received your written instructions,
and also fully understood your noble intentions.
The kindness and effort are deep and profound.
I, a humble monk, cannot but feel deeply grateful.
I humbly note the county’s report which states:
It is necessary to report to the prefecture and wait for ten-odd days.
Only when the prefectural office has made a decision
will it be possible to travel east or west.
My humble thoughts consider this;
the reasoning is clear.
However, the journey I intend to undertake
is over ten thousand *lǐ*.
As a distant traveler, my private hope
is not for this public matter. I humbly believe that the county's report to the prefecture
may not be immediate.
If there is delay and time is wasted,
the travel season will enter the hot period.
I humbly request
that you once again extend your gracious consideration.
I, Yuánrén,
whose journey is over perilous paths,
am devoted to seeking the Way,
and am particularly eager to depart early,
not fearing criticism or blame.
I lightly trouble
Your Excellency with this small matter.
Although my shame and apprehension accumulate,
I cannot remain silent.
This is because I admire Your Excellency's protection.
I humbly hope
that you will again exert pressure and urge
an early decision.
In doing so,
your great benevolent reputation
will spread far overseas,
and the good root of seeking the Dharma
will be bound together in deep friendship.
I cannot contain my utmost reverence and longing.
I respectfully send my disciple Wéizhèng
to present this petition on my behalf.
Undisclosed, respectfully presented.'
The first day of the second month.
Petition from the Dharma-seeking monk Yuánrén to
Zhāng Yáyá.
Received a report from the yáyá, saying:
'Another envoy has been sent to report.
I earnestly believe it will not be long before a response comes.
For now, I wish the guest not to worry unduly.'
'Since the time the Abbot arrived and stayed in my humble residence,
many people have been bustling about all day.'
On the seventh day, the senior disciple, the novice monk Shī Jìng,
left the monastery and went west.
On the eleventh day, at dusk,
the monastery abbot's disciple, the novice monk Yǒng Xián,
secretly led the abbot's junior disciple, Shī Jùn.
The two, with one mind,
secretly left and ran away.
No one, old or young, in the monastery
heard or knew.
On the fourteenth day, at the invitation of the Silla monk Cháng Jì,
I went to Liú Cūn.
Upon arriving there, I saw that the white stone Maitreya statue was covered in earth.
I asked about the reason.
They replied:
'There was a Silla man named Wáng Xiàn here.
He dreamed one night that a monk
came and said:
"I am Mañjuśrī.
The ancient Buddha hall has fallen into disrepair,
and for years no one has repaired it.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are buried in the earth.
Seeing your faithful devotion,
I have come to inform you.
If you wish to know the truth,
by the precious map to the southeast of my humble abode,
you will see them."
He awoke in surprise and wonder.
He spoke of the dream
to various monastics and laypeople.
They went far to the edge of the ancient map
and dug the earth.
When they dug down to the knee,
they found the Buddha and Bodhisattva statues.
Today, they have unearthed one Maitreya Buddha statue,
one Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva statue,
one Samantabhadra Bodhisattva statue,
two Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva statues,
one Mahāsimhanāda Bodhisattva statue,
one Rāhula statue,
and Buddha relics in an iron casket, weighing over twenty *jīn*.
All who saw them
found them extremely wondrous.'
That night, they worshipped the Buddha.
Monastics and laypeople gathered,
giving alms all night.
On the fifteenth day, there was a vegetarian feast without limit to the number of people.
I then saw Zhāng Yáyá.
I received a report from the yáyá,
saying:
'Regarding the westward journey,
I will immediately dispatch a person to the prefecture
to obtain another decision.
For three to five days,
please pay attention and wait.
If it is urgently desired,
I will specially order the relevant person to escort you to the county.
It is also permissible to proceed continuously from there.'
Within fifteen days,
Cuī Yáyá's ship arrived from Yángzhōu.
It was at Rǔshān Pǔ.
On the seventeenth day, for Cuī Yáyá,
I left a letter
and entrusted it to the monastery abbot.
I also gave a letter
to Zhāng Dàshǐ.
The letter is as follows:
Unfolding the changing year.
Virtuous words are rarely heard.
Diligence accumulates and deepens.
The spring scene is already warm.
I humbly reflect that
Your Excellency, Yāyá, is in good health and prosperity.
Currently, Yuánrén, having received grace, is separated by a cloud path,
unable to meet you in person.
My longing grows deeper day by day.
How can I express my admiration in song?
Yuánrén has remained in the mountain monastery,
happily having passed the year.
I have received abundant benevolence and virtue from the monks,
which greatly comforts my traveler's heart.
This is truly Your Excellency Yāyá’s benevolent creation.
Your protection extends far and wide.
How could a humble person
be able to repay it?
It is deeply engraved in my heart and bones,
only increasing my gratitude and shame.
Previously, I received your fragrant instructions,
that at the beginning of spring, a special envoy would be sent
to grant a boat
to transport me to Wéinán from Liánshuǐ.
Recently, I heard about the spiritual sites on Táishān,
and I cannot but yearn to visit them.
Yuánrén’s original intention
is specifically to seek Buddhist teachings.
Having fortunately heard of this sacred place,
how could I not go?
Because of this wish,
I will first go to Táiyuè.
Since I have broken my sincere promise,
and the matter did not go as planned,
I am deeply ashamed of your noble intentions.
I also fear that
the envoy you dispatched
will have exerted effort in vain.
Please do not blame me.
After seeking the Dharma,
I will return to Chìshān.
From Qīnghǎizhèn,
I will then return to my home country.
I humbly hope that
you will consult with Ambassador Zhāng
and fully explain the situation.
When Yuánrén returns,
roughly in the autumn of next year,
if there are ships and people traveling to and from that region,
please issue a high command
to specially send someone to look for us.
When the monks return home,
we will rely entirely on your great salvation.
My respectful longing knows no bounds.
I have respectfully left an empty document to substitute for a personal presentation.
Not fully declared, respectfully presented. On the 17th day of the 2nd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng.
Yuánrén, Dharma Master of Transmission of the Lamp and Seeker of Dharma for Benefit of Japan.
To Yāyá Cuī,
and Pànguān Nán,
may your esteemed bodies be blessed with ten thousand fortunes.
Although I have not yet met you in person,
I have already learned of you,
as if I had met you face to face.
I humbly reflect that
you are fully aware of the situation as before.
Please do not mind my difficulties in finding paper to write on.
My heart has no paper, so I cannot write a separate letter.
I would be very fortunate if you would forgive me.
Respectfully empty.
I have not yet served you in person in my lifetime,
but have long heard of your noble reputation.
My admiration and respect only increase.
Mid-spring is already warm.
I humbly reflect that
Your Excellency, the Ambassador,
is well in all your actions and demeanor.
Currently, Yuánrén
remotely receives your benevolence and virtue.
My respectful longing knows no bounds.
Yuánrén,
to fulfill an old wish,
has lingered in the land of Táng.
My humble self is very fortunate
to travel in the land of Your Excellency's original vows.
Beyond gratitude and joy,
it is difficult to express in words.
Yuánrén,
when bidding farewell to my homeland,
humbly received a letter from the Governor of Chíkuzén,
to be presented to the Ambassador.
Suddenly, the ship sank in shallow waters, and goods were lost.
The entrusted letter also sank with the waves.
My sorrow and regret
have accumulated daily.
I humbly hope you will not blame me.
The time for serving you in person has not yet come,
but my longing and attachment only increase.
I respectfully present this letter to inquire about your well-being.
Not fully declared, respectfully presented.
On the 17th day of the 2nd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng.
Presented by Yuánrén, Dharma Master of Transmission of the Lamp and Seeker of Dharma Monk of Japan.
To Ambassador Zhāng of Qīnghǎizhèn.
Presented by Yuánrén, Seeker of Dharma Monk of Japan.

Request to be granted official travel documents to proceed to Wǔtái and other famous mountains and various places to tour sacred sites, seek masters, and learn the Dharma: Monk Yuánrén, disciples Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo, attendants Dīng Xióng and Mǎnyuán, with their robes and alms bowls, etc.

The above Yuánrén and others, with great aspiration, admire the Buddhist teachings and practice the Buddha Way. They have heard from afar that Wǔtái and other places in China are the origin of Buddhist Dharma and the transformation sites of great saints, where eminent monks from Xītiān crossed dangers and traveled far to the land of Hàn, and renowned figures traveled here to attain the Way. Yuánrén and others, filled with admiration, crossed the sea to visit and seek, but have not yet fulfilled their long-cherished wish. In the 6th month of the 4th year of Kāichéng, they arrived at Chìshān Xīnluóyuàn in Qīngníngxiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn. They separated from their relatives across the vast ocean and forgot their homeland on the seashore. Fortunately, they were permitted to travel east and west to Your Excellency's territory. Now, they wish to visit various places to pay homage at sacred sites, seek masters, and learn the Dharma. They fear that local prefectures, counties, garrisons, city gates, streets, passes, ferries, stations, villages, and monasteries may not understand their itinerary. Therefore, they humbly request that official travel documents be granted as proof. As stated above, they respectfully request a decision. As stated above, this official document is respectfully presented.
On the 3rd day of the 3rd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng.
Yuánrén, Dharma Master of Transmission of the Lamp and Seeker of Dharma Monk of Japan.
Yuánrén, Seeker of Dharma of Japan,
humbly received several official gifts.
For my humble self,
I cannot bear the burden of such gratitude.
Yuánrén
is an ordinary monk from a foreign land.
How dare I accept such a generous gift?
It is truly difficult to acknowledge and thank you for it,
only increasing my awe and shame.
I humbly reflect that
Your Excellency the Governor is loyal and righteous, in accord with the will of heaven.
Your noble rank places you among the pillars of the state, with a pure and lofty reputation.
Your benevolent influence spreads far,
and the military command is at peace.
Both monks and laypeople admire you.
Yuánrén,
for the sake of seeking Buddhist teachings,
came from afar, moved by your virtue.
I linger and travel in your noble territory,
fortunately bathed in your benevolence and virtue.
As a humble person,
my gratitude and joy know no bounds.
On the 19th day of the 2nd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng.
Presented by Yuánrén, Dharma Master of Transmission of the Lamp and Seeker of Dharma Monk of Japan.
On the 19th, after the meal, I left Chìshān Xīnluóyuàn and entered the county.
The monastery abbot, Monk Fǎqīng,
accompanied me to the residence of Yāyá Zhāng, who supervises Silla envoys.
Yāyá met me and said,
"Just now I received an official document from the county.
I was about to send someone to report,
but Your Reverence has arrived in person.
I truly believe this journey has been very auspicious.
I deeply congratulate you."
Then I saw the county document.
Official Document from Wéndēng Xiàn to the Office of the Yāyá in Charge of Silla Affairs.
Our county previously reported to the higher authorities
regarding the four Japanese ship-borne monks including Yuánrén.
This document states:
Upon examining the records and receiving a notice, it is stated that
the aforementioned guest monks
previously resided at Chìshān Monastery.
They entirely wish to go to various places for pilgrimage due to the warmth of spring.
Fearing unfamiliarity with procedures,
we now wish to permit them to travel east and west.
A report has been submitted as we cannot make a decision independently.
According to the notice, they should be permitted to go.
There is no corresponding notice yet.
This document is sent to Yāyá Zhāng, who supervises Silla affairs,
requesting a decision.
According to the report, a document is to be issued to Yāyá Zhāng.
Respectfully presented.
On the 10th day of the 2nd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng.
Document from Diǎn Wángzuǒ.
Hú Jūnzhí, Registrar and Acting Commandant.
County seal stamped in three places.
Dēngzhōu Dūdùfǔ, Official Document from Wéndēng Xiàn.
Regarding the four Japanese guest monks, including Yuánrén:
Monk Yuánrén, disciples Monk Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo, attendants Dīng Xióng and Màn Yú, along with their robes and alms bowls, etc.
This document states:
Upon examining the records, we received the aforementioned monk's petition.
In the 6th month of the 4th year of Kāichéng,
they arrived with their country's tribute ship
and took lodging at Chìshān Xīnluóyuàn in Qīngníngxiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn.
Now, having been permitted to travel east and west,
they wish to go to various places for pilgrimage.
They fear that local prefectures, counties, passes, ferry ports, roadsides,
may not understand their itinerary.
Therefore, they humbly request
that official travel documents be granted as proof.
Requesting a decision:
Upon examination, the aforementioned guest monks do not yet have a corresponding document.
Grant official travel documents.
Requesting a decision: according to the previous petition,
grant official travel documents as proof.
Respectfully presented.
On the 23rd day of the 2nd month of the 5th year of Kāichéng. Document from Diǎn Wángzuǒ.
Hú Jūnzhí, Registrar and Acting Commandant.
At night, I stayed at Yāyá's residence.
On the 20th, Yāyá issued a document to Yuánrén and others,
sending it to the county office
to have official travel documents issued.
He also dispatched an official,
Lǐ Míngcái, to accompany us into the county.
Then I bid farewell to Yāyá
and also to Abbot Fǎqīng of Chìshān Monastery, etc.
After saying our farewells,
we traveled north for twenty *lǐ*
to Wángjiāduàn in Wànghǎicūn.
After the meal, we traveled north for fifty *lǐ*.
At night, we arrived at Wéndēng Xiàn.
We stayed overnight at Jílè Shālí's residence in Huìhǎi Sì.
On the 21st, early morning court.
Entered Huìjù Sì to temporarily look for lodging.
Settled in the north courtyard.
At mealtime, went to the Jílè Shé Lí Yuàn at Huìhǎi Sì to have lunch.
Lǐ Míngcái,
in the early morning, went to the county yámén.
By that time, the official document for the Yāyá had not yet been approved by the superior.
Had not yet obtained the official travel permit.
According to Tángguó customs and laws,
officials manage government affairs
with two court sessions a day:
morning court and evening court.
One must listen for the drum sound
before taking one's seat in the yámén.
When private guests or public visitors await the court session,
they can then see the officials.
On the 22nd, ate gruel and rice at this temple.
Because the superior official requested leave, he did not come out,
so the official travel permit was not obtained.
Also heard
that Emperor Kāichéng
passed away on the 3rd day of the first month of this year.
Throughout the realm, people mourned and wore mourning clothes for three days.
Also heard
that the new emperor ascended the throne.
Over four thousand people in the city were executed.
These were people who had received imperial favor during the previous emperor's reign.
On the 23rd, it was Hánshí Jié.
Fires were extinguished for three days.
After the meal, Hú Zhǔbù, Zhèng Zhǔbù, and others from the county magistracy,
a total of several tens of people, came to the temple.
They met and offered condolences.
We fully explained our original intention for coming from afar and staying.
Wéndēng Xiàn
is at the western root of the Bóhǎi Sea,
and the eastern border of Tángguó.
When Qín Huáng ruled the empire,
he toured and enjoyed this place.
A Buddhist temple was consequently established,
named Huìjù.
It is now south of the county seat.
On the 24th, early morning court.
Obtained an official document from the county.
The text is as explained elsewhere.
Lǐ Míngcái handled the official travel permit and finished.
Returned to Zhāng Yāyá's place.
On the 25th, in the hour of Sì (9-11 a.m.),
went to the county to bid farewell to the officials, then returned to the temple.
After the meal, departed.
Gāngwéi, Diǎnzúo, and others
came to the wilderness west of the county to bid farewell.
Traveled 30 lǐ from the county
and stayed at Zhāoxián Guǎn.
The curator, Gāo Nù,
lived in the guesthouse
and acted as a diligent host.
On the 26th, at dawn,
departed from Zhāoxián Guǎn in the early morning.
Traveled 30 lǐ
and stopped for lunch at Lóngquán Cūn Xiéshān Guǎn.
The curator, Liáng Gōngdù,
lived in the guesthouse.
He was neither bad nor good.
Because of a footache,
could not travel.
So, stayed at the guesthouse.
On the 27th, early morning,
departed and arrived at Fánchē Cūn Cǎi Rìchéng Zhái for lunch.
Asked for soy sauce, vinegar, salt, and vegetables.
There was absolutely nothing of any kind.
Could not eat the soup or rice.
Traveled seven lǐ along the northwest coast
and arrived half a lǐ east of Mùpíng Xiàn city.
There was Lúshān Sì.
At the hour of Wèi (1-3 p.m.),
entered the temple to stay.
There were only Sāngāng,
Diǎnzúo,
and Zhísuì, a total of five people.
There were no other monks.
The Buddha hall was dilapidated.
The monastic cells were all occupied by laypeople,
having been transformed into lay residences.
The county city was one and a half lǐ from east to west,
and over two lǐ from north to south.
On the 28th, Lúshān Sì held a vegetarian feast for Dēngzhōu Cìshǐ Wū Jūn.
Two monks from this temple:
the temple master, monk Yī Xíng,
and the Zhísuì monk Cháng Biǎo.
And three Japanese monks.
A total of five people.
Over twenty villagers
each, from their own homes,
prepared and brought food according to their means.
Temple Master Yī Xíng expressed his admiration.
The villagers shared the vegetarian meal in the hall, each at their designated place.
On the 29th, departed early.
Traveled 30 lǐ northwest
to Zhīyáng Guǎn for lunch.
After the meal, traveled 20 lǐ
and stayed at Mùchéng Cūn Gāo'ān Zhái.
The host was not bad.
On the 1st day of the 3rd month, departed at dawn.
Traveled 10 lǐ to Gùxiàn Guǎn.
Traveled 20 lǐ northwest
to Shù Tàisūn Huāmào Zhái for lunch.
Entered the house directly without announcing our arrival.
This surprised the host.
But the host was diligent and cordial.
After the meal, traveled 30 lǐ northwest
and stayed at Wángtíng Cūn Sì in Wàngxiān Xiāng, Pēnglái Xiàn district.
It thundered and rained in the night.
In Tángguó, a marker post is erected every five lǐ.
Two marker posts are erected every ten lǐ.
Earthen mounds are built at four corners,
narrow at the top and wide at the bottom,
varying in height from four to five or six chǐ.
They are called "lǐgézhù" (mile-interval posts).
On the 2nd, departed at dawn.
Traveled 20 lǐ to Ānxiāng Cūn Tíngyàn Zhái for a meal.
Traveled 20 lǐ to Dēngzhōu and stayed at Kāiyuán Sì.
Dēngzhōu is 400 lǐ from Chìshān Pǔ.
At first, we walked up and down mountain slopes, our feet became sore.
We walked with staffs, stepping with our knees.
Qíao Gǎilái, from the southern city boundary, came to request an account of our journey.
Therefore, a travel record was written and given to him, as follows:
Japanese monk Yuánrén, disciple monks Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo, and lay practitioner Dīng Xióngmǎn, seeking the Dharma.
The above Yuánrén and others,
on the 13th day of the 4th month of the 5th year of Chénghé in Japan, boarded a ship with the tribute envoys.
Departed from our homeland's border.
On the 2nd day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Dà Táng Kāichéng, arrived at Báicháo Zhèn, Hǎilíng Xiàn, Yángzhōu.
On the 28th day of the 8th month, arrived in Yángzhōu and temporarily stayed at Kāiyuán Sì.
On the 21st day of the 2nd month of the 4th year of Kāichéng, departed from Yángzhōu by ship.
On the 7th day of the 6th month, arrived at Qīngníng Xiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn, and temporarily stayed at Chìshān Xīnluó Yuàn.
Spent one winter.
On the 19th day of the 2nd month of this year, departed from Chìshān Yuàn.
On the 2nd day of this month, arrived at this Kāiyuán Sì at dusk and stayed.
We respectfully present the account of events as above.
2nd day of the 3rd month, 5th year of Kāichéng.
Memorial of the Japanese monk Yuánrén, seeking the Dharma.
Dēngzhōu Dūdū Fǔ city is one lǐ east,
and one lǐ north to south.
Southwest of the city boundary,
there is Kāiyuán Sì.
Northeast of the city,
there is Fǎmó Sì.
Southeast, there is Lóngxīng Sì.
There are no other temples.
Outside and near the city, there are private residences.
Below the city is Pēnglái Xiàn.
The monastic cells in Kāiyuán Sì are quite numerous,
but all are occupied by official guests.
There are no vacant rooms.
When monks arrive,
there is no place to settle them.
North of the city is the vast sea.
One and a half lǐ from the city.
On the coast, there is Míngwáng Miào, standing alone by the sea.
Due east of the city is the market.
Millet costs 30 wén per dòu.
Polished rice costs 70 wén per dòu.
On the street south of the city, to the east,
there are Xīnluó Guǎn and Bóhǎi Guǎn.
From the Chìshān border of Dēngzhōu
to Dēngzhōu,
residences along the road are rare.
It is mostly mountainous wilderness.
From Mùpíng Xiàn
to Dēngzhōu,
the path runs along the northern sea.
This year, there has been an insect plague.
The common people are hungry and poor,
eating acorns as food.
On the 3rd, early morning,
an envoy from the county magistrate came to invite us.
Went to meet the magistrate.
Entered the prefecture and met the Lùshì.
Then entered the Pànguān's yámén.
After meeting the Pànguān,
entered through Zàimén to meet the Cāncǐ Jūn (governor).
Was invited to the main hall to drink tea.
The Cāncǐ Jūn personally wrote to bestow two shí of rice,
two shí of flour, one dòu of oil,
one dòu of vinegar,
and one dòu of salt.
And thirty roots of firewood,
to serve as travel provisions.
On the 4th, it was Guójì (a national day of mourning).
The Cāncǐ Jūn, Pànguān, Lùshì, county officials, and others,
all went to Kāiyuán Sì to offer incense.
The Cāncǐ Jūn, Pànguān, and others
drank tea in the treasury.
They summoned the monks seeking the Dharma and offered them tea.
They asked about the customs of our home country.
At mealtime, went to Zhāng Jiā's invitation.
The three Japanese monks
and the Diǎnzúo monk from this temple had lunch there.
On the fifth day, there was an early morning audience.
I presented a memorial.
To thank the Shǐjūn for providing provisions.
Another memorial requested an official permit.
The memorials are as follows.
From Yuánrén, a monk from the country of Rìběn seeking the Dharma.
I humbly received the gift of two shí of rice,
two shí of flour,
one dǒu of oil,
one dǒu of vinegar,
one dǒu of salt,
and thirty bundles of firewood.
These were specifically for my humble self.
My gratitude is immeasurable.
Yuánrén is an ordinary monk from a foreign land;
how dare I accept such kindness and generosity?
It is truly difficult to express my thanks adequately;
it only increases my apprehension and shame.
I humbly reflect
that the Shǐjūn’s loyalty is in harmony with Heaven’s will,
and his honor and nobility extend to myriad cities.
His pure character is a lofty standard,
and his benevolent governance spreads far and wide.
The military prefecture is peaceful,
and both monks and laity look up to him with admiration.
Yuánrén,
having traveled far to seek the Buddhist teachings, feeling your virtue, has arrived in your esteemed domain.
Fortunately, I have received your benevolent virtue,
and you have specially extended your compassionate care,
nurturing a poor traveler.
My humble self’s gratitude and joy are boundless.
I respectfully present this memorial to express my thanks.
Without further ado, I respectfully submit this memorial.
The fifth day of the third month of the fifth year of Kāichéng. Submitted by Yuánrén, a monk from the country of Rìběn seeking the Dharma.
To the Shǐjūn.
Submitted by Yuánrén, a monk from the country of Rìběn seeking the Dharma.
I humbly request the favor of an official permit
to travel to Wǔtái and other famous mountains, and various other places,
to visit sacred sites,
and to seek teachers and learn the Dharma.
Monk Yuánrén,
disciples Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo,
and attendant Dīng Xióngwàn.
Regarding my personal razor, robes, and alms bowl, etc.
The aforementioned Yuánrén and others,
whose original intention was to admire the teachings of Śākyamuni
and practice the Buddhist Way.
Having heard from afar
that the roots of the Buddhist Dharma are in Zhōnghuá, Wǔtái, and other places,
and that these are the places of transformation of the Great Sages,
where eminent monks from Xītiān
crossed dangerous lands and traveled far to arrive,
and where renowned virtuous monks from the Táng kingdom
traveled and attained the Way.
Yuánrén and others
have long held admiration and longing.
We crossed the sea to visit and seek,
but our long-cherished wish has not yet been fulfilled.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Kāichéng,
we arrived at the Xīnlúo Temple on Chìshān in Qīngníng Township, Wéndēng County.
We crossed the boundless ocean, severing ties with our former lives,
and cast off thoughts of our homeland on the coast.
Fortunately, we were allowed to travel east and west and arrived in the benevolent territory of the Shǐjūn.
Now we wish to proceed to various places,
to pay homage at sacred sites,
and to seek teachers and learn the Dharma.
We fear that the local zhōu, xiàn, customs barriers, postal stations, and temples, etc.,
may not understand our reasons for travel.
We humbly hope that the Shǐjūn, in your benevolence, will specially grant an official permit as proof.
We humbly request your order.
This dispatch addresses the aforementioned memorial.
Respectfully dispatched.
The fifth day of the third month of the fifth year of Kāichéng.
Submitted by Yuánrén, a monk from the country of Rìběn seeking the Dharma.
I received a report from the Shǐjūn stating:
“Our office has examined it.”
Then, from the capital,
a decree from the new Son of Heaven arrived.
Inside the zhōu city, in front of the gate of the residence, in the courtyard,
two carpets were spread.
On the north steps of the main gate, a small table was placed.
On the table, a purple curtain was spread.
On it was placed the imperial decree.
It was written on yellow paper.
The Zhōupànguān, Lùshì, etc.,
Xiànlìng, Zhǔbù, etc.,
Bīngmǎshǐ,
military commanders,
military officials,
common people,
monks and nuns,
and Daoist priests,
each lined up according to their rank and class.
They stood on the east side of the courtyard,
facing west.
From inside, the Shǐjūn came out.
Twenty military commanders
were in front of the Shǐjūn,
leading ten people each to the left and right.
The Lùshì, xiàn officials, etc.,
seeing the Shǐjūn emerge,
prostrated themselves, almost touching the ground.
The Shǐjūn called out, “Common people!”
Everyone together shouted, “Nuo!”
The Shǐjūn stood on one carpet.
The Pànguān also stood on one carpet.
All stood facing west.
There was one military commander
who called out the names of the various officials.
The ranks of the Lùshì and xiàn officials all shouted “Nuo!” at once.
Next, he called out the ranks of the various army commanders, Yáyá, generals, and Bīngmǎshǐ.
The ranks of the army all shouted “Nuo!” at once.
He then said, “Various guests!”
Immediately, the various official guests and Zàitài shouted “Nuo!”
Next, he said, “Common people!”
The common people, young and old, all shouted “Nuo!”
Next, he said, “Monks and Daoists!”
Monks, nuns, and Daoist priests all shouted “Nuo!”
Then, two military commanders
brought the table with the imperial decree.
They placed it in front of the Shǐjūn and bowed once.
The Shǐjūn took the imperial decree with his hands,
raised it to his forehead, and saluted it.
One military commander knelt,
received the document on his sleeve,
and held it up to the center of the courtyard,
standing facing north.
He called out,
“By imperial edict!”
The Shǐjūn, Pànguān, Lùshì, various military officers, etc.,
all bowed twice together.
One military commander said,
“Common people, bow!”
The common people bowed twice.
However, monks, nuns, and Daoist priests did not bow.
He ordered two Yámén officials to open the imperial decree.
These two people wore green robes.
There were two other Yámén officials
who took turns reading.
Their voices were loud, similar to the sound of proclaiming policies in our own country.
The imperial decree, about four or five pages long, was read aloud.
It took quite a while, and no one sat down.
When the imperial decree was finished,
the Shǐjūn and all others bowed twice.
Next, one Lùshì
and one military commander
came out into the courtyard
and expressed their thanks to the Shǐjūn.
They then walked back to their original positions.
The Shǐjūn announced to the various departments,
“Each of you, diligently attend to your duties!”
The Pànguān and those above him all shouted “Nuo!”
Next, the Dūshǐ called out, “Monks and Daoists!”
Monks, nuns, and Daoist priests shouted “Nuo!”
Next, he said, “Common people!”
They shouted “Nuo!”
Next, the imperial decree was brought to the Shǐjūn, who bowed again.
The Shǐjūn stepped off the carpet
and covered himself with his sleeve.
Several tens of official guests and others
came before the Shǐjūn,
prostrating themselves and bending their bodies to stand.
A military commander called out, “Dismissed!”
They all shouted “Nuo!” at once.
Officials, military officers, monks, Daoists, and common people then dispersed.
On the fifth day, the rice and flour provided by the Shǐjūn
were used to prepare an offering at the storehouse.
Five dǒu of rice, one shí of flour, vinegar, salt, oil, thirty bundles of firewood.
The above items are due to the Shǐjūn’s benevolence.
I should not keep them for myself alone.
Therefore, the aforementioned items
will be used at the permanent temple
to prepare a vegetarian meal.
Tomorrow, it will be offered to all the monks of the monastery.
Respectfully submitted.
The sixth day of the third month. Yuánrén, a monk from the country of Rìběn seeking the Dharma.
To the Gāngwéi of this temple.
On the sixth day, at noon,
I had a meal with over ten monks from the monastery. We were then interrupted.
At the shēn hour (3-5 PM),
Wáng Chángzōng, the Jūnshì Yáyá of this zhōu,
donated a donkey
to carry provisions.
On the seventh day, I partook in a vegetarian meal at the residence of Vice-Prefect Wáng.
This is on the north wall inside the hall of Venerable Sēngjiā, outside the west corridor of the Buddha Hall of Kāiyuán Temple.
It depicts the Western Pure Land,
and also Mount Pǔtuóluò Pure Land.
It was the wish of the envoy from Japan.
Immediately on the wall,
the缘起 (yuánqǐ, 'circumstances of the origin') were written down.
All of them have been erased,
only the three characters '日本國' (Rìběn Guó) are visible.
To the left and right of the Buddha image,
the names of the wish-makers are written.
These are all officials' ranks and names of Japanese people.
Lùshì (Record Keeper) Zhèngliùwèishàng Jiànbìgǎn.
Lùshì (Record Keeper) Zhèngliùwèishàng Yǔfēngxiáng.
Záshǐ (Miscellaneous Envoy) Cóngbāwèixià Qínyù. Záshǐ (Miscellaneous Envoy) Cóngbāwèixià Báiniúyǎng.
Zhūlì (Various Clerks) Cóngliùwèixià Qínhǎiyú.
Shǐxià (Subordinate Envoy) Cóngliùwèixià Xíngsànwèi Dùjiān.
Rén (Person) Cóngqīwèixià Liánxióngzhēn.
Jiān (Attendant) Cóngbāwèixià Jìcháochén Zhēnxún. No one could tell me their original purpose when I inquired.
I do not know in which year a tribute envoy
arrived at this prefecture.
On the morning of the eighth day,
I drafted a memorial to the Prefect,
and also urged for the official permit.
It is extremely warm in late spring.
I respectfully reflect,
may your honorable personage, Sǐjūn, be well in all your movements and repose.
Yúanrén has received your grace here.
The path of a monk is limited.
For several days, I have not been able to pay my respects.
My humble feelings are boundlessly fearful.
I respectfully send my disciple, the monk Wéizhèng, to present this memorial.
Not fully expressed, respectfully memorialized.
The eighth day of the third month of Kāichéng fifth year – Memorial from Yúanrén, a monk from Japan seeking the Dharma.
To Sǐjūn.
Yúanrén, a monk from Japan seeking the Dharma.
Respectfully, Yúanrén's original wish is to go to Mount Tái to spend the summer,
then travel to various places
to pilgrimage to sacred sites.
Fearing that changing circumstances might hinder my journey,
I previously submitted a memorial
to trouble your excellency for an official permit.
I respectfully request your decision.
This communication regarding the above memorial
is respectfully submitted.
The eighth day of the third month of Kāichéng fifth year – Memorial from Yúanrén, a monk from Japan seeking the Dharma.
The Prefect sent word saying,
"He will arrive now."
At mealtime,
I went to the invitation of Vice-Prefect Jiāng.
Together with four monks from this temple,
we had a vegetarian meal at his residence.
On the ninth day, I received a report from the Superintendent saying,
"The prefectural dispatch should be received tomorrow.
It is intended to be entrusted to the Venerable [Yúanrén],
to report to the envoy and request a decision."
The Venerable himself will bring the dispatch to the Jìdùfǔ (Military Governorship) of Qīngzhōu to obtain the official permit.
At noon,
we had a vegetarian meal at the residence of Liú Zìzhèng.
On the tenth day, it rained.
We went to the Zhāng family for a vegetarian meal.
On the eleventh day, at sìshí (9-11 am),
I received two prefectural dispatches: one for the Liúhòuguān (Retained Official),
and one to be presented to the envoy. I took the dispatch
and entered the prefecture to thank the Prefect
and bid farewell.
I also obtained a copy of the prefectural dispatch.
Dēngzhōu Dūdūfǔ (Dengzhou Military Governor's Office) dispatch – To the Superior Liaison Envoy of the Two Border Districts.
Regarding the memorial from the Japanese monk Yúanrén and others,
requesting an official permit
to go to Wǔtái Mountain and other famous mountains and various places
to pilgrimage to sacred sites
and seek teachers to learn the Dharma, etc.
The monk Yúanrén,
his disciples, the monks Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
and the practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn,
along with personal items such as a razor, robes, and alms bowl.
The dispatch states:
Upon investigation, it is found that the said monk’s memorial indicates
that his original intention is to admire the Buddhist teachings
and practice the Buddha Way.
He has heard from afar that various places in Zhōnghuá, such as Wǔtái,
are the root source of Buddhist law,
and places where great sages manifested their teachings.
High monks from Xītiān (India)
crossed perilous distances to come here,
and renowned virtuous ones from Táng Guó (China)
traveled here to attain the Way.
Yúanrén and others
have long admired this
and crossed the sea to seek it,
but have not yet fulfilled their long-cherished wish.
In the sixth month of Kāichéng fourth year, they arrived at Chìshān Xīnluóyuàn in Qīngníng Xiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn.
Separated by the boundless ocean of this life,
they forgot their homeland at the seashore.
Now they wish to go to various places to pay respects at sacred sites
and seek teachers to learn the Dharma.
Fearing that local prefectures, counties, customs posts, and inns,
as well as monasteries, etc.,
may not understand their purpose,
they respectfully hope
that a special official permit will be granted
as proof.
According to the investigation, the Japanese monk Yúanrén and others,
as previously reported by Wéndēng Xiàn,
on the twelfth day of the sixth month of last year,
the Japanese envoy who came to the capital for tribute returned on his ship
and landed at Chìshān Dōnghǎikǒu in Qīngníng Xiāng within the county’s jurisdiction.
They departed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Subsequently, a report from the county was received, stating
that the Japanese ship returning to its country abandoned
the monk Yúanrén
and four practitioners.
The prefectural administration has already reported the circumstances
to the envoy.
It is respectfully stated as above.
It is unclear whether an official permit will be granted.
The Prefect, judicial officer, and prefectural administration have no basis
to directly issue an official permit.
It was submitted to Ānlù to report to the Shàngshū for a decision.
And it was decided to send the monk
to personally carry the memorial to see the Shàngshū
to obtain a decision.
It is respectfully stated as above.
There has been no request to the envoy for a decision.
A memorial has been submitted to the envoy.
It is respectfully recorded and submitted.
Respectfully memorialized.
The ninth day of the third month of Kāichéng fifth year – Dispatch issued by Fǔshǐ Kuāngcóngzhì.
Memorial submitted to
the Shàngshū. The tenth day, Xínggù.
One dispatch has been issued by Diǎnkūangcóngzhì, Guānfùyīn. Two seals.
On the twelfth day, at dawn, we departed.
We traveled thirty *lǐ* to the west
and stopped for lunch at the residence of Wáng Xú in Xiànqìng Village.
Then we departed, traveling forty *lǐ*,
and stayed overnight at the residence of the Shàoyǔn (Assistant Administrator) in Jiǔlǐ Zhàn Village, Huáng Xiàn.
The host was impolite.
I dreamed of Abbot Yúan chéng.
On the thirteenth day, we departed in the early morning.
We traveled twenty *lǐ* to the west
and arrived at Zhànzhāiguǎn (Zhàn Vegetarian Hall).
We had a vegetarian meal at the residence of Dōng Huán.
The host was extremely stingy.
I begged for a plate of vegetables,
and only after repeated requests did he give it.
After the meal, we departed.
We traveled twenty-five *lǐ* to the west
and ate *bǐng* (flatbread) at Chéngfūguǎn (Chéngfū Inn).
We traveled twenty-five *lǐ*
and arrived at Xú Sòng Village in Yè Xiàn, Láizhōu.
We stayed overnight at the residence of Jiāng Píng.
The host was straightforward.
I dreamed of Venerable Yìzhēn.
On the fourteenth day, we departed.
We traveled thirty *lǐ*
and stopped for lunch at the Wáng family in Túqiūguǎn (Túqiū Inn).
The host was initially unwilling when we first met,
making everything difficult.
However, in the end, he provided enough salted vegetables.
After the meal, we traveled ten *lǐ*
and ate *bǐng* at the Wáng family in Qiáocūn (Qiáo Village).
We traveled twenty *lǐ*
and arrived at Zhōnglǐcūn (Middle Li Village), which has over twenty households.
We passed five or six residences
looking for a place to stay.
Every household had
The sick person did not allow guests to stay.
Finally, they arrived at a family's home.
Again, they were not allowed to stay.
After repeated scolding and cursing,
they went further to Féngfēng's residence to stay.
The host had a sincere heart for the Dao.
On the fifteenth day, they departed.
They traveled fifteen *lǐ*.
They arrived at Chéngjiā Duànzhōng in Píngxú Cūn.
The host was very hospitable.
After the meal, they traveled fifteen *lǐ* to Láizhōu.
The prefectural city was one *lǐ* southeast.
It was more than two *lǐ* from north to south.
The outer corridors extended about three *lǐ* in each direction.
Inside the city, people's homes and buildings were well-maintained.
Outside the city, to the southeast, they stayed at Lóngxīng Sì.
In front of the Buddha hall, the thirteen-story brick pagoda base and steps were dilapidated.
The surrounding corridors were ruined.
The monastery had no community of monks.
There were only two monks.
The abbot (sìzhǔ) and the director of monastic affairs (diǎnzùo) had common dispositions,
and did not understand the etiquette for hosts and guests.
Láizhōu administered four counties:
Yè Xiàn,
Chāngyáng Xiàn,
Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn.
Outside the prefectural city, to the southwest, a market was established.
A *dǒu* of millet cost fifty *wén*.
A *dǒu* of polished rice cost ninety *wén*.
On the morning of the sixteenth day,
the permanent monastic community provided porridge.
The monastery had no cooked rice,
so everyone sought their own food.
They ate their own food,
without sharing with others.
Each cut their own portion
to offer to the monks.
Afterward, they departed northwest, traveling fifteen *lǐ*.
By the roadside was the tomb of Wáng Fǔjūn.
An inscription was carved on stone.
After many years,
the inscribed stone had fallen to the ground.
Alongside Běihǎi Pǔ,
they traveled more than twenty *lǐ*.
They arrived at Fáyún Sì in Yī Cūn to stay.
The officer in charge (zhīguǎn) handled matters.
The official lodging (táiguǎn) was originally a Buddhist monastery.
Later, it became a lodging.
People at the time called it Jiàntái Guǎn.
In front of the lodging were two pagodas.
One was two *zhàng* high and five stories.
It was constructed of carved stone.
The other was one *zhàng* high.
It was made of cast iron.
It had seven stories.
Its stele inscription read:
"Wáng Xíngzé,
following an imperial edict, went to conquer the fallen eastern barbarians.
Over a hundred people on the same boat
were all captured by bandits
and sent to the land of Wō.
He alone escaped
and fortunately returned.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of Líndé second year,
this precious pagoda was built."

On the twenty-ninth day, they departed early, traveling thirty *lǐ* northwest to Zhīyáng Guǎn for a meal. After the meal, they traveled twenty *lǐ* to Móuchéng Cūn, staying at Gāo'ān's residence. The host was not bad.

On the first day of the third month, they departed at dawn, traveling ten *lǐ* to Gùxiàn Guǎn. Traveling twenty *lǐ* northwest, they arrived at Shùtài Sūn Huāmào's residence for a meal. Without reporting, they entered the house, which surprised the host, but the host was very hospitable. After the meal, they traveled thirty *lǐ* northwest to a monastery in Wàngxiān Xiāng, within Pénglái Xiàn. Thunder and rain came at night. In Tángguó, after traveling five *lǐ*, a marker was erected; after ten *lǐ*, two markers were erected. Earth mounds were built, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, four, five, or six *chǐ* high, not fixed, and called "lǐgézhù" (distance markers).

On the second day, they departed at dawn, traveling twenty *lǐ* to Chíyàn's residence in Ānxiāng Cūn for a meal. Traveling twenty *lǐ*, they arrived in Dēngzhōu and stayed at Kāiyuán Sì. Dēngzhōu is four hundred *lǐ* from Chìshān Pǔ. Suddenly, they encountered mountain slopes, their feet worn out from walking, using their staffs and stepping with their knees. Qíao, from the area south of the city, came to ask for the travel log, so the travel history was written for him as follows:
Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén, disciple monk Wéizhèng, practitioner Wéixiǎo, Dīng Xióngwàn.

The above Yuánrén and others, from Japan, on the thirteenth day of the fifth year of Chénghé, traveled with the tribute envoy by boat, departing from their homeland. On the second day of the seventh month of Kāichéng third year in Great Táng, they arrived at Báihú Zhèn, Hǎilíng Xiàn, Yángzhōu. On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month, they arrived in Yángzhōu and stayed at Kāiyuán Sì. On the twenty-first day of the second month of Kāichéng fourth year, they departed by boat from Yángzhōu. On the seventh day of the sixth month, they arrived at Qīngníng Xiāng, Wéndēng Xiàn, and stayed at the Silla Monastery in Chìshān, spending a winter. On the nineteenth day of the second month of this year, they departed from Chìshān Monastery. At dusk on the second day of this month, they arrived.

The sick person did not allow guests to stay. Finally, they arrived at a family's home. Again, they were not allowed to stay. After repeated scolding and cursing, they went further to Féngfēng's residence to stay. The host had a sincere heart for the Dao. On the fifteenth day, they departed, traveling fifteen *lǐ*. They arrived at Chéngjiā Duànzhōng in Píngxú Cūn. The host was very hospitable. After the meal, they traveled fifteen *lǐ* to Láizhōu. The prefectural city was one *lǐ* from east to west and more than two *lǐ* from north to south. The outer corridors extended about three *lǐ* in each direction. Inside the city, people's homes and buildings were well-maintained. Outside the city, to the southeast, they stayed at Lóngxīng Sì. In front of the Buddha hall, there was a thirteen-story brick pagoda base and steps which were dilapidated. The surrounding corridors were ruined. The monastery had no community of monks, there were only two monks. The abbot (sìzhǔ) and the director of monastic affairs (diǎnzùo) had common dispositions, and did not understand the etiquette for hosts and guests. Láizhōu administered four counties: Yè Xiàn, Chāngyáng Xiàn, Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn. Outside the prefectural city, to the southwest, a market was established. A *dǒu* of millet cost fifty *wén*. A *dǒu* of polished rice cost ninety *wén*. On the morning of the sixteenth day, the permanent monastic community provided porridge. The monastery had no cooked rice, so everyone sought their own food.
After the meal, it rained, so they did not depart.
On the seventeenth day, they departed at dawn.
They headed southwest.
They mistakenly entered the road to Mìzhōu.
After traveling five *lǐ*,
they accidentally met someone who guided them to the correct path.
After traveling fifteen *lǐ*,
they arrived at Pān Cūn, Pānjiā for a meal.
The host was mean and unkind.
They did not observe proper etiquette.
They asked the host
for vegetables, soy sauce, vinegar, and salt.
They received nothing at all.
So they took out one *jīn* of coins
and bought some pickled vegetables.
They were not palatable.
After the meal, they traveled forty *lǐ*.
They arrived at Liúqīng's residence in Sān'é Cūn, within the boundary of Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn, to stay.
The housewife was angry.
Her husband tried to mediate.
Thirty *lǐ* southeast of the village
was Jiāoshuǐ Xiàn.
On the eighteenth day, they traveled five *lǐ*.
They crossed the Jiāohé ferry.
Within Láizhōu's boundary,
people were unyielding.
The common people were poor and hungry.
Walking alongside the river for fifteen *lǐ*,
they arrived at the Bǔjiā farm in Tiánzhuāng, within the boundary of Qīngzhōu Běihǎi Xiàn, for a meal.
The host was hospitable.
There was no shortage of vegetarian dishes.
After the meal, they walked alongside the Jiāohé for thirty *lǐ*.
They arrived at Gěngjiā in Gěng Cūn, east of Fúróng Yì, to stay.
One *lǐ* west of Gěngjiā
was an ancient city.
People at the time called it Chāngguó Chéng.
The city's circumference was twelve *lǐ*.
It was wide from east to west
and narrow from north to south.
Inside the city, thirty households of common people were seen living. They asked a village elder,
who said,
"Since this city was abandoned,
more than a thousand years have passed.
We do not know which king resided here."
In the ground within the city,
gold, silver, pearls, jade, ancient coins, horse locks, etc. are still found.
Many treasures
are scattered in the ground.
They are collected after every rainfall.
The host of Gěngjiā was kind and good.
On the nineteenth day, they departed at dawn.
Traveling twenty *lǐ*,
they arrived at Zhàojiā in Wángkuí Cūn for a meal.
The host had a sincere heart for the Dao and provided abundant dishes.
After the meal, they traveled forty-five *lǐ*.
They arrived at Běihǎi Xiàn.
They stayed at Guānfǎ Sì.
The Buddha hall and monks' quarters were dilapidated.
The Buddha statues were exposed.
There were about twelve monks in the monastery,
all residing in lay families' homes.
Inside the monastery, there was one director of monastic affairs (diǎnzùo) monk.
In the county, one *dǒu* of rice cost sixty *wén*.
Also, one *dǒu* of small beans cost thirty-five *wén*.
The county city was two *lǐ* from east to west
and one *lǐ* from north to south.
It was the former Wéizhōu.
Now it is Běihǎi Xiàn.
On the twentieth day, they departed early.
Traveling twenty *lǐ* west,
they encountered the Bóhǎi envoy returning from Shàngdū to his country in the wilderness. Traveling another five *lǐ*,
they arrived at Gūshān Cūn to eat.
The host was extremely stingy.
A pinch of vegetables,
a *è* of soy sauce and vinegar,
were not given without money.
After the meal, thirty *lǐ* further,
they arrived at Lǐjiā in Bànchéng Cūn, within the boundary of Shòuguāng Xiàn, to stay.
The host was greedy
and stopped guests to collect lodging fees.
On the twenty-first day, they departed.
Traveling thirty *lǐ*,
they arrived at Zhāngjiā in Jiǔwèi Diàn for a meal.
The host was fair-minded.
After the meal, they traveled thirty *lǐ*.
They arrived at Lóngxīng Sì in Qīngzhōu Fǔ to stay.
The monastery staff recorded their origins and reported to the prefecture.
It was five hundred forty *lǐ* from Dēngzhōu.
On the twenty-second day, they entered the prefectural office in the morning to see the registrar (lùshì) and judicial officer (sīfǎ).
Next, they arrived in front of the Shangshū's (Minister's) office, which oversaw the two barbarian envoys.

At dawn,

Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
We, Yuánrén and others,

We humbly request your disposition.

From Déngzhōu's Wéndēng County

Yuánwài.
