Fifty donkeys
were carrying sesame oil.
Also saw Jùjiān and three other monks from Tiāntái Guóqīngsì
who were heading towards Wǔtái, stating that
at Tiāntái Guóqīngsì,
there was one Japanese monk,
one *shāmí* disciple,
and one *xíngzhě*.
They were currently residing there.
On the twenty-fourth day, the sky was overcast.
Departed from the mountain valley.
Traveled twenty-five *lǐ* northwest.
Encountered a shepherd driving about five hundred sheep.
Crossed a ridge.
Arrived at Liánglǐng Pǔtōngyuàn.
The院主 was not present.
Prepared food oneself.
There had never been porridge or rice in the院.
This was because of insect plagues in recent years,
so there was no grain now.
After the meal, traveled along the mountain valley.
Thirty *lǐ* northwest.
Arrived at Guǒyuàn Pǔtōngyuàn to lodge.
Thunder roared and rain fell.
On the 25th, it rained.
Pǔtōngyuàn.
Deep in the mountains, there was no congee or rice.
We ate a small amount of beans as a meal.
From Zhàozhōu until this place,
for three or four years there has been a locust plague.
The five grains did not ripen.
Food was hard to come by.
After the meal, the rain stopped. We looked for a valley heading west.
We traveled thirty *lǐ*.
We arrived at Jiěpǔtōngyuàn.
For the pilgrimage to Wǔtáishān,
the offering people, monks, nuns, and women,
totaled over one hundred people.
We all stayed overnight in the temple.
On the 26th, the weather was clear.
After eating congee,
we continued to travel twenty *lǐ* through the mountain valley.
We arrived at Jìngshuǐpǔtōngyuàn to have a meal.
The temple was poor.
The mountain wind gradually cooled.
Green pines connected the ridges.
We crossed two mountain ridges.
We traveled thirty *lǐ* west to Tángchéngpǔtōngyuàn.
Passing the temple, we continued west.
The ridges were high and the valleys deep.
Emerald peaks exhaled clouds.
Stream water cascaded in a green flow.
From Tángchéng, we traveled fifteen *lǐ* west.
At *shēn* hour,
we arrived at Lóngquánpǔtōngyuàn for the night.
Behind, on a hill, in the dragon hall,
a spring emerged, clear and cold.
The temple was near this spring.
It was called Lóngquánpǔtōngyuàn.
The temple had rice and congee.
On the 27th, we departed.
From the mountain valley, we traveled twenty *lǐ* west.
We arrived at Zhānghuāpǔtōngyuàn.
A total of nine monks had their mid-day meal.
The temple had congee and rice.
After the meal, we traveled ten *lǐ* through the valley.
We arrived at Jiēpùpǔtōngyuàn.
Passing the temple, we traveled ten *lǐ* west.
We crossed Dàfùlǐng.
East of the ridge, the stream water flowed east.
West of the ridge, the stream water flowed west.
After crossing the ridge, it gradually descended.
Sometimes we went west,
sometimes we went south.
Pine forests on the peaks,
trees in the valleys,
were straight and tall.
Bamboo groves and hemp gardens
were incomparable.
The mountain cliffs were rugged and steep,
seeming to touch the Milky Way.
The green pines reflected the blue sky.
West of the ridge, the tree leaves had not yet opened.
The grass had not yet reached four inches.
From Jiēpù, we traveled thirty *lǐ*.
At dusk,
we arrived at Juéshīpǔtōngyuàn for the night.
The temple had no congee or rice.
On the 28th,
we entered a flat valley.
We traveled thirty *lǐ* west.
At *sì* hour,
we arrived at Tíngdiǎnpǔtōngyuàn.
Before entering the temple,
looking northwest,
we saw the Central Terrace.
We prostrated ourselves in worship.
This is the realm of Wénshūshīlì.
The five peaks are round and high.
No trees are visible.
It is shaped like an overturned copper basin.
As we gazed at it from afar,
tears flowed unconsciously.
The trees and exotic flowers are unlike those elsewhere.
The wondrous scenery is particularly profound.
This is the Pure and Cool Mountain, the Golden World.
Wénshūshīlì currently manifests to benefit and transform beings.
We then entered Tíngdiǎnpǔtōngyuàn.
We prostrated ourselves before the statue of Wénshūshīlì Púsà.
Then we saw on the wall of the west pavilion,
an inscription that read:
"The great virtuous monk, Língxiān, who served the scriptures in Japan,
arrived at this hermitage
on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the fifteenth year of Yuánhé."
The monks in the temple, seeing a monk from Japan,
were surprised and showed him the inscription on the wall.
Therefore, I have recorded it.
At noon, we had a meal in the refectory.
After the meal, we saw several dozen monks going on a pilgrimage to the Southern Terrace.
Towards evening, thunder rumbled and rain fell.
From *shēn* hour on the 23rd, when we entered the mountains,
until today,
we have traveled through mountain valleys,
for a total of six days.
We have not yet reached the source of the mountains or Wǔtái.
Since the nineteenth day of the second month,
when we left Chìshānyuàn,
until this place,
we have traveled over two thousand three hundred *lǐ*.
Excluding rest days,
we have been traveling on the road for exactly forty-four days.
I am ashamed (of my condition).
On the road, I had no illness or burdens.
On the 29th, Tíngdiǎnyuàn held a hundred-monk vegetarian feast, and we were invited to partake.
Because the monk Jùjiān from Guóqīngsì in Táizhōuguó was returning to his own temple,
I entrusted two letters to him.
They were to be delivered to the Venerable Yuánzài.
After the meal, we saw several dozen monks going on a pilgrimage to the Southern Terrace.
In an instant, the clear sky suddenly became overcast.
Wind and clouds rapidly darkened.
Drizzling rain turned to hail.
In the evening, we saw them return.
Their bamboo hats were broken by the hail.
On the first day of the fifth month, the weather was clear.
We planned to go on the pilgrimage to the Terraces.
The donkey we brought,
we left at Tíngdiǎnyuàn, entrusting it to the head monk of the temple,
to manage its fodder.
From Tíngdiǎn, we traveled seventeen *lǐ* west.
Then, heading north, we crossed a high ridge for fifteen *lǐ*.
We arrived at Zhúlín Temple for our mid-day meal.
After the meal, we toured the temple buildings.
There was a *bānzhōu* practice hall.
The Venerable Fǎzhào once recited the Buddha's name in this hall.
There was an imperial edict posthumously conferring the title "Great Awakened Venerable."
He passed away two years ago.
Now a statue has been made and placed in the hall.
Also, there is a painting of Fútuópōlì arriving at Táishān in the first year of Yífèng,
and an image of him when he met the old man.
In the hall of Huáyányuàn,
there was a full set of Vajradhatu Mandala.
On the second day, we entered Zhēnyuán Jièlǜyuàn.
We went upstairs to worship the Mandala of the seventy-two worthy saints and various venerable ones, the national meritorious works.
The colorful paintings were exquisitely beautiful.
Next, we opened the Ten Thousand Saints Precept Platform.
It was made of jade and stone.
It was three *chǐ* high.
Its octagonal base was filled with fragrant mud.
On the platform, a silk carpet was spread,
its width and length matching the platform.
The beams, purlins, and pillars
were subtly decorated and painted.
We met the venerable old monk guarding the platform.
His Dharma name was Língjué.
He was one hundred years old.
He had seventy-two summers (of monastic life), and his appearance and bones were extraordinary.
He was a great virtuous monk who had ascended the platform.
He greeted guests cordially.
He said
that in the sixth month of last year, three monks from Nàlántuó Temple in Central India
came to visit Wǔtái.
They saw five-colored clouds and a round light enveloping their bodies, taking them back to Central India.
Zhúlín Temple has six compounds:
the Vinaya compound,
the Treasury compound,
the Huáyán compound,
the Fǎhuā compound,
the Pavilion compound,
and the Buddha Hall compound.
The entire temple has about forty monks.
This temple does not belong to Wǔtái.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
the temple held a vegetarian feast for seven hundred and fifty monks.
All the temples held similar feasts.
All were provided by the donor from Língyánsì in Qízhōu.
Zhúlín Sì Zhai Ceremony for Worshipping the Buddha.
At noon, the bell rings.
All monks enter the hall.
Elder monks, śrāmaṇeras, laypeople, children, and women
sit in rows according to their turns.
The Biǎotàn Shī strikes the mallet and chants, "Everything reverent, respectfully worship the abiding Three Jewels, everything universally mindful."
Next, two young monks from the temple
hold golden lotuses and strike the lìbá (cymbals).
Three or four people chant together in unison.
The offering host performs the incense offering.
Regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, male or female,
the incense offering is completed by everyone.
The Biǎotàn first reads the donor's offering inscription.
Next, the eulogy is recited.
Then, "Everything universally mindful" is chanted.
The elder monks chant in unison, "Móhē Bōrě Bōluómì."
Next, the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are chanted.
The assembly learns the lyrics.
Together, they pay homage to Shìjiāmóuní Fó,
Mílè Zūn Fó,
Wénshū Shīlì Púsà,
Dàshèng Pǔxián Púsà,
the Ten Thousand Bodhisattvas,
Dìzàng Púsà,
all Bodhisattvas,
and Mahāsattvas.
For the twenty-eight heavens, Śakra, Brahmā, and other kings,
they respectfully worship the abiding Three Jewels.
For the endless transformation by saints,
they respectfully worship the abiding Three Jewels.
For today's offering hosts and the solemn adornment of all good deeds,
they respectfully worship the abiding Three Jewels.
For teachers, monks, parents, and all sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
they respectfully worship the abiding Three Jewels.
Striking the mallet, it is chanted,
"Food offering mantra and vows."
The senior monk completes the mantra and vows.
Food is distributed to everyone, old and young, monastic and lay, male and female, as an equal offering.
After all monks have finished eating their vegetarian meal,
water for rinsing their mouths is offered.
Next, the mallet is struck, and the Buddha's name is recited.
The Biǎotàn Shī strikes the mallet and says,
"For today's donors, for their solemn adornment of good deeds, and for all sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
recite Móhē Bōrě Bōluómìduō."
The assembly recites in unison
Shìjiāmóuní Fó,
Mílè Zūn Fó,
Dàshèng Wénshū Shīlì Púsà,
the Ten Thousand Bodhisattvas,
all Bodhisattvas,
and Mahāsattvas.
After reciting the Buddha's name,
the mallet is struck, and the assembly disperses as they wish.
Towards evening, thunder rumbled and hail rained.
The pavilion courtyard was solemnly adorned as a sacred Dharma hall,
offering to seventy-two enlightened ones.
The abbot, monk Chángqīn,
had a written notice.
He sent it around to inform the various courtyards.
Together, they invited the Japanese monk.
He then attended the invitation, entering the Dharma hall to observe the ritual of reverence and chanting.
Along the walls inside the hall,
seventy-two portraits of enlightened ones were arranged in order.
Precious banners and precious pearls,
made of the finest silks of the world,
were displayed and arranged.
Assorted colored felt blankets
were spread extensively on the ground.
Flower lanterns, famous incense, tea, medicine, and food were offered to the enlightened ones.
After dusk,
the elder monks gathered.
One monk ascended the ritual seat.
First, he struck the lìbá.
Next, he explained the origin of the Dharma ritual.
He chanted each donor's name and the colors of their offerings one by one.
He recited the Buddha and Bodhisattva names for the donors.
Next, he respectfully invited the seventy-two enlightened ones, calling each name individually.
After each name was called,
they all chanted, "We sincerely wish for your compassion and pity on us; please descend to this Dharma hall and accept our offerings."
He performed seventy-two standing prostrations.
Only then did he descend from the seat.
Another Dharma master then ascended the seat.
He recited a eulogy to the Buddha
and exhorted and invited the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, saying,
"With one mind, we respectfully invite the Great Master Shìjiāmóuní Fó.
With one mind, we respectfully invite the future Mílè Zūn Fó, who will descend to be born.
The Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha with his twelve great vows,
the Great Saint Wénshū Shīlì Púsà,
the Great Saint Pǔxián Púsà,
the Ten Thousand Bodhisattvas."
Each began with "With one mind, we respectfully invite."
Next, they chanted the text for offering scattered flowers in unison.
There were several tunes.
Next, there was a nun Dharma master,
who also delivered a eulogy, etc.,
exactly like the monk Dharma master.
Next, the monk Dharma master and the various monks
chanted praises in unison.
Then, the lìbá were struck.
They chanted Āmítuó Fó in unison.
Then they paused.
Next, the assembly of nuns praised the monks,
also as before.
They took turns praising the Buddha in this manner
until the ceremony concluded at midnight.
They all left the Dharma hall and dispersed.
The invitation and praise texts
were recorded separately.
On the seventh day,
a donor in the pavilion courtyard
arranged a seven-day monastic vegetarian meal.
The Dharma procedures during the meal
were generally the same as yesterday, but during the incense offering,
for the sounds of offerings in the Dharma hall,
the Biǎotàn Shī did not chant "Everything reverent," etc.
Instead, he only stood as a Biǎotàn.
Another monk struck the mallet to perform.
Other Dharma rituals and food were according to the rules.
On the fourteenth day,
at night, Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
along with dozens of śrāmaṇeras who had traveled far,
received the full precepts at the Báiyù Tán.
On the sixteenth day, attended morning court.
Departed Zhúlín Sì.
Followed the valley eastward for ten *lǐ*.
Then went northeast for ten *lǐ*.
Arrived at Dàhuāyán Sì.
Entered the Kùyuàn and stayed there.
After the vegetarian meal, entered the Nièpányuàn.
Met Xián Zuòzhǔ.
In the Mígāogé Diàn,
he was lecturing on *Móhē Zhǐguān*.
There were over forty monks
seated in rows listening to the lecture.
Then saw Tiāntái Zuòzhǔ Zhìyuǎn Héshang at the lecture assembly,
listening to *Zhǐguān*.
The hall's adornments were exquisite and difficult to describe.
The Zuòzhǔ said,
"The fourth scroll has been completed."
After the lecture, went to Zhìyuǎn Héshang's room to pay respects.
The Héshang offered earnest comfort and inquiry.
Fǎjiān Zuòzhǔ had just arrived from Xījīng.
Wénjiàn Zuòzhǔ had long resided on this mountain.
Together with the over forty people listening to the lecture,
all of them were of the Tiāntái Zōng.
They gathered to express mutual comfort and joy at meeting during the lecture assembly.
Zhìyuǎn Héshang himself spoke, saying,
"Japan's Zuìchéng Sānzàng,
in the twentieth year of Zhēnyuán,
came to Tiāntái to seek the Dharma.
The Prefect of Táizhōu, Lù Gōng,
personally provided paper and scribes
to copy several hundred scrolls
for Chéng Sānzàng.
The Sānzàng obtained the scriptures and returned to his native country."
Then he inquired about the prosperity of Tiāntái in Japan.
I briefly explained the matter of Nányuè Dàshī's birth in Japan.
The assembly was greatly pleased.
Yuǎn Zuòzhǔ was extremely happy to hear about Nányuè Shī's birth in Japan and his propagation of the Dharma.
The monks of the fifteen courts of Dàhuāyán Sì
all regarded Yuǎn Zuòzhǔ as their head monk.
He did not accept alms or benefits.
He ate only one meal a day.
He did not miss the six-time bowing and repentance.
He constantly cultivated the Fǎhuā Sānmèi.
The 'one mind, three contemplations' was at the core of his being.
The elder monks and resident elders in the temple all showed him great respect.
After drinking tea,
I entered the Nièpán Dàochǎng
to pay respects to the Nirvāṇa image.
It depicted him lying on his right side under the twin Sāla trees,
with a stature of sixteen feet.
There was an image of Māyā fainting and falling to the ground,
and the Four Kings, Eightfold Divine Legions, dragons, and gods,
and all the holy multitude,
some raising their hands in sorrowful lament,
others closing their eyes in contemplation.
All the events described in the scriptures
were rendered as images.
Next, I entered Bōrěyuàn
to pay respects to Wénjiàn Zuòzhǔ.
He was of the Tiāntái Zōng and had lectured on *Zhǐguān* several times.
He also painted a portrait of Tiāntái Dàshī for long-term供養 (*gōngyǎng*).
Our conversation and his expressions of comfort and inquiry were very earnest.
I also saw the portrait of Dàhéshang,
who had practiced on this mountain.
He had toured Wǔtái fifty times,
and stayed on the summit of Zhōngtái for three years, never descending in winter or summer.
Consequently, he received the blessings of the Great Sage,
and obtained a large *dàhé* (alms bowl) one foot high
and one foot five inches long.
The large one weighed twenty-five *jīn*,
and the small one ten *jīn*.
They were displayed before the portrait.
The Héshang had once made fifteen thousand monastic robes and given them to fifteen thousand monks.
He offered seventy-five thousand oblations.
He had a portrait made and placed for *gōngyǎng* in a high pavilion.
This Qīngliáng Shān,
on nights in May, is extremely cold.
People usually wear padded jackets.
The trees on the ridges and in the valleys are straight and tall,
without a single crooked or twisted tree. When entering the realm of the Great Sage,
even when seeing the lowest of people,
one dares not harbor any contempt.
If one encounters a donkey or other animal,
one also feels a sense of doubt,
fearing it might be a manifestation of Wénshū.
Everything seen with the eyes
evokes the thought that it is a manifestation of Wénshū.
The land of the sacred spirit
naturally inspires a feeling of reverence in people when they encounter its sights.
On the twenty-eighth day, entered Pínggǔ.
Walked thirty *lǐ* westward.
At *sìshí*, arrived in front of Tíngdiǎn Pǔtōngyuàn.
For the first time, I saw the summit of Zhōngtái.
This is the Qīngliáng Shān, where Wénshūshīlì resides,
the Zhōngtái among the Wǔtái.
I prostrated myself and paid distant respects.
Unbeknownst to me, tears flowed.
Looking afar at the peak of the *tái*,
it was round and high, with no trees visible.
Then I entered Tíngdiǎn Pǔtōngyuàn.
Paid respects to the Wénshū image.
On the west pavilion wall, I saw an inscription that read,
"Língxiān, a great virtuous monk who serves the nation by translating scriptures from Japan.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, fifteenth year of Yuánhé,
arrived at this *lǎnruò*."
At noon, entered the dining hall for the vegetarian meal.
I saw that on the upper monk's seat,
a Wénshū image was placed.
I did not see a seat for Bīntóulú.
I was puzzled and asked the monks.
They replied,
"All the pictures on this mountain are like this."
After the meal, I saw several tens of monks heading south to Nántái.
Suddenly, from a clear sky, it became overcast in a single moment.
Wind and clouds battled, darkening the sky.
Hail and rain fell together.
In the evening, I saw them return.
Their straw hats were broken by the hail,
and they came back drenched.
From the *shēnshí* on the twenty-third of this month, when I first entered the mountain,
until today,
I have walked in the mountain valleys every day.
It took six days to finally reach these Wǔtái.
Departing from Chìshānyuàn on the nineteenth of the second month,
I have traveled all the way here,
a distance of over two thousand three hundred *lǐ*.
Excluding rest days,
I have actually been on the road for forty-four days.
I am ashamed.
My companions have suffered no illness or hardship.
On the twenty-ninth day,
there was a vegetarian meal for a hundred monks in the monastery.
I also attended the invitation.
Also, because Jùjiān, a monk from Guóqīng Sì in Táizhōu, was returning to his temple after touring the *tái*,
I entrusted him with two letters to be sent to Yuánzài Shàngrén.
On the first day of the fifth month, the sky was clear.
I set out to tour the Wǔtái.
From Tíngdiǎn Pǔtōng, I walked about seventeen *lǐ* westward.
Then, crossing a high ridge northward,
I walked fifteen *lǐ*.
Arrived at Zhúlín Sì Duànzhōng.
Still saw several tens of *shāmí* from various prefectures who had come to seek ordination,
waiting for the day at the temple.
After the meal, I toured the temple.
There was a Bānzhōu Dàochǎng.
Fǎzhào Héshang had once
cultivated *niànfó sānmèi* in this hall.
He was bestowed the posthumous title Dàwù Héshang by imperial edict.
It had been almost two years since his passing, and now his portrait was made and placed in the hall.
Also, a portrait of Fótuópōlì
was painted, depicting him arriving at the mountain gate in the first year of Yífèng and seeing an old man.
In the Buddha hall of Huāyányuàn, there was a set of Vajradhātu Maṇḍala.
On the second day,
I entered the upper floor of Zhēnyuán Jìlǜyuàn.
Paid respects to the Maṇḍala of the seventy-two worthy saints and venerables, the meritorious achievements of the nation.
The colored paintings were exquisite.
Next, the Myriad Saints' Ordination Platform was opened for viewing.
It was made purely of white jade stone,
three feet high and octagonal.
The bottom of the platform was filled with fragrant mud.
On the platform was spread an octagonal carpet of five-colored silk threads,
its width and length exactly matching the platform.
The elder who guarded the platform,
whose Dharma name was Língjué,
was one hundred years old,
with seventy-two monastic years.
His appearance and bones were extraordinary.
He was a great virtuous monk who ascended the platform.
He treated guests with earnestness.
He said that in the sixth month of last year, three *sānzàng* from Nālántuó Sì in Central India came to tour Wǔtái,
and saw five-colored clouds,
circular light,
and light that encompassed the body,
before returning to Central India.
This Zhúlín Sì has six courts:
the Lǜyuàn,
Kùyuàn,
Huāyányuàn,
Géyuàn,
and Fódiànyuàn.
The entire temple has about forty monks.
This temple does not belong to Wǔtái.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
there was a vegetarian meal for seven hundred and fifty monks.
All temples jointly hosted it.
It was all provided by the供主 (*gōngzhǔ*) of Língyán Sì in Qízhōu.
In the evening, I happily participated.
On the fourteenth night,
only Zhèng and Xiǎo,
together with several tens of people,
received the full precepts on the White Jade Platform.
On the sixteenth day, morning court.
Departed from Zhúlín Sì and traveled ten lǐ east along the valley.
Then traveled over ten lǐ to the northeast.
Arrived at Dàhuāyán Sì.
Checked into the Kùyuàn to stay.
After the meal, went to the Nièpán Yuàn.
Met the Head Monk Xián.
He was lecturing on Zhǐguān from a high building.
The fourth scroll was nearing its conclusion.
Over thirty monks were listening together.
Then saw the Venerable Zhìyuǎn listening to Zhǐguān below the讲 seat.
The interior and exterior of the hall were adorned with a splendor difficult to describe.
After the lecture, paid respects to the Venerable Zhìyuǎn, the lecturing Head Monk,
and the assembled monks.
The Venerable and others offered sincere comfort and inquiries.
The Head Monk had recently come from Xījīng.
Head Monk Wénjiàn had lived on the mountain for a long time.
He had lectured on the Zhǐguān and Fǎhuā Jīng several times.
All the listeners were disciples of the Venerable Zhìyuǎn.
Perhaps there were also some who came to listen from other places.
The Venerable Zhìyuǎn said,
"In the twentieth year of Zhēnyuán,
I met the Tripitaka Master Zuì Chéng from Japan.
He entered Tiāntái to seek the Dharma.
Lù Gōng, the Prefect of Táizhōu, personally provided paper, ink, and scribes,
who copied several hundred scrolls
for Tripitaka Master Chéng.
The Tripitaka Master also obtained seals and credentials
and then returned to his homeland."
Then I asked about the prosperity of the Tiāntái宗 in Japan.
I roughly explained how the Great Master Nányuè was born in Japan and propagated the Dharma.
The Venerable Zhìyuǎn and the assembly were very pleased.
Dàhuāyán Sì has twelve courtyards,
and the monastic community is very large.
All regard the Venerable Zhìyuǎn as their head monk.
The Venerable does not accept alms or benefits.
He eats only one meal a day.
His precepts and conduct are pure and lofty.
He performs six-session repentance rituals
without missing a single session.
He constantly practices the Fǎhuā Sānmèi,
taking the 'one mind, three contemplations' as his core.
His aspiration transcends the mundane world.
All the elder monks in the various temples throughout the mountain show him reverence.
His profound intention
is to meet the Bodhisattva Pǔxián in this life
and attain the Fǎhuā Sānmèi.
After eating rice porridge,
entered the Nièpán Dàocháng.
Prostrated before the image of the Buddha's Parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha lay on his right side between the twin sāla trees.
The figure was sixteen feet tall.
There was an image of Lady Móyé
fainting and falling to the ground.
The Four Kings, Eightfold Divisions, dragons, spirits, devas, humans,
and all the holy multitude
were depicted either raising hands in sorrowful lament
or closing their eyes in contemplation.
Everything was made according to the scriptural descriptions.
Next, entered the Bōrě Yuàn.
Paid respects to Head Monk Wénjiàn.
Also paid respects to the image of the Great Master Tiāntái.
Head Monk Wénjiàn's joy was boundless.
He then said,
"This temple has established two lecture seats
to widely transmit the Tiāntái teachings.
It is truly a profound response to see a monk from a distant country come here seeking the Tiāntái teachings!"
Also saw the image of the Venerable Dàxié.
He once practiced asceticism on this mountain.
He toured Wǔtái fifty times.
He also stayed on the summit of Zhōngtái.
He did not descend in winter or summer,
staying on the summit for three years.
Consequently, he received empowerment from the Great Sage.
He wore large shoes,
one chi five cùn high.
The larger pair weighed twenty-five jīn,
and the smaller pair weighed ten jīn.
The shoes are currently displayed in front of his image.
The Venerable once made fifteen thousand sets of robes and stoles
and bestowed them upon fifteen thousand monks.
He made seventy-five thousand offerings.
His image is placed in a high pavilion for veneration.
On the seventeenth day, when the thirty articles of the matter concerning the Yánlì-sì had not yet been decided,
they were presented to the Reverend Zhìyuǎn.
He was asked to make a decision and explain.
The Reverend Yuǎn said:
"I have heard it said
that Tiāntái Mountain has already resolved this doubt.
It should not be resolved again."
He refused to comply.
In the evening,
I went with several monks
up to the Púsà-táng-yuàn.
I saw the Reverend Chíniàn.
He was seventy years old,
but looked like he was only about forty.
People said,
"He is old, but his complexion is robust;
this is due to the power of his chanting."
I entered the hall and reverently prostrated before the great Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva statue.
Its countenance was majestic,
exceedingly solemn and dignified.
The statue rode a lion.
It filled a five-bay hall.
The lion's spiritual essence
was vibrantly lifelike,
with the potential for movement.
Moisture seemed to emanate from its mouth.
I gazed at it for a long time,
and it truly seemed to be moving.
The old monk said:
"When this Bodhisattva was first made,
it was created and then it cracked.
It was carved six times,
and it cracked and crumbled six times.
The sculptor was disheartened and said:
'My skill
is known throughout the world,
and all acknowledge its singular excellence.
Throughout my life, I have carved Buddha statues,
and I have never seen one crack or break.
Now, making this statue,
I have fasted and purified myself with utmost sincerity,
employing the peak of my craftsmanship,
desiring to make it an object of reverence for all people,
specifically a source of inspiration.
Yet, having made it six times,
it has crumbled and cracked all six times.
This surely must displease the Great Saint's heart.
If this is truly the case,
I humbly pray,
Great Saint Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
to personally manifest your true form for me,
that I may personally behold your golden countenance,
and then imitate it in carving.'
As soon as he finished his vow,
he opened his eyes and saw
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva riding a golden lion,
appearing before him.
After a long while, it rode on five-colored clouds
and soared away into the sky.
The sculptor, having seen the true form,
was filled with joyful tears and grief.
He then realized that what he had made before was incorrect.
He immediately changed the original design,
altering its length, breadth, and size,
and its facial features.
Taking the manifested form
as his guide, he carved this statue for the seventh time.
It no longer cracked or broke.
Everything was made easy,
and all his wishes were fulfilled.
When that man had finished making this statue
and placed it in this hall,
he shed tears of bright light from his eyes
and then said:
'How wondrous!
What I had never seen before
I now have seen.
May I, through countless kalpas and lives, always be a disciple of Mañjuśrī.'
Having spoken, he passed away.
Thereafter,
this statue frequently emitted light and manifested auspicious signs.
Whenever such phenomena occurred,
they were fully recorded and reported to the emperor.
An imperial edict then bestowed a *jiāshā*,
and the one currently draped over the Bodhisattva's body
is one of them.
Because of this, an imperial envoy annually sent one hundred *jiāshās*
as a symbol of bestowal upon the mountain monks.
Annually, another imperial envoy was specially dispatched to send incense and flowers,
precious canopies,
pearl banners and canopies,
jade pendants,
precious jewels,
seven-gemmed precious crowns,
gold-filigreed incense burners,
large and small bright mirrors,
flower carpets,
white felt blankets,
and precious and artificial flowers and fruits, etc.
These gradually accumulated in great numbers.
They are displayed in the hall,
but there is no end to them.
The rest are all stored in the treasury,
and are kept there to this day.
Furthermore, contributions from various provincial and prefectural officials and private donors
are innumerable each year.
Now, the Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva statues made in the various temples on Wǔtái Mountain
all follow the model of this sacred statue.
However, they only capture one part out of a hundred."
Inside and outside the hall,
seven-gemmed parasols
are suspended above the Bodhisattva's head.
Precious colored flower banners
and wondrous pearl garlands, etc.,
are spread throughout the hall.
The number of jeweled mirrors,
both large and small, is unknown.
Exiting to the north of the hall,
one can see the Northern Terrace and the Eastern Terrace.
Their rounded peaks rise high,
completely devoid of trees.
Short grasses display their colors.
Looking at them from afar,
they present the scenery of autumn in summer.
Returning to the front of the hall,
one can see the Southern Terrace from afar.
It is also without trees.
The terrace peak stands out alone,
connected to the azure sky,
towering transcendently above the other peaks.
The Western Terrace is separated by the Central Terrace
and cannot be seen.
In front of the Púsà-táng,
overlooking a precipice, there is a three-bay pavilion.
Its floor is covered with planks,
and it has high railings on all four sides.
Below the pavilion is a sheer, dangerous cliff thousands of *rèn* deep.
The old monk said:
"In ancient times, the Japanese monk Língxiān Sānzàng
beheld ten thousand Bodhisattvas
in this very pavilion."
After completing the circumambulation and prostration,
I went to the Géyuàn and met the dharma master Xuánliàng.
Since April, he has been lecturing on the *Fǎhuā Jīng* (Lotus Sutra)
and the *Tiāntái Shū* (Commentary on Tiāntái).
The audience numbered over forty people,
all disciples of the Reverend Yuǎn.
In the morning, he lectured on the *Fǎhuā Jīng* in the Géyuàn,
and in the evening, he lectured on *Zhǐguān* (Cessation and Contemplation) in the Nièpán-yuàn.
The congregations of both courtyards
came and went to listen.
Many also came from other courtyards to listen.
The abbot of this temple, Hongjī,
together with the Reverend Yuǎn, deliberated
and invited these two dharma masters
to open these two lecture series.
It can truly be said that the Dàhuáyán-sì on Wǔtái Mountain is a branch of Tiāntái.
I went up to the pavilion with the monks
to worship and accumulate merit.
The adornments inside and outside the pavilion,
all the precious objects,
were similar to those in the Púsà-táng.
I saw the skull bone of a Pratyekabuddha.
Its color was a dull white,
resembling the light stones of our country.
The bone was solid inside.
It was about two *shēng* in size.
It was the bone from above the forehead.
White hairs grew on it,
about five *fēn* long,
as if they had been shaved and grown back.
It was brought by a Western monk during the Zhēngguān era.
There were also Sanskrit-leaf copies of the *Fǎhuā Jīng*,
and Buddha relics,
placed in a lapis lazuli bottle.
The *Fǎhuā* in gold characters
and the *Fǎhuā* in small characters
were extremely exquisite.
In front of the pavilion, there was a pagoda,
two-storied and octagonal,
magnificently adorned with jewels.
An Aśoka pagoda was placed at its base,
buried underground,
not permitted for people to see.
This is one of the eighty-four thousand pagodas built by King Aśoka.
Next, I entered the Shànzhù-géyuàn to rejoice.
There were over fifty Chan monks,
all wearing coarse robes and carrying tin staffs,
who had come from various regions on pilgrimage.
This was an imperially designated 'Nation-Guarding Daochang'.
There were Tiāntái school monks
lecturing on the *Sìfēn Lǜ* (Four-Part Vinaya),
who were also disciples of the Reverend Yuǎn."
On the eighteenth day, [I] attended the invitation of the abbot of Shànzhùgé.
Arriving there, [I found them] in the midst of deliberation.
Still, [I] saw the document brought from Guóqīngsì in Táizhōu.
Previously in Chǔzhōu,
it had been entrusted to the student monk, Venerable Yuánzài,
concerning thirty undecided items sent to Yánlìsì on Tiāntáishān.
Zuòzhǔ Xiū of Guóqīngsì
had already fully resolved them.
Then, [he] requested Táizhōu's official seal.
The Cìshǐ had already affixed the seal.
Zuòzhǔ Jìngwén of Xiūchánsì transcribed it in full
and sent it to Táishān,
to promote the teachings of Tiāntái.
Also, the document sent by Héshàng Wúxíng from Rìběnguó to Tiāntái,
Tiāntái Xiū Zuòwáng had already fully resolved it.
The document requesting the prefectural official seal,
the Cìshǐ of Táizhōu approved it,
and the document granting the official seal
had been transcribed in full and delivered.
On the twentieth day, I began my tour of the terraces.
From Huáyán Sì, I headed west.
I ascended the slope for about seven *lǐ*.
I arrived at Wángzǐ Sì and had tea.
I headed west, ascending the slope for six or seven *lǐ*.
I reached Wánghuā Sì.
Then I continued west, ascending the slope for over ten *lǐ*.
I arrived at Zhōngtái.
On the south side of the terrace,
there is Qiúyǔ Yuàn.
From the院 (yuàn), I ascended for about half a *lǐ*.
I reached the summit of the terrace.
Near the south of the summit,
there are three iron stupas.
They have no tiers, *xianglun*, or other features.
Their form
resembles an inverted bell.
Each is about four arm-spans in circumference.
The central stupa is quadrangular
and about one *zhàng* high.
The ones on either side are round
and both about eight *chǐ* high.
Empress Wǔ Péi
built them to guard Wǔtái.
Wǔ Péi
is Empress Zétiān.
To the north of the iron stupas,
there is a four-bay hall.
Inside are statues of Wénshū Shīlì and Buddhas. From here, one and a half *lǐ* to the north
is the center of the terrace summit.
There is Yùhuā Chí,
about forty *chǐ* square on each side.
It is called Lóng Chí.
On a small island in the center of the pond, there is a small hall.
It houses a statue of Wénshū. People of the time call it Lóngtáng.
The pond water is clear and pure,
about three *chǐ* deep.
From the bank, the sand at the bottom is visible.
It is clean, with no dust or weeds.
The terrace summit is flat,
with a circumference of over a hundred *dìng*.
It rises majestically and singularly,
like a double peak.
The terrace is round and soaring.
From here, one can see the other four terraces: Xītái
and Běitái
are relatively close to Zhōngtái.
Going down from Zhōngtái and then ascending northward
is the southern cliff of Běitái. Also, going down from Zhōngtái and then ascending westward
is the eastern cliff of Xītái.
The three terraces' terrain is closely connected.
Dōngtái and Nántái
are both about fifty *lǐ* from Zhōngtái.
The eastern foot of Zhōngtái,
a long ridge of varying heights,
winds and meanders
for fifty *lǐ* to the south.
The land then connects with the northwestern foot of Nántái.
The northeastern foot of Běitái,
the ridge descends and then ascends again.
A long ridge of varying heights
extends for over forty *lǐ* to the east.
It then connects with the western foot of Dōngtái.
However, the Five Terraces rise conspicuously above all other peaks.
The Five Terraces have a circumference of five hundred *lǐ*.
Outside, there are layers of high peaks,
rising high across valleys,
encircling the Five Terraces, forming a wall-like barrier.
The peaks vary in height,
and the trees are dense and lush.
Only the upper half of the five summits
are devoid of trees.
Zhōngtái,
however, is the center of the four terraces.
Water springs from the ground all over the terrace.
The soft grass grows to over an inch,
thick and dense,
covering the ground.
It bends when stepped on
and rises again when the foot is lifted.
Every step is wet with water,
which is as cold as ice.
Everywhere there are small hollows,
all filled with water.
Throughout the terrace, countless stone stupas are interspersed among the sand and rocks.
Fine, soft grass entwines with moss and spreads.
Although the ground is wet,
there is no muddy brine.
This is because the roots of the moss and soft grass are densely spread,
thus preventing travelers from soiling their shoes and feet.
Exotic flowers of unusual colors
blossom fully across the mountainsides.
From the valleys to the summits,
all four sides are covered with flowers,
like spread brocade.
The fragrance is rich and sweet,
perfuming people's clothes.
People say:
"Though it is May, it is still cold here.
The flowers are not yet in full bloom.
In June and July,
the flowers will bloom even more profusely.
The colors of these flowers
are unlike any seen in the human world."
From the summit of the terrace, to the east,
going down the slope for about half a *lǐ*,
there is Púsà Sì.
In summer, it provides porridge and meals
only for monks and laypeople touring the terraces.
From in front of the iron stupa, I gradually descended westward.
After traveling over ten *lǐ*,
I descended a steep slope for about two *lǐ*.
Then I ascended westward for about half a *lǐ*.
I arrived at Xītái Gōngyǎng Yuàn.
Behind the院 (yuàn), there are three large rock peaks,
precipitous and straight.
The three peaks rise together,
named Xiāng Shān.
In the past, an Indian monk came
and, seeing these three peaks, said,
"I lived in Xi Guó on Xiāng Shān for a long time.
Now that I have come here, I see Xiāng Shān again.
Has it appeared early here?"
From Gōngyǎng Yuàn,
I ascended westward for five or six *lǐ*.
I arrived at the summit of Xītái.
The terrace summit is flat,
with a circumference of about ten *dìng*.
The terrace body is narrow north-south
and wide east-west. Looking from east to west,
the east is narrow, and the west is wide. In the center of the terrace summit,
there is also a Lóng Chí.
Each side is about fifty *chǐ* square.
In the center of the pond,
there is a four-bay Lóngtáng housing a statue of Wénshū.
To the southeast of the pond,
there is one iron stupa from Zétiān.
It is round, without tiers,
about five *chǐ* high
and twenty *chǐ* in circumference.
Moss and soft grass entwine around the rocks.
The stone stupas are unusual.
The flowers and grasses are no different from those on Zhōngtái.
Water springs from the ground,
flowing hidden beneath the grass.
Water collects in hollows.
Three sides are precipitous cliffs,
but the eastern bank slopes gradually down and connects with the base of Zhōngtái.
From the west of the terrace, I descended the slope for five or six *lǐ*.
Near the valley, there is the place where Wénshū and Wéimó debated. Two large rocks face each other, rising high.
One to the south, one to the north,
each about thirty *chǐ* high.
The tops of the rocks are all flat.
Both have large stone seats.
It is said that
this is the place where Wénshū Shīlì Púsà
and Wéimó met and debated.
Between the two seats, on the stone below, there are lion paw prints
pressed into the stone surface,
about an inch deep.
In front of the rocks, there is a six-bay pavilion,
built facing east.
At the south end, a statue of Wénshū is placed,
riding a pair of lions.
At the east end, a statue of Wéimó is placed,
sitting on a quadrangular seat. The old man's hair is white,
his topknot is doubly coiled.
His forehead is pale white,
and it hangs forward
as if wearing a lotus.
He wears a yellow-red robe and a white skirt, and over the robe, he drapes a fur coat.
The fur is mottled, red, white, and black.
Both hands do not enter the fur sleeves. His right knee is bent,
resting on the seat,
and his left knee is raised,
stepping on the seat.
His right elbow is on the low table,
with his palm open and five fingers extended.
His left hand holds a whisk,
with his wrist pressing on his left knee.
His mouth is open, revealing his teeth,
as if in the act of speaking.
Near the front of the seat,
on the west side, there is a Tiānnǚ,
and on the east side, there is a Púsà,
standing and holding a bowl full of rice.
Also, in front of this pavilion,
there is another six-bay pavilion facing it.
People say
that it was built in the image of its manifestation.
Walking about a hundred paces east of the pavilion,
there is Bā Gōngdé Chí.
Water springs from the bottom of a large rock.
I continued my tour until night
and then returned to Gōngyǎng Yuàn to stay.
On the twenty-first, after the fast,
we returned to the Púsà Temple on Zhōngtái to drink tea.
Looking out towards the northeast,
we saw dozens of *mǔ* of land deep in the valley bottom
glistening with a silvery color.
People said,
“This is ice that has been frozen for a thousand years.
Year after year, the snow does not melt,
accumulating into frozen ice.
The valley is deep and shady, overshadowed by the cliffs in front, so sunlight has never reached it.
Therefore, since ancient times,
there has never been a time when the snow melted even a little.”
The ridge in front of the valley
is the eastern foot of Zhōngtái.
From Púsà Temple, we went north along the eastern slope of Zhōngtái,
meandering downhill for about ten *lǐ*.
Then we went uphill for more than ten *lǐ*,
arriving at Běitái.
The summit of the terrace is about six *mǔ* in circumference.
The body of the terrace is round.
At the southern end of the summit there is a Lóngtáng.
Inside the hall is a pond.
Its water is deep and dark,
a clear, deep pool filling the hall.
One part of the hall is divided into three sections.
The middle section is the Lóngwáng Palace.
A statue of the Dragon King is placed above the pond water.
A bridge is built over the pond,
leading to the Dragon King's seat.
This Dragon King is
the king of the five hundred poisonous dragons of Wǔtái.
Each terrace has one hundred poisonous dragons,
all of whom
consider this Dragon King their sovereign.
This Dragon King and his people
were subjugated by Wénshū
and converted, no longer daring to commit evil.
To the left and right of the Dragon Palace,
separated by wooden partition walls,
Wénshū statues are placed.
In front of the Lóngtáng,
there is a Gōngyǎngyuàn.
We saw a monk there
who had not eaten cooked food for three years,
eating only once a day.
He ate earth and then fasted.
He had vowed for three years
not to leave the summit of the terrace.
There are several disciples' quarters.
The front quarters overlook a deep valley.
The terrace cliff is towering
and perhaps a thousand *rèn* deep.
This valley is where Wénshū once manifested a golden bell and a precious tower.
It is now called Zhōnglóugǔ.
The western source of the valley
is the bottom of the eastern slope of Zhōngtái.
To the south of the valley is a high ridge.
The northern slope of the ridge is extremely perilous,
and drops deep down to the valley bottom's thousand-year-old ice.
It lies in the secluded depths, shining brightly.
Then, looking southeast,
we saw the Dàhuáyán Temple.
In the center of the terrace summit,
there is a Tiānzétiě Tǎ,
surrounded by many stone stupas.
Soft grass and moss
cover the ground everywhere.
Every three or four steps,
there are countless small well-like ponds,
named Lóngchí.
Water gushes from the sandy bottom, clear and shallow.
The due north and due east banks are steep and high,
overlooking deep valleys.
The northern valley is named Sònggǔ.
It was where a monk, following Zhìzhě of Tiāntái,
practiced the Fǎhuā Sānmèi
and performed rituals of repentance,
and saw Pǔxián Púsà and the Duōbǎotǎ.
The southern side, though the path is perilous,
has a path that can be climbed.
The northwest bank gradually descends, forming a curtain,
eventually becoming a deep valley.
At the eastern end of the terrace summit there is a high mound
called Luóhàntái.
There are also no trees anywhere on this terrace.
From Luóhàntái,
we descended southeast.
By the roadside, there were many scorched stones covering the ground.
They formed a circular stone wall-like structure,
filled with scorched stones.
This is the place where hell was manifested.
In the past,
the Governor of Dàizhōu,
who had a violent disposition
and did not believe in cause and effect,
did not believe when he heard about hell.
One day, while sightseeing and touring the terraces,
he arrived at this spot.
He was enraged when he saw fierce flames
burning the rocks,
and black smoke rising to the sky.
The burning stones and charcoal glowed intensely
and formed a surrounding corridor.
Hell-guards appeared before him, furious and lamenting.
The Governor, terrified,
sought refuge with the Great Saint Wénshū Shīlì.
The fierce flames immediately extinguished.
Their traces are still visible today.
Scorched stones are piled up to form a wall
about five *zhàng* in circumference,
filled with black stones.
On the twenty-second,
after gruel, we walked along the eastern flank of Běitái, heading northeast, winding downhill.
After walking about twenty *lǐ* along the ridge eastward,
we arrived at the Shàngmǐpǔtōngyuàn.
Inside the hall, we suddenly saw five rays of light
shining directly into the hall.
Suddenly, they disappeared.
Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo, and others
were in the hall with us.
All said
they saw nothing.
We found this most peculiar.
After the fast,
we followed the ridge eastward,
gradually ascending for twenty *lǐ*,
and arrived at Dōngtái.
At the eastern end of the terrace there is a Gōngyǎngyuàn.
We entered the院 to drink tea.
Going uphill south for about two *lǐ*,
we reached the summit of the terrace.
There is a three-room hall
with stone walls,
each side about five *zhàng* long,
and about one *zhàng* high.
Inside the hall is placed a statue of Wénshū Shīlì.
Near the northwest of the hall are three Tiānzétiě Tǎ,
their forms similar to those on the other terraces.
There is no Lóngchí on the summit,
and no water on the ground.
The grass grows somewhat deep.
The circumference of the terrace summit
is about ten *zhàng* on each side.
The body of the terrace is gradually longer from north to south,
and narrow from east to west.
The northern base is about one *lǐ* long.
To the south of the terrace is a ridge,
varying in height and extending for about three *lǐ*.
However, the terrace summit is the highest and most prominent,
and without trees.
From the summit, heading directly east for half a *lǐ*,
on a steep cliff there is a cave
named Nàluóyán Kū.
People say
that in the past, Nàluóyán Fó
practiced there in this cave
and later went west.
The inside of the cave is damp,
with water dripping at the entrance,
which is six *chǐ* wide.
The cave is dark inside,
likely harboring dragons.
In the evening,
we returned to the Gōngyǎngyuàn for the night.
As dusk approached,
the sky suddenly clouded over.
At the bottom of the eastern valley,
white clouds gathered densely,
suddenly red, suddenly white, flying up.
Thunder rumbled
and echoed in the deep valley.
People looked down from the high summit.
Wind, rain, and hail fell together in confusion.
It stopped late at night.
On the 23rd, after the fast, descended from the terrace.
Then arrived at Shàngmǐ Pǔtōngyuàn.
Proceeded directly south down the slope.
After walking about eighteen lǐ, entered a valley.
Then walked three or four lǐ further southeast.
Then walked about one lǐ further west into a valley.
Arrived at Jīngāngkū.
The cave is by the valley side.
The Western monk Fótuóbōlì (Buddhapālita) arrived empty-handed
at the mountain gate.
Wénshū, appearing in human form, did not allow him to enter the mountain.
Instead, Wénshū instructed him to go to the Western regions to retrieve the Fódǐngzūnshèngtuóluóní Sūtra.
The monk then returned to the Western Heavens.
After retrieving the sūtra, he arrived at this mountain.
Wénshū received and guided him.
They entered this cave together.
As soon as Bōlì (Buddhapālita) entered,
the cave entrance sealed itself.
It has not opened to this day.
The cave wall is firm and dense, tinged with yellow. In front of the cave entrance, there is a tall building.
The cave entrance is beneath the building.
People cannot see it.
At the eastern end of the building,
there is a供養yuàn.
Above the building at the cave entrance,
there is a zhuǎnlúnzàng.
It is built hexagonally.
This is seen in the cave record.
Within the cave, there are many holy relics from the Western Heavens. During the time of Wéiwèi Fó,
Xiāngshān Mólì Dàxiān
created three thousand kinds of seven-jeweled musical instruments.
After that Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
Wénshū Shīlì brought them
and placed them in this cave.
During the time of Jūliúqín Fó (Krakucchanda Buddha),
Dōulǜ Tiānwáng (Tuṣita Deva-king) made a bell.
It could hold one hundred and twenty shí.
Those who heard its sound
might attain the four fruits
or the first bhūmi, etc.
After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
Wénshū Shīlì
brought this bell
and placed it in this cave.
During the time of Jiāyè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha),
a silver kōnghóu was made.
It had eighty-four thousand melodies.
Eighty-four thousand melodies,
each curing one affliction.
After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
Wénshū Shīlì
brought this kōnghóu
and stored it in the cave.
The full-body stupa of the second Buddha of the Xīngxiùjié (Bhadrakalpa), with one thousand three hundred levels.
Wénshū Púsà brought this stupa
and stored it in this cave.
Silver paper and gold-inked writings from Zhèndàn Guó,
as well as texts from the hundred billion four continents.
Wénshū Púsà
stored them in this cave.
About a hundred paces up the slope from the cave,
there is Wénshū Táng
and Pǔxián Táng.
This is where Dàchāo Héshàng
saw the golden world.
In the evening,
returned to Dàhuāyángāngwéi Sì.
Was led to Nípán Yuàn and settled in a room beneath the阁.
This was the room of Zuòzhǔ Xuánliàng Shàngrén,
who lectures on the Fǎhuā Jīng.
Because the Zuòzhǔ was lecturing,
he temporarily resided in the 閣yuàn of Yuǎn Héshàng and Zuòzhǔ Wénjiàn.
Tiāntái teachings, records, and documents were all complete.
On the 23rd, began copying Tiāntái documents that were not yet available in Rìběn Guó.
On the 6th day of the 6th month,
an imperial envoy arrived.
In the monastery,
all the monks came out to greet him.
It was the usual custom that every year,
the emperor would send robes, alms bowls, incense, flowers, etc.
The envoy delivered them to the foot of the mountain and distributed them among the twelve great monasteries.
Five hundred fine pèi,
five hundred túns of cotton,
one thousand duāns of kasāya cloth,
dyed blue.
One thousand liǎngs of incense,
one thousand jīn of tea,
one thousand tiáos of hand towels.
Additionally, an imperial decree commanded the provision of alms-meals at the twelve great monasteries.
For seven days, an imperial alms-meal was held at this monastery.
After the meal,
one volume of the Huāyán Jīng was chanted.
In the evening,
the imperial envoy, along with several dozen monks,
ascended Púsà Táng to seek manifestations.
Arrived at Nípán Yuàn.
Prostrated before Yuǎn Héshàng.
On the 8th, the imperial envoy hosted an alms-meal for one thousand monks.
On the 9th, after the meal,
the imperial envoy went to Jīngé Sì.
On the 11th, it was the birthday of the current emperor (Deyang Day).
An imperial decree commanded that in all temples on Wǔtái,
a birthday alms-meal be held.
All temples rang their bells simultaneously.
Five or six of the eldest and most senior monks
rose from their seats to perform the incense ritual.
It was heard that the imperial envoy, after performing the incense ritual at Jīngé Sì, was returning to the capital.
On the 21st, the sky was beautifully clear.
The sky was azure blue,
without a single blemish.
Together, Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo,
and several monks in the monastery
saw a cloud of colored light
in the courtyard in front of the monastery阁.
The light was brilliant and shining.
Its color was exceptionally beautiful,
radiantly flowing through the sky.
It was directly above their heads.
After a long while, it disappeared.
Several dozen monks in the monastery
who did not come out
could not see it.
There was a ascetic monk from Fénzhōu,
who for ten years had been providing offerings to the twelve temples of Wǔtái
and other common aranyakas.
His name was Yìyuán.
He came to deliver this year's offerings
and also saw the auspicious light.
With tears in his eyes, he said,
"Yìyuán has been making this vow for ten years.
Every year, I have sent offerings throughout the mountain without fail.
I have never seen a single phenomenon.
Today, together with the foreign Tripitaka Master,
I have seen the cloud of light.
I truly know that although our birthplaces are in different regions,
we are all graced by the great saint's transformation, as we are all destined.
From now on, let us form a common connection
and forever be among the retinue of Wénshū Shīlì Púsà."
On the 29th,
the copying of the Tiāntái teachings and records was completed.
A catalog was made.
It was presented to Yuǎn Héshàng,
who was asked to inscribe his Dharma name.
On the first day of the seventh month,
I prepared to go to Cháng'ān.
I packed my luggage.
I heard people say,
"From Wǔtái to Cháng'ān,
head southwest,
over two thousand *lǐ*,
and you will reach Cháng'ān."
Before the meal,
I bowed to the venerable old monks
and the two *zuòzhǔ* who lectured on the Tiāntái *Zhǐguān Wénjù*,
as well as the general assembly.
The abbot, the monk Guǎngchū,
offered a simple meal as a send-off.
After the meal, I departed.
The assembly within the monastery sent me off,
reaching beyond the Sānmén.
We parted, wiping tears and holding hands.
I took the Zhúlín road,
passing in front of Zhúlín Sì,
heading southwest.
After crossing a high ridge,
I arrived at Bǎomó Zhènguó Jīngé Sì Jiāngù Púsà Yuàn to stay overnight.
The host monk Yìyuán, who offered universal offerings throughout Wǔtái,
also returned to Fénzhōu.
Today, from Huáyán Sì,
he continued to come and stay in the same monastery.
The monastery monk, while serving tea, said,
“The Japanese monk Rúxiān Sānzàng
once lived in this monastery for two years.
Afterward, he moved to Qīfó Jiàojiè Yuàn and passed away.
That *Sānzàng*
peeled off a piece of his own hand skin, four *cùn* long and three *cùn* wide,
painted a Buddha image on it,
and had a bronze pagoda made to house it.
It is now kept beneath the Jīngé in this temple,
and has been offered to for many years.”
On the second day,
together with Yìyuán, the offering master, and several other monks from the temple,
we opened the Jīngé.
We paid homage to the sacred image of Dàshèng Wénshū Púsà riding a blue-maned lion.
The golden countenance
was so solemn and beautiful as to be incomparable.
We also saw Rúxiān Shèngrén's
hand skin Buddha image and the bronze pagoda.
We also saw the Pìzhīfó's teeth
and the Buddha's corporeal relics (*shèlì*).
Above the *Púsà*'s head hung a canopy of seven treasures.
These were imperial gifts.
The pavilion had nine bays and three stories,
over one hundred *chǐ* high.
The walls, eaves, rafters, and pillars
were painted everywhere.
The interior and exterior were adorned
with all the world's precious and rare objects.
It stood majestically alone above the cedar forest.
White clouds freely descended and drifted,
and the azure layers rose loftily and conspicuously.
Next, we ascended to the second story
to pay homage to the five Buddha images of the Jīngāngdǐng Yújiā.
These were commissioned by the state
and created by Bùkōng Sānzàng,
modeled after the Nàlánpúó Sì in Tiānzhú.
Each Buddha had two attendant *xiéshì*,
all arranged on a wooden platform.
Next, we ascended to the third story
to pay homage to the five golden Buddha images of the Dǐnglúnwáng Yújiā Huì.
Each Buddha had one attendant *Púsà*.
Two *Púsà* made *hézhǎng* gestures
and stood in front of the Buddha, facing south.
The Buddha and *Púsà* mudras and countenances
differed from the images on the second story.
On the inner surface of the plaster walls
were painted *Mántuóluó* of various deities.
The coloring was not yet finished.
These were also commissioned by the state and created by Bùkōng Sānzàng.
After finishing our veneration,
we descended from the pavilion to Pǔxián Dàochǎng.
We saw the Jīngzàng Gé,
which contained over six thousand scrolls of the Great *Sūtra* Collection.
All were written on dark blue paper with gold and silver characters,
and had axes made of white sandalwood, jade, and ivory.
Upon inspecting the prayer dedication,
it stated that Zhèng Dàojué,
a native of Cháng'ān,
on the fourteenth day of the fifth month of Dàlì fourteen,
toured Wǔtái,
personally saw ten thousand great *Púsà* and the golden world.
Thus, he resolved
to transcribe six thousand scrolls of the Great *Sūtra* Collection in gold and silver characters.
There were also painted footprint images with a thousand-spoked wheel design,
and a written statement saying,
"During the Zhēnguān years,
Emperor Tàizōng sent envoys with *jiāshā* to Tiānzhú.
They saw the ancient temple of Āyù Wáng,
where there was a Buddha footprint on a stone,
one *chǐ* eight *cùn* long
and six *cùn* wide.
They made a rubbing of the Buddha footprint
and brought it back to the capital.
It was then reproduced here for placement."
Next, we opened the Chínìan Mántuóluó Dàochǎng
and paid homage to the venerable images.
This was where Bùkōng Sānzàng's disciple Hánguāng,
to ensure the long-lasting prosperity of the Lǐ family,
offered prayers by imperial edict.
The altar for performing rituals was three *zhǒu* in length.
It was made by mixing mud
with white sandalwood sap and applying it.
Whenever the wind blew,
its fragrance was carried far.
There were many bronze ritual implements,
all placed on the altar.
Next, we opened the Pǔxián Táng
and paid homage to the image of Pǔxián Púsà.
Three horses stood abreast,
with a *Púsà* image placed on their backs.
The interior and exterior of the hall were adorned
with colorful paintings and carvings,
too numerous to describe fully.
There were treasure boxes for *sūtra*s made of seven gems,
and Buddhas embroidered with pearls.
Pearls were strung with thread
and embroidered onto silk.
The workmanship was wonderfully exquisite.
Other items
were too numerous to record.
After finishing our homage and viewing,
we returned to the monastery courtyard.
After the meal,
together with the offering master, the *tóutuó* monk Yìyuán, and several others,
we formed a group
and headed toward Nántái.
To the west of Jīngé Sì,
about five *lǐ* from the temple,
is Qīngliáng Sì.
It now administers Nántái.
This Wǔtái Shān
is entirely known as Qīngliáng Shān.
Among the temples built on the mountain,
this temple was the very first,
hence it is called Qīngliáng Sì.
Within the temple is the Qīngliáng Shí.
Led by the *tóutuó*,
we headed towards Nántái.
We did not reach that temple.
Exiting the Sānmén of Jīngé Sì,
we followed the ridge southward.
Climbing an incline for twenty *lǐ*,
we reached the western end of Nántái.
Heading east,
along the southern edge of the plateau,
we walked four or five *lǐ*
to reach the top of the plateau.
There were no trees.
On the southeast side of the plateau
was a Gòngyǎng Yuàn.
From the courtyard, heading north,
climbing an incline for about three hundred paces,
we finally reached the summit of the plateau.
Inside a three-bay hall,
was placed an image of Wénshū Púsà
made of white jade stone,
riding a white jade lion.
Soft grass grew thickly,
and fragrant flowers of *línglíng*
perfumed the entire plateau.
The body of the plateau, to the northwest and southeast,
had long ridges, high and low,
stretching and gradually receding into the distance.
The west and north faces
had steep cliffs overlooking deep valleys.
From the summit, looking north,
the four plateaus were seen in the distance,
distinctly visible before our eyes.
Turning our heads, we surveyed the five rounded and high peaks,
soaring conspicuously above all other peaks.
A thousand peaks and a hundred ridges,
with luxuriant pines and firs,
interspersed beneath the five peaks.
Deep ravines and profound valleys, their bottoms unseen.
Secluded springs and stream waters;
only their flowing sounds were heard.
Strange birds soared above the many peaks,
their wings reaching high,
but those that flew to the top of the plateau were rare.
The area of the five peaks,
for five hundred *lǐ* beyond,
had high peaks arranged on all four sides,
enveloping Wǔtái,
extending for perhaps a thousand *lǐ*.
All their sharp edges
formed a perimeter of heavy enclosures.
Peaks and valleys, layer upon layer,
one knows not how many layers.
And from the east, entering Táishān,
walking through the mountain valleys,
five hundred *lǐ*,
up to the top of craggy cliffs,
down to the bottom of deep valleys.
After traveling for seven days,
one finally reaches the land of Wǔtái Shān.
For the other three directions and four cardinal points,
one also traverses mountains and valleys,
before finally arriving at Wǔtái.
It is truly known that Wǔtái Shān
is the center of myriad peaks.
Five hundred venomous dragons lurk in the mountains,
breathing out wind and clouds.
During the four seasons and eight solar terms, thunder ceases,
and hail frequently descends.
The sky quickly clears,
but travelers do not see the spectacle of eternal light.
Whenever it is clear,
observing Wǔtái,
it appears as a light yellow color.
On the peak, a speck of cloud suddenly appears,
and in a short while,
heavy clouds cover the entire mountain.
Those who enter this mountain
naturally develop a mind of equality.
Alms are offered in the mountains,
without distinction of monastics or laypeople, men or women, old or young.
They are equally provided for,
without regard for their status or size.
Everyone is regarded as Mañjuśrī.
In the past,
a grand alms-giving ceremony was held at Dàhuáyán Sì.
All ordinary men and women,
beggars and the poor,
came to receive offerings.
The patrons grumbled, saying,
"We traveled far over mountains and slopes
to make offerings here,
intending only to support the monastics in the mountain.
But now these common beggars and their ilk
all come to eat.
This is not our original intention.
If we were to support these beggars,
we could just hold the ceremony in our hometown.
Why bother coming all the way to this mountain?"
The monastics advised them to give food to everyone.
Among the beggars,
there was a pregnant woman.
After sitting and receiving her portion of food,
she asked for a portion for the child in her womb.
The patrons cursed her and refused.
The pregnant woman insisted repeatedly, saying,
"Though my child in the womb
has not yet been born,
it is still a person.
Why not give it food?"
The patrons said,
"You are foolish.
Although the child in your belly is counted,
if it doesn't come out and ask for food,
who will eat it?"
The woman replied,
"If the child in my belly doesn't get food,
then I also should not eat."
She then stood up and walked out of the dining hall.
As soon as she exited the hall door,
she transformed into Mañjuśrī,
radiating brilliant light
that filled the hall with dazzling splendor.
With a visage like pure white jade, riding a golden-maned lion,
surrounded by myriad bodhisattvas,
she ascended into the sky and departed.
The assembly,
thousands of people,
all rushed out at once,
and, bewildered, fell to the ground.
They cried out in repentance and apology,
weeping tears like rain.
At once, they chanted "Dàshèng Wénshū Shīlì!"
until their voices were hoarse and throats parched,
but they never received a glance in return.
She vanished as if a fleeting image.
The assembly
found their food tasteless.
Each made a vow that from this day forward,
when making offerings and holding alms-giving ceremonies,
without distinction of monastic or lay, male or female, old or young, noble or humble, rich or poor,
all must be equally provided for.
The custom of the mountain
thus established this principle of equality.
Other spiritual transformations
frequently manifested many auspicious signs,
known throughout the world.
Now, during the alms-giving ceremony in the dining hall,
men are in one row,
women in another.
Some hold infants,
and the infants also receive a share.
Children are in one row,
novice monks in another,
great monks in one row,
and nuns in another.
All sit on benches to receive offerings.
The patrons distribute food equally.
If someone asks for an unusually large portion,
they are not blamed.
Regardless of how much,
it is given to them.
It is often cold in the mountains.
In May, June, and July,
throughout the five hundred *li* of Wǔtái,
exotic flowers
bloom like brocade.
The mountains and valleys are filled with fragrance,
and the air is perfumed.
On each peak, there are many onions and leeks growing.
In the past,
Emperor Xiàowén
resided here at Wǔtái for leisure.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva transformed into a monastic
and asked the emperor for a piece of land the size of a meditation mat.
The emperor granted it.
When the monastic received permission,
he spread out a meditation mat,
which covered five hundred *li* of land. The emperor was astonished, saying,
"I only granted land for a meditation mat!
This monastic spread out a meditation mat
that covers all of Wǔtái! How extraordinary!
I do not wish to reside with this person."
So he scattered onions and leeks
all over Wǔtái
and left the mountain.
The monastic, following behind,
scattered *línglíngxiāng* seeds
over the onions and leeks to remove their strong odor.
Today, on every peak,
onions and leeks grow everywhere, but no strong odor is smelled.
*Línglíngxiāng* grows abundantly all over the peaks,
and its fragrance permeates the air.
It is said
that Wǔtái, for five hundred *li*,
is the land of that one meditation mat.
Now, on the Southern Peak,
together with several dozens of *tóutuó* practitioners and others,
we collectively sought a manifestation of the Great Sage.
But we saw nothing by night,
so we returned to the monastery to rest.
In the early night,
across a valley to the east of the peak,
in the sky above a ridge,
a holy lamp was seen.
Everyone saw it together and bowed.
The light of the lamp
was initially as large as a bowl,
then gradually grew as large as a small house.
The assembly, with utmost sincerity,
loudly chanted the Great Sage's name.
Then another lamp
appeared near the valley.
It was also initially like a hat,
then gradually grew larger.
The two lamps were separated by
about ten *zhàng* when viewed from afar, their flames burning brightly,
until midnight,
when they faded and disappeared.
After three days of alms-giving,
together with the *tóutuó* practitioners and others,
we set out as a group.
The *tóutuó* said,
"I will accompany you all the way to Fénzhōu
and be your host on the way."
From the peak of the *tái*, heading south,
after descending about seventeen *li*,
in a valley,
there was a ruined, abandoned temple building
named Qīfó Jiàoyuàn.
The plaque above the gate read:
"The eighth *dì* transcends the *āraṇya*."
The Japanese monk Língxiān once lived here and passed away.
The Bóhǎi monk Zhēnsù
wrote a poem mourning Reverend Língxiān,
which was inscribed on a board
and nailed to the wall.
It reads as follows:
A Poem Mourning the Venerable Virtuous Monk Língxiān, Imperial Patron of Japan
By the Monk Zhēnsù of Bóhǎi Kingdom
He who roused me was called Yìng Gōng.
Gōng served and learned.
He followed his master to Fúsāng.
From small, he became great.
He stood firm and was seen in Zīlín.
I too was destined to descend among things.
Carrying my satchel, I came to follow the hegemonic enterprise.
In the eighth year of Yuánhé,
the scene of late autumn,
we met in a guesthouse.
A single word brought us together in accord.
We conversed from the heart.
From humble origins, could Zhōu Yán Xiǎozi be anything but worthy?
Not long after,
he already headed towards Gēyuán.
The wagtail arrived.
Foot pain, then heartache.
This Xiān Dàshī
was my Yìng Gōng's master.
The profound principle was first revealed to the Primordial.
In the second year of Chángqìng,
he entered a chamber on Wǔtái.
He always endured his body as a vessel of green and purple decay,
and would not let his heart listen to the cries of white apes.
In the fifth year of Chángqìng,
the Great King of Rìběn bestowed a hundred gold pieces from afar.
It arrived in Cháng'ān.
Xiǎozi then received the golden letter
and sent it to Tiěqín.
Xiān Dàshī received the gold.
He entrusted one hundred thousand relics,
two new sutras,
and five imperial edicts, etc.,
to Xiǎozi,
requesting him to go to Rìběn
to express gratitude for the national favor.
Xiǎozi readily agreed.
How could a promise be deterred by ten thousand miles of heavy waves, so that Zhōng Wúwài’s destined encounter for a grand future might be fulfilled?
On the day of return,
he again attached a hundred gold pieces.
On the seventh day of the fourth month of the second year of Dàhé,
I returned to Língjìng Sì.
I sought out Xiān Dàshī.
Many days had passed since he left.
My blood congealed,
my heart ached.
Then I sailed across the four-layered sea,
regarding death as a homecoming.
Five companions and their luggage followed continuously.
In the blink of an eye, this was due to Yìng Gōng’s original friendship.
I believe in beginning and ending again.
May spirits and mortals all know.
Only the sound of the stream's gurgling remains for a thousand autumns.
Still, the melancholy of clouds and pines extends for ten thousand miles.
On the fourth month, the mallows fell, like the ear that hears a road poem longing for the capital.
Not disturbed by worldly thoughts, tears flowed spontaneously.
Emotion, because of the dharma eye, entered the hidden spring.
If tomorrow one asks the guest of the blue waves, they will surely say that the lost shoes and white feet have returned.
Written on the fourteenth day of the fourth month of the second year of Dàhé
in a small grotto.
Seven Buddha statues are placed facing the grotto entrance.
There is a hall.
On the south side of the hall,
there is a small hermitage.
Below the hall are two rooms.
Both are dilapidated.
The courtyard is overgrown with weeds and deserted.
Formerly, in front of this grotto,
the Seven Buddhas appeared.
Going south for about three *lǐ*,
one reaches Dàlì Língjìng Sì.
I asked an old monk about the whereabouts of Língxiān Sānzàng's tomb.
He said,
Língxiān Sānzàng
had previously spent much time in Tiěqín Lánruò
and Qīfó Jiàojiè Yuàn.
Later he came to this temple
and lived in the Yùshì Yuàn.
He died from poisoning by medicine given by someone.
His disciples buried him,
but the location is unknown.
On both sides of the temple's three gates,
there are statues of Shèng Jīngāng Púsà.
Formerly,
in the three jiedushi prefectures of Tàiyuán and Yōuzhèng,
they all manifested a vajra body.
They said,
"I am Lóuzhì Fó.
I transform my body into a spirit
to protect the Buddha Dharma.
Buried in the ground,
accumulating years, turning into dust,
I reappear."
Now they are inside the three gates of Táishān Língjìng Sì.
The jiedushi of the three prefectures were surprised and amazed.
They fully recorded their appearances
and each sent envoys to search.
There are two vajras
on the left and right sides of the temple gate.
Their appearance and physique
are identical to the body colors seen in their original prefectures.
Their envoys returned to their respective regions to report this.
Consequently, envoys from the three prefectures came
specifically to restore the old statues.
There were many spiritual manifestations,
as detailed in the stele inscription,
which is copied separately.
Near the corner by the three gates
is a mountain elm tree.
Its roots are hollow, forming a grotto
called Shèng Zhōng Kū.
From time to time, a bell rings inside the grotto.
When the sound is emitted,
the mountain peaks vibrate.
Legend says
this is a manifestation of the Great Saint Wénshū.
It is popularly called Shèng Zhōng Gǔ.
Due east of the temple,
about ten *lǐ* from the temple,
there is a high peak
called Bǎoshí Shān.
Inside the grotto, there are many small stones.
Each stone displays a circular light, an aura encompassing the body, and five-colored clouds.
This is also caused by the manifestation of a saint.
After the four-day fast,
I headed southwest, entered a valley, and crossed a ridge.
After traveling fifteen *lǐ*,
I arrived at Dàlì Fǎhuā Sì.
Multi-storied pavilions are built on steep cliffs.
The cliff faces on all four sides
are entirely adorned with flower towers and treasure halls.
Depending on the terrain's height and lowliness, halls and residences are arranged like teeth on a comb.
Sutras, images, and treasures
are exquisitely beautiful beyond words.
I toured the various courtyards,
then entered Fǎhuā Yuàn.
I saw the portrait of Shéndào Héshang.
This Reverend, when alive,
practiced according to the Tiāntái Fǎhuā Sānmèi method.
He continuously recited the Fǎhuā Jīng
and did not leave the courtyard for forty-three years.
He achieved purification of the six sense organs.
He passed away several years ago.
His portrait and the Fǎhuā Jīng he held,
as well as the Sānmèi practice method,
and the large chair where he sat when he attained samadhi,
are all still present today.
From Fǎhuā Sì,
fifteen *lǐ* northwest,
is Fóguāng Sì.
After the five-day fast,
I traveled two *lǐ* southwest
and stayed at Shàngfáng Pǔtōng Yuàn.
I set off early on the sixth day,
traveling about five *lǐ* southwest.
Looking south from afar, I saw a high ridge.
The summit of the cliff was rugged and steep.
In its center was a large hole,
through which the empty space on the other side could be seen.
This hole, seen from afar,
was about the size of a bamboo hat.
This was where Emperor Xiàowén
shot an arrow through.
Traveling about seven *lǐ* southwest,
I reached Sīyáng Lǐng.
Formerly, in the first year of Yífèng,
a Brahman monk from Western Heaven,
Fótuópōlì,
arrived here.
He shed tears and bowed from afar to Táishān.
This moved the Great Saint to transform into an old man
and arrange for him to return to Tiānzhú to retrieve the Buddha's crown.
Today, a treasure banner is erected.
Inscribed on the banner are the Buddha's Crown Dhāraṇī and a preface narrating Fótuópōlì's encounter with the old man.
From Sīyáng Lǐng,
traveling thirteen *lǐ* southwest,
one reaches Dàxián Lǐng.
In Pǔtōng Yuàn,
the road passes over the ridge.
At the top of the ridge is a multi-layered mountain gate tower.
This is the southern mountain gate of Wǔtái.
After the fast,
traveling about five *lǐ* southwest,
one reaches Wǔtái Xiàn, under the jurisdiction of Dàizhōu.
Traveling thirty *lǐ* southwest,
crossing Hútú Hé,
one reaches Jiàn'ān Sì to stay overnight.
After the fast on the eighth day,
traveling thirty *lǐ* southwest,
one reaches Qīyán Sì in Xīnzhōu Dìngxiāng Xiàn to stay overnight.
I set off early on the ninth day,
traveling about thirty *lǐ* southwest,
and stopped for a break at Húcūn Pǔtōng Yuàn.
I set off early on the tenth day,
traveling about thirty *lǐ*,
and stopped for a break at Sòngcūn Pǔtōng Yuàn.

At the mountain gate, there was a small temple

As for the origin of obtaining the *shèlì*:
One night, the monk who recited the Sūtra was in his room,

Three beams of light came and shone,
filling the room with brightness
and illuminating the entire temple.
Following the source of the light,

emerging from under the cliff.
Every night it illuminated his room and the temple.
After several days, the monk

He dug the ground more than one *zhàng* deep

In a blue *liúlí* bottle were seven *shèlì*.
In a white *liúlí* bottle
were five *shèlì*.
In a golden bottle

He carried them and placed them in the Buddha hall for veneration.
From Dàyuánchéng and all the villages,

We entered Chūnmíng Mén.
We stayed overnight at the Xīchányuàn of Dàxīngshàn Sì.
On the twenty-third day, after the meal,
we went to the Zuǒjiē Gōngdé Xúnyuàn.
We met Zhīxúnyāyá Jiāncháschìyùshǐ,
whose surname was Zhào and given name Liàn.
We presented our petition,
requesting to reside temporarily in various temples within the city to seek teachers.
The petition text is as follows:
“Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén,
and his disciples, monks Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
and lay practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn,
all with official documents from Qīngzhōu, state:
The above-mentioned Yuánrén and others,
in the third year of Kāichéng,
came with the tribute envoys of our country to seek and visit Buddhist teachings.
In the third month of this year,
they requested official documents from Qīngzhōu
to enter Wǔtái Shān
to pay homage to the holy sites.
They then arrived here,
intending to study the sacred Dharma.
We humbly request
to reside temporarily in temples within the city
to seek teachers and listen to their teachings.
The foregoing is respectfully submitted.
We await your decision.”
The attached petition is as above.
Respectfully submitted.
Kāichéng, fifth year, eighth month, twenty-third day. Petition from Yuánrén, Japanese monk seeking the Dharma.
Zhīxún Shìyù
dispatched one patrol officer
to lead the monks
to be housed in Zīshèng Sì.
On the twenty-fourth day, at *chén* time,
the Xúnyuàn Yāyá
drafted a document dispatching a patrol officer,
ordering him to meet the Gōngdéshǐ.
The Zuǒjiē Gōngdéshǐ Hùjūn Zhōngwèi Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Zhī Nèishěngshì Shàngjiāngjūn Qiú Shìliáng,
enfeoffed with three thousand households.
The monks, accompanied by the patrol officer and attendant,
went north from the temple.
They passed four wards and entered Wàngxiān Mén.
Next, they entered Xuánhuà Mén.
They further passed the Nèishě Shǐ Mén
and Zǒngjiānyuàn.
They entered one more gate
and arrived at the southern gate of the Shǐ Yámén.
Inside the gate was the Zuǒ Shéncè Bùmǎ Mén.
Having passed a total of six gates,
they arrived at the Shǐ Yámén desk to present the petition,
requesting a decision.
After detailed questioning about their background,
another petition was drafted,
which contained the relevant facts,
as follows:
“Japanese monk Yuánrén,
and his disciples, monks Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
and lay practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn.
The above-mentioned Yuánrén and others,
in the fourth month of the third year of Kāichéng,
traveled by boat across the sea
with the tribute envoys of their country.
They arrived
on the second day of the seventh month
at Báihúzhèn in Hǎilíng Xiàn, Yángzhōu.
In the eighth month, they arrived in Yángzhōu
and resided temporarily at Kāiyuán Sì.
They stayed through one winter.
In the second month of the fourth year of Kāichéng,
they left Yángzhōu
and arrived in Chǔzhōu.
They resided temporarily at Kāiyuán Sì.
By the seventh month,
they arrived at Chìshānyuàn in Wéndēng Xiàn, Dēngzhōu, and stayed through one winter.
By the second month of this year,
they left Dēngzhōu
and arrived in Qīngzhōu in the third month.
