They temporarily resided at Lóngxīng Sì.
Ten days later,
they obtained official documents from Jíedùshǐ Shòu Shàngshū.
On the first day of the fifth month,
they arrived at Wǔtái Shān
to tour and pay homage to the holy sites.
On the first day of the seventh month,
they came from Wǔtái Shān.
Today, the twentieth day of the third month,
they arrived in the city.
They now request
to temporarily reside in temples within the city
to seek teachers and listen to their teachings,
and then return to their home country.
The foregoing is respectfully submitted.
We await your decision.”
The attached petition is as above.
Respectfully submitted.
Kāichéng, fifth year, eighth month, twenty-fourth day. Petition from Yuánrén, Japanese monk seeking the Dharma.
Because the Kāifǔ was not present,
the petition could not be submitted.
Officer Hé Pànguān at the desk delivered it.
They were housed in Nèi Hùguó Tiānwáng Sì.
The temple was north of the Zuǒ Shéncè Jūn Qiúchǎng.
The temple was separated from the Great Inner Palace by a wall,
which was the northeast corner of the inner wall of the imperial city.
Two or seven monks were permanently stationed there to chant prayers.
The monks circled and greeted the guests.
On the twenty-fifth day, after the meal,
an envoy from the Shǐyuàn summoned the monks.
They followed the envoy into the Shǐ Yámén.
They received a document from the Gōngdéshǐ stating,
“Temporarily reside at Zīshèng Sì.
Ordered that the Gāngwéi provide supplies.”
Zhīxún Shìyù
then, according to the envoy's document, forwarded the order to Zīshèng Sì.
A patrol officer was immediately dispatched
to escort them to the temple.
They were temporarily housed in the west pavilion of the treasury.
On the twenty-sixth day, it rained.
In the evening,
the Gāngwéi arranged rooms and courtyards
and housed them in Jìngtǔ Yuàn.
The abbot of the *yuàn* was monk Shī Ān.
He had a devout heart.
Upon seeing the visiting monks,
he offered sincere comfort and inquiries.
He often asked the various monks
about those who held prayers and understood the Dharma.
He had not yet found a definite answer.
On the fifth day of the ninth month,
at night, he focused his thoughts on Píshāmén
and vowed to seek a guide to the Dharma.
It was heard
that Lǐ Déyù, the Jíedùshǐ of Yángzhōu,
received an imperial edict to enter the capital.
On the third day of the ninth month,
he entered the palace to assume the position of Zǎixiàng.
On the sixth day, there was an early morning imperial audience.
The monastery's monk, Huáiqìng,
whose occupation was chanting sūtras,
brought five relics of the Buddha
and asked us to bow to them.
He said:
"If you wish to practice esoteric dharma,
I know of someone in the city who is skilled in the Great Dharma:
Rùn Heshang of Qīnglóng Sì.
He is skilled only in the Garbhadhātu (Tāicáng)
and has mastered one particular practice.
Everyone in the city considers him highly skilled.
Although there are monks from the Western Regions in that temple,
they do not understand much of the language.
Their chanting practice
is not widely understood.
Wénwù Shélí of Dàxīngshàn Sì
understands the Vajradhātu (Jīngāngjiè).
He is considered highly skilled in the city.
Yìzhēn Heshang of Qīnglóng Sì understands both sections.
Dàxīngshàn Sì has Yuánzhèng Heshang,
who deeply understands the Vajradhātu.
He understands both the principles and the practices.
Although there is Nántuó Sānzàng from the Western Regions in that temple,
he does not understand much Táng speech.
Dà'ān Guósì has Yuánjiǎn Shélí,
who is skilled in the Vajradhātu,
and also understands Siddhaṃ and painting,
and can write Sanskrit characters.
Fǎquán Heshang of Xuánfǎ Sì
deeply understands the three sections of the Great Dharma.
The new emperor has built a new temple
in Xuānyáng Fāng.
Its temple name has not yet been bestowed.
It was built by Empress Dowager for Yuánhé Shàng.
The present emperor and Empress Dowager
separately issued an imperial edict for its new construction.
An imperial edict was sent to the various temples in the city
to select over fifty monks
to be assigned to this temple."
On the seventh day, at mealtime,
Zhào Liàn, the supervisor of the Left Street Bureau of Merit and a patrol commandant,
came to this temple
and selected seven monks.
From the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month
to the tenth day of the ninth month,
it rained incessantly.
On the fourteenth day, I composed a letter
to the attendant and censor who supervises the patrols.
It reads as follows:
"Late autumn is gradually becoming cold.
I humbly presume
that Your Excellency's esteemed body is in perfect health.
I, Yuánrén, have received your grace.
Limited by official duties as a guest,
I have been unable to call upon you.
My sincerity and earnestness
are difficult to express.
Yuánrén previously troubled you greatly
due to a small matter.
Having just obtained a room in the courtyard,
I wished to visit and offer my thanks.
However, due to several tens of days of overcast and rainy weather,
I have not been able to fulfill my wish.
I am deeply apprehensive.
I humbly request
that you do not blame me.
A visit is imminent,
and my eagerness only increases.
I respectfully send my disciple, the monk Wéizhèng,
to present this letter of greeting.
I will not elaborate further. Respectfully submitted."
The fourteenth day of the ninth month of Kāichéng fifth year. Submitted by Yuánrén, the monk seeking dharma from Japan.
To the attendant and censor who supervises the patrols.
The attendant and censor's reply is in a separate document.
Later, the attendant and censor sent a message saying:
"How are things since your recent arrival as a guest?
There are no communal meals in this temple.
The food may not be as it should be.
Heshang, please write a letter and bring it.
I will present it to the governor-general
to arrange for your placement in a temple with communal meals."
On the eighteenth day,
I wrote a letter
and presented it to the attendant and censor.
Yuánrén, the monk seeking dharma from Japan.
"I, Yuánrén,
humbly received your gracious instruction the other day,
and was specially granted comfort and security.
My humble feelings are filled with boundless joy and gratitude.
However, Yuánrén and others,
upon our recent arrival, have already received the benevolent arrangements of the emissary's office,
and have been temporarily placed in this temple.
We are deeply grateful and fortunate.
We have no further wishes.
If I were to request a move to a temple with communal meals,
I humbly fear disturbing the high official.
I now request to reside at Zīshèng Sì.
I wish to travel to various temples
to seek teachers and listen to teachings,
and to pursue dharma as I wish.
At night, I will return to my original temple.
I humbly beg Your Excellency's grace and arrangement,
and especially request permission.
I have respectfully stated the above.
I humbly request your disposition."
A note accompanying this letter states the above.
Respectfully noted.
The eighteenth day of the ninth month of Kāichéng fifth year. Note from Yuánrén, the monk seeking dharma from Japan.
The attendant and censor sent a message saying:
"Let Heshang's wishes be followed.
If there is anything else you need, please let me know.
I will make sure Heshang is comfortable."
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month,
I sent Wéizhèng
together with Huáiqìng Shélí
to Qīnglóng Sì
to meet the dharma teachers.
In the East Pagoda Courtyard
was Yìzhēn Heshang,
who understood the Garbhadhātu.
Xíng Shélí from Japan studied dharma here.
There was also Fǎrùn Heshang,
who understood the Vajradhātu.
He was seventy-three years old
and frail from wind-stroke and old age.
On the sixteenth day, I sent someone to Dàxīngshàn Sì
to select a dharma teacher.
In the Translation Institute was Yuánzhèng Āshélí,
who understood the Vajradhātu.
He had abundant chanting and textual materials.
Nántuó Sānzàng from India did not understand much Táng speech.
Wénwù Shélí was not as good as Zhèng Āshélí.
On the seventeenth day, I sent a letter of greeting to Zhèng Āshélí,
and also requested to borrow the practice methods of chanting.
"I have long admired your excellent conduct,
but have not had the opportunity to meet you.
My admiration
is difficult to express in words.
Yesterday, I was honored by your inquiry,
which greatly comforted my humble self.
Early winter is gradually becoming cold.
I humbly presume
that Your Reverence's spiritual body is in perfect health.
I, Yuánrén,
have traveled far from my homeland
to seek Buddhist teachings.
Having arrived in the city,
I have not yet been able to serve you.
I humbly hear
that Your Reverence's virtue is lofty and your teaching profound,
that you thoroughly understand the dharma treasury
and expound the true teachings.
Although I, Yuánrén,
have not yet personally met you,
I greatly admire your virtuous conduct.
I humbly submit
that due to official guest duties, I have not been able to make a dedicated visit.
My earnest longing has accumulated in vain.
I have not yet seen your esteemed face,
and my eagerness only increases.
I respectfully send my disciple, the monk Wéizhèng,
to present this letter on my behalf.
I will not elaborate further. Respectfully submitted."
The seventeenth day of the tenth month of Kāichéng fifth year. Submitted by Yuánrén, the monk from Japan.
To Zhèng Heshang of Xīngshàn Sì.
At Chìshān Sì,
I dreamed that I bought a scale.
The person selling the scale said:
"This is a scale that weighs the light and heavy of the three-thousand great thousand worlds."
Hearing this, I was extraordinarily joyful.
I borrowed the practice methods of chanting
and began copying them on the eighteenth day.
On the twenty-ninth day,
I went to Dàxīngshàn Sì
and entered the Imperial Translation Institute.
I met Yuánzhèng Heshang
and began to receive the Great Dharma of the Vajradhātu.
I entered the consecrated maṇḍala for the abhiseka (guàndǐng).
I bowed to all the great maṇḍalas.
I offered offerings
and received the abhiseka.
Also, on the wall of the Translation Hall,
there were paintings of Jīngāngzhì Heshang and Bùkōng Sānzàng.
To the south of the Translation Hall
is the relic stūpa of Dàbiànzhèng Guǎngzhì Bùkōng Heshang.
Jīngāngzhì and Bùkōng, the two Sānzàngs,
had previously translated sūtras in this institute.
On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month of Kāichéng fifth year,
I dreamed at night of painting a Vajradhātu maṇḍala.
Upon arriving in my homeland,
the Great Master unfolded the maṇḍala
and was extremely joyful.
I intended to bow to the Great Master,
but the Great Master said:
"I dare not receive your bow.
I will now bow to you."
I joyfully and diligently painted the maṇḍala.
On the third day of the eleventh month, snow fell.
On the thirteenth day, snow fell.
The 26th day was the Winter Solstice festival.
The monks offered congratulations, saying:
"We humbly wish
that the Hóshàng may long abide in the world
and widely benefit sentient beings."
Junior monks and Shāmí
spoke to the senior monks.
This was entirely in accordance with the ceremonial regulations.
The Shāmí, facing the monks,
knelt with their right knee on the ground,
and recited words of congratulation for the festival.
When eating gruel,
wontons and fruits were served.
On the 8th day of the 12th month,
by imperial edict, all monasteries performed incense offerings and held vegetarian feasts.
At this monastery,
Prime Minister Lǐ Déyù and the imperial envoy performed the incense offering.
This was the death anniversary of Emperor Xuánzōng of the Dàlì era.
All expenses were covered by government funds
for the vegetarian feast.
At the Dàochǎng within this monastery, Dàdé Zhīxuán Fǎshī, who discussed the three teachings, gave an appreciative address.
On the 22nd day, Wáng Huì of Yǒngchāng Fāng was ordered
to begin painting four copies of the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala.
On the 25th day, the new year began.
The assembled monks ascended the hall
and ate gruel, wontons, and various fruits.
While the monks were eating gruel,
the Gāngwéi and Diǎnzùo
(Jísuì) presented the accounts of various expenditures in money and goods from the monastery's estates, transactions, and guests over the past year.
These were read aloud before the assembly.
On the 1st day of the 1st month of Kāichéng 6th year,
monks and laypeople exchanged New Year greetings at the monastery.
On the 3rd day, food was offered to the monks.
On the 4th day, it was a national day of mourning.
By imperial edict, an incense offering was performed at the Jiànfú Sì in honor of the late emperor.
One thousand monks were invited.
On the 6th day, it was the Lìchūn festival.
Húbǐng (sesame cakes) were bestowed.
Húbǐng were served during the monastery's gruel time.
The same was true in lay households.
Furthermore, by another imperial edict, a Dàjiāngjūn of the Zuǒ Jīnwú Wèi was appointed.
This was an imperial relative,
the current emperor's maternal uncle.
Originally poor,
last year he traveled around the wards and monasteries,
carrying baskets of chrysanthemums, etc., for sale.
Now, newly favored by imperial grace,
he was made Dàjiāngjūn of the Jīnwú.
He entered the palace to receive the appointment.
When he came out, he was escorted by twenty pairs of golden-armored guards leading horses.
Fifty or sixty mounted generals followed.
They cleared the way with staffs.
About a hundred infantry guards escorted the retinue.
The infantry were all dressed in brocade.
They wore brocade hats and robes.
The Dàjiāngjūn himself
wore court attire, cap, and boots,
all embroidered with patterns of birds guarding auspicious grasses.
He was appointed
after his posting in Nánjùn
as Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng Fǔ.
On the 7th day, the Son of Heaven visited Tàiqīng Gōng for a vegetarian feast.
On the 8th day, at dawn,
he left the city
and proceeded to the Nánjùn altar.
The altar was in front of Míngdé Mén.
The various guards and the left and right armies,
numbering two hundred thousand, followed.
Countless
wondrous and unusual things occurred.
On the 9th day, at the fifth watch,
the Nánjùn ceremony was completed.
He returned to the city at dawn.
He proceeded to Dānfèng Lóu
and changed the era name.
Kāichéng 6th year was changed
to Huìchāng 1st year.
An imperial edict was also issued to the seven monasteries of the left and right streets
to open public lectures.
In four places on the left street:
At this Zīshèng Sì,
Dàdé Hǎi'àn Fǎshī, who had been granted purple robes from Yúnhuā Sì, was ordered to lecture on the Huāyán Jīng.
At Bǎoshòu Sì,
Sēnglù Tǐxū Fǎshī of the left street, who discussed the three teachings, had been granted purple robes, and guided imperial carriages, was ordered to lecture on the Fǎhuā Jīng.
At Pútí Sì,
Gōngfèng Dàdé Qígāo Fǎshī from Zhāofú Sì, who discussed the three teachings, was ordered to lecture on the Nièpán Jīng.
At Jǐnggōng Sì,
Guāngyǐng Fǎshī was ordered to lecture.
In three places on the right street:

At Huìchāng Sì, Gōngfèng Dàdé Wénxù Fǎshī, who discussed the three teachings, had been granted purple robes, guided imperial carriages, and recorded imperial activities, was ordered to lecture on the Fǎhuā Jīng.
Among the public lecturers in the city,
this Fǎshī was considered the foremost.
The names of the Fǎshī lecturing at Huìrì Sì and Chóngfú Sì were not obtained.
An imperial edict was also issued to open lectures on Daoist teachings.
On the left street, Fèi, the Jǔlìng of Tàiqīng Gōng Gōngfèng, who had been newly summoned from Jiànnán Dào by imperial edict,
was ordered to lecture at Xuánzhēn Guàn
on Nánhuá and other sūtras.
In one place on the left street,
the name was not obtained.
All were ordered to lecture by imperial edict.
Lectures had been abolished since Dàhé 9th year.
The present emperor newly reinstated them.
They began on the 15th day of the 1st month
and ceased on the 15th day of the 2nd month.
On the 8th day of the 2nd month, the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala paintings were completed.
An imperial edict also ordered Jìngshuāng Fǎshī of Zhāngjìng Sì to spread the Pure Land practice of Amitābha recitation at various monasteries.
From the 23rd to the 25th day,
at this Zīshèng Sì,
the practice of念fó (Buddha recitation) was transmitted.
He also toured various monasteries,
spending three days at each monastery.
This monthly circuit continued without interruption.
Furthermore, at Dàzhuāngyán Sì,
an exhibition of the Śākyamuni Buddha's tooth relic was opened.
From the 8th day of the 3rd month
to the 15th day,
the Jiànfú Sì opened an exhibition of the Buddha's tooth relic.
Lántián Xiàn also held one from the 8th to the 15th day.
Unlimited tea and food were provided.
Monks and laypeople from all directions came to eat.
Sēnglù Tǐxū Fǎshī of the left street
presided over the assembly.
Various monasteries gathered, each setting forth precious offerings.
A hundred kinds of musical entertainments and food,
rare and exquisite fruits and flowers,
and all kinds of fragrant decorations were prepared
to offer to the Buddha's tooth.
The offerings and displays under the corridors of the pavilion
were immeasurable.
The Buddha's tooth was placed in the pavilion.
The Dàdé of the city
were all on the upper floor
rejoicing and praising.
The entire city came to prostrate and make offerings.
Some offered one hundred shí of polished rice and twenty shí of millet.
Some offered unlimited sustenance for heads and feet.
Some offered unlimited money for miscellaneous expenses.
Some offered unlimited thin pancakes.
Some offered unlimited provisions for the Dàdé and venerated elders of various monasteries.
In this way, each [person] made vows and gave donations
to adorn the Buddha's tooth assembly.
Towards the Buddha's tooth pavilion,
money was scattered like rain.
Monks seeking the Dharma,
on the 10th day,
went there to rejoice.
They ascended the Buddha's tooth pavilion
and personally saw the Buddha's tooth.
They revered and prostrated before it.
They also entered the Fānjīng Yuàn
and saw the image of Yìjìng Sāncáng.
On the wall was written "Sāncáng touches the crown."
At Xīngfú Sì on Sōngshù Jiē West,
the Buddha's tooth offering was also opened
from the 8th to the 15th of the 2nd month.
Chóngshèng Sì
also opened a Buddha's tooth offering.
There were four Buddha's teeth in total in the city.
One Buddha's tooth at Chóngshèng Sì
was brought from heaven
by Nèzhā Tàizǐ
and given to Xuānlǜshī of Zhōngnán Shān.
One Buddha's tooth at Dàzhuāngyán Sì
was brought from Tiānzhú inside a leg of meat.
The protector deity Jiāpíluó Shénjiàng brought it.
One was brought by Fǎjiè Hóshàng
from Yútián Guó.
One was brought from Tǔbō.
This has been transmitted since ancient times.
Now, these four Buddha's teeth
were offered at four monasteries in the city.
On the 13th day of the 2nd month,
the great Vajradhātu Dharma was received.
Offerings were made to the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala, and the Dharma transmission anointing was received.
With five bottles of water,
the crown of the head was anointed, and the twelve celestial beings were offered to until night.
Every event was auspicious.
They also ascended the pagoda of Cí'ēn Sì.
On the 15th day, Xīngtáng Sì established an anointing Dàochǎng for the nation.
From the 15th day
to the 8th day of the 4th month,
those with karmic connections came
to form connections through anointing.
On the 25th day of the 3rd month,
they went to Chóngshèng Sì
to revere the Śākyamuni Buddha's tooth assembly.
Many people said
that the Hóshàng of Zhōngnán Shān,
accompanying Vīśramaṇa's crown prince,
obtained this Buddha's tooth.
Nèzhā Tàizǐ
brought it from heaven
and gave it to the Hóshàng.
It is now placed in this monastery for offerings.
On the 1st day of the 4th month,
Dàxīngshàn Sì's Fānjīng Yuàn
opened an anointing Dàochǎng for the nation,
continuing until the 23rd day.
On the fourth day, went to Qīnglóng Sì.
Entered the East Pagoda Courtyard.
Carefully inquired about and saw various Mandalas.
On the seventh day, went to Dàxìngshàn Sì.
Entered the Guàndǐng Dàochǎng to participate in the joyous occasion.
And ascended the Dàshèng Wénshū Gé.
On the ninth day, Kāifǔ welcomed the stele.
Praising Kāifǔ’s merits and achievements,
And his virtuous governance.
From Dà’ānguó Sì,
Entered Wàngxiān Mén.
It was erected to the left of Shéncè Jūnlǐ.
The inscription read:
“Qióu Gōng Jì Gōngdé Zhèng Zhī Bēi” (Stele Commemorating Qióu Gōng’s Merits and Virtuous Governance).
The welcoming of the stele by the army and horses, and the various preparations,
Were innumerable.
The present emperor
Watched from Wàngxiān Lóu.
On the thirteenth day, summoned the painter Wáng Huì
To discuss the payment for painting the Tái Zàng scrolls.
On the fifteenth day, after the vegetarian meal,
Slept and dreamed that an old monk from this temple brought forty bolts of silk, saying:
“There is a patron
Who knows that the Reverend
Intends to make the Tái Zàng image,
Therefore, this donation has been sent.”
In the room, there were about ten lay people
Who together rejoiced, saying:
“The Reverend should make the Tái Zàng Mandala soon.
Money and goods are abundant, with no place to store them.” Received the items.
Also dreamed that a monk brought a letter, saying:
“Coming from Wǔtái Shān,
Residing as a Dhuta at the North Terrace,
I send this letter to inquire after the Japanese Reverend.”
Immediately opened the letter and read it.
The initial note said:
“Though we have not met in person since your birth,
We met once before on Wǔtái.
I convey my full greetings.
I send a white silk belt and a small knife.”
Both were old and excellent.
Received the items.
Held them with joy.
In the evening,
Doctor Wáng Huì came.
The payment for painting the scrolls was settled,
Fifty strings of cash,
To make five sets of scrolls.
On the twenty-eighth day, began painting the Tái Zàng scrolls.
Early summer is gradually getting hot.
Respectfully,
May the Reverend’s health be blessed with myriad good fortunes.
I, Yuánrén, have been released from
Being detained for copying documents.
Unable to frequently present myself in person,
I feel deeply ashamed.
I will come specially in a day or two
To pay my respects, though it is not yet settled,
My longing only increases.
I respectfully send my disciple, the monk Wéixiǎo,
To present my respectful greetings.
Not further expressed. Respectfully,
Huìchāng Yuánnián, fourth month, [date]. Respectfully presented by Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma from Japan.
To Reverend Zhēn of Qīnglóng Sì.
Three bolts of silk.
These items, though light and few,
Are respectfully offered as a token of support.
Yuánrén has been a traveler for several years,
And is poor in means.
Though the time for respectfully meeting is near,
There are no offerings to present.
These humble items mentioned above
Respectfully express my profound intention.
I humbly hope you will accept them.
Please do not despise their lightness or scarcity.
Not further expressed. Respectfully,
Huìchāng Yuánnián, fourth month, [date]. Respectfully presented by Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma.
To Reverend Zhēn of Qīnglóng Sì.
The newly translated scriptures from Xìngshàn Sì,
Recitation methods, etc.,
Were copied on the twenty-second day of the fourth month.
The Reverend said:
“My understanding of the great Vajra Realm Dharma
Has been entirely transmitted.
Its Dharma gates have all been copied.
If there is anything still lacking,
Seek it elsewhere.”
To Reverend Yuánzhèng, a total of twenty-five liǎng of gold were given, both before and after.
Beyond this, there were no limits to the amount.
Ten strings of cash.
These, though humble,
Respectfully express my profound sincerity.
I humbly hope you will accept them.
Yuánrén has come from afar for the Dharma,
And is delighted to meet the Reverend and seek to learn the great Tái Zàng Dharma.
I humbly request your compassion and special bestowal of instruction.
I humbly wish for the widespread propagation of the Buddha Dharma,
Benefiting sentient beings.
Unable to express my utmost reverence and respect,
I respectfully present this petition. Respectfully,
Huìchāng Yuánnián, fourth month, twenty-eighth day. Respectfully presented by Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma from Japan.
To Reverend Zhēn of Qīnglóng Sì.
On the twenty-eighth day,
Began painting the Tái Zàng scrolls.
On the thirtieth day at dusk,
Painted the Vajra Realm Nine Assemblies Mandala.
The payment for the work was discussed
And settled at sixty wén, excluding the painting silk. Reverend Zhēn instructed lay people to assist with an additional forty-six chi of silk,
Which was granted as painting silk.
On the first day of the fifth month,
Sent the attendant Dīng Xióngwàn to express gratitude.
Yesterday,
I humbly received your kind instruction.
Wishing for all matters to be accomplished,
My joy knows no bounds.
I deeply thank the Reverend for instructing and bestowing forty-six chi of silk.
To be used for painting virtuous merits, your compassionate connection is exceptionally profound.
This is entirely due to Yuánrén.
My gratitude is boundless.
The summer night has arrived.
May the Reverend’s health be blessed with myriad good fortunes.
I, Yuánrén, having received release, am currently prevented by a small matter from personally presenting my thanks.
My fear and shame are deeply felt.
I will come specially to the courtyard in a few days to offer my thanks in person, though it is not yet settled,
My longing only increases.
Unable to express my profound gratitude, shame, and joy,
I respectfully send Dīng Xióngwàn
To present this petition.
Not further expressed. Respectfully,
Huìchāng Yuánnián, fifth month, first day. Respectfully presented by Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma.
To Reverend Zhēn of Qīnglóng Sì.
On the first day of the fifth month,
An imperial edict ordered the opening of lectures on Buddhism in the ten temples of the two districts,
And lectures on Daoism in the two monasteries.
In this temple, the Great Virtue Sībiāo Fǎshī, a court-appointed lecturer, lectured on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Yuánjìng Fǎshī of Qīnglóng Sì
Lectured on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra at Pútí Sì.
Other details cannot be fully written.
On the third day, began painting five sets of Vajra Realm Nine Assemblies Mandala scrolls.
The payment was six thousand wén, excluding the painting silk.
This was the payment for the painting.
On this day, at Qīnglóng Sì,
Offerings were made.
Then, at the imperially established Guàndǐng Dàochǎng for one’s birth year,
Received the consecration and cast flowers.
Began receiving the great Dharma of the Tái Zàng Vairocanā Sūtra,
As well as the great Susiddhi Dharma.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month,
Ate ripe melons.
On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
The present emperor’s birthday.
Vegetarian meals were served in the palace.
Great Virtues and Daoists from the two districts gathered for discussions on scriptures.
Four pairs debated.
Two Daoists were granted purple robes.
The Great Virtues of the Buddhist school
Were generally not allowed to wear them.
The Tripiṭaka Master Bǎoyuè from Southern India entered the palace to meet the emperor.
From his bosom, he pulled out a memorial and presented it, requesting to return to his homeland.
He did not consult Kāifǔ beforehand, which angered him.
On the fifth day, he was detained by the army.
Because he committed the crime of unauthorized departure, three of Bǎoyuè’s disciples
Each received seven strokes.
The interpreter monk received ten strokes.
The Tripiṭaka Master
Was not beaten,
And was not allowed to return to his homeland.
On the seventh day of the eighth month,
For the purpose of returning to his homeland,
A petition was drafted and submitted to the Zīshèng Sì.
Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma from Japan,
His disciple, the monk Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo,
And attendant Dīng Xióngwàn.
We, Yuánrén and others,
On the twenty-third day of the eighth month last year,
Came from Wǔtái Shān
To the city.
Humbly receiving the benevolence of Kāifǔ,
We were allowed to temporarily reside at Zīshèng Sì.
Now we intend to return to our homeland.
We dare not act unilaterally.
We respectfully state the above.
We humbly await your disposition.
This memorial is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
Huìchāng Yuánnián, eighth month, [date]. Respectfully submitted by Yuánrén, a monk seeking Dharma from Japan.
On the first day of the ninth month,
An imperial edict ordered all temples in the two districts
To open popular lectures.
On the seventh day, heard that three disciples of the Japanese monk Huì’è
Arrived at Wǔtái Shān.
Their master had vowed
To seek offerings from monks in all directions before returning to his homeland.
He left two disciples
To reside on Tái Shān.
On the twenty-third day, a heavy snow fell
For one day and one night.
Trees were broken and collapsed.
On the first day of the eleventh month.
The Winter Solstice festival.
A comet appeared.
A few days later,
it gradually grew larger.
The Emperor (Guānjiā) ordered all monasteries to recite sūtras.
On the third day of the twelfth month,
moved to live in the West Courtyard.
On the fourth day, the moon and the Great Bear Star (Dàbó Xīng)
traveled close together.
On the eighth day, was the National Commemoration Day (Guójì).
The monastery held an official vegetarian feast.
Various monasteries in the city offered baths.
The comet gradually disappeared.
On the first day of the first month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year,
every household erected bamboo poles and hung banners,
praying for longevity in the new year.
Various monasteries held popular lectures (sújiǎng).
On the first day of the second month,
an imperial edict promoted Qiú Kāifǔ (仇開府)
to be Commissioner of Imperial Armies (Guānjūnrúngshǐ),
thereby giving him command over all military affairs in the realm.
On the seventeenth day,
was the Cold Food Festival (Hánshí Jié).
One day before and one day after,
a total of three days' holiday.
Every household visited graves.
On the nineteenth day, was the Pure Brightness Festival (Qīngmíng Jié).
On the twenty-ninth day, at Xuánfǎ Sì (玄法寺), from Ācháolí (阿闍梨) Fǎquán (法全),
I first received the Great Dharma of the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala (Tāicáng Dàfǎ).
Also, at Dà'ān Guósì (大安國寺), from Ācháolí (阿闍梨) Yuánjiǎn (元簡),
I re-examined and decided on the Siddhāṃ chapter.
On the third day of the third month,
Chancellor Lǐ (Lǐ Zǎixiàng) presented a memorial regarding regulations for monks and nuns.
An imperial edict was issued, ordering all unnamed monks
who were outside protection not to keep child novices (shāmí).
On the eighth day, at Jiànfú Sì (薦福寺), it was heard that a Buddha tooth offering was being made.
I went to the monastery to participate joyfully in the offering.
At Xīngfú Sì (興福寺) west of the street,
a Buddha tooth assembly was opened.
A circulated notice was sent to Xīngshàn (興善), Qīnglóng (青龍), Zīshèng (資聖) and other three monasteries:
Foreign monks and Saṃghatrāyas (Sānzàng), etc.
“Regarding the instruction from the Military Guest Department:
The aforementioned foreign monks
are all to be protected and kept.
They are not to be expelled.
It is necessary to circulate this notice.
All are expected to act in accordance with this instruction and report back.”
In accordance with the document, this notice was circulated.
Notice dated the fifth day of the third month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year.
Yāyá Zhīxún (押衙知巡) Hé Gōngzhēn (何公貞).
On the eleventh day,
I went to Xīngfú Sì (興福寺) to venerate the Buddha tooth for one night.
On the twelfth day in the evening, due to the patron of Mount Táishān (Táishān) Yīyuán (義圓) returning to the mountain,
I sent offerings for 150 monks.
Yuánrén (圓仁), a monk seeking dharma from Japan,
and his disciples Wéizhèng (惟正),
Wéixiǎo (惟曉),
and practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn (丁雄萬),
respectfully send offerings for 150 monks on Qīngliáng Shān (清凉山).
The intention of Yuánrén (圓仁) and others in making this offering
is that they may succeed in seeking the Dharma,
cross the sea without difficulty,
reach their destination safely,
and greatly benefit all sentient beings.
In every kalpa and every life,
may they always be attendants of the Great Saint Mañjuśrī (Wénshū),
benefiting the ten directions
and all sentient beings in the Dharma realm,
so that they may all partake of this blessing.
Respectfully submitted.
On the twelfth day of the third month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year.
Respectfully submitted by Yuánrén (圓仁), a monk seeking dharma from Japan, and others.
Uighur (Huíhú) troops entered Tang territory and invaded.
They are now in Qínfǔ (秦府).
The state has mobilized military forces from six jiedushi (jiédùshǐ) commands
and dispatched them to the Uighur (Huíhú) border.
There are several hundred Uighurs (Huíhú) in the capital city.
By imperial edict, they are all to be beheaded.
The same rule applies to those in other prefectures.
Circulated notice to Zīshèng Sì (資聖寺):
“Japanese monk Yuánrén (圓仁),
and his disciples Wéizhèng (惟正)
and Wéixiǎo (惟曉),
and practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn (丁雄萬), etc.
Regarding the dispatch order received from the Imperial Envoy:
It orders the expulsion of foreign monks
who are outside protection from the monastery.
However, regarding Yuánrén (圓仁) and others,
we dare not presumptuously expel them.
We have received an instruction from the Military Guest Department
not to expel them.
They are to be retained as before.
In accordance with the document, this notice is circulated.
The monastery is expected to act in accordance with the envoy's instruction.”
Notice dated the tenth day of the third month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year.
Yāyá Zhīxún (押衙知巡) Hé Gōngzhēn (何公貞).
It is now said that
Uighur (Huíhú) troops
have entered and are occupying the city of Qínfǔ (秦fǔ).
The Jiedushi (Jiédùshǐ) has fled.
The newly appointed Jiedushi (Jiédùshǐ) on the way dares not enter.
The Sūtra Master (Zuòzhǔ) Fǎquán (法全) of Xuánfǎ Sì (玄法寺),
who understands the Great Dharma of the Three Sections,
bestowed three volumes of the Great Ritual for the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala (Tāicáng Dàguǐyí),
along with three volumes of separate deity rituals (bié zūnfǎ),
and hand seals for the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala (Tāicáng Shǒuqì),
to be widely propagated in distant lands.
I am sending a letter of gratitude and an exhibition.
My fervent desire to meet you has been difficult to realize in summer. I respectfully pray
that the Sūtra Master's (Zuòzhǔ) spiritual body is in excellent health.
Yuánrén (圓仁) has received your grace,
but due to a minor ailment,
he is unable to come for the exhibition.
He feels deeply remorseful.
Thank you,
Sūtra Master (Zuòzhǔ), for mercifully bestowing six volumes of Dharma teachings
for widespread propagation.
I am overcome with gratitude and shame.
I shall propagate them in distant lands
to repay your Dharma grace.
However, I have no offerings yet,
which causes me great anxiety.
In a day or two,
I will come to your courtyard myself
to express my gratitude in person, but in the meantime,
my eagerness only grows.
I respectfully dispatch a junior monk to present this letter.
I do not declare all. Respectfully, this letter.
On the [blank] day of the fourth month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year.
Letter from Yuánrén (圓仁), a monk seeking dharma from Japan.
To Sūtra Master (Zuòzhǔ) Fǎquán (Fǎquán).
On the twenty-third day of the fourth month,
the Emperor was on the imperial tower to confer an honorary title.
Troops and horses from various departments
lined up in front of the tower.
Civil officials, Buddhist monks, and Daoist priests stood in their ranks.
The Chancellor (Zǎixiàng) presented the honorary title.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict ordered popular lectures (sújiǎng) to be held.
Five venues in each of the two districts (liǎngjiē).
On the twenty-fifth day, Yuánzài (圓載), a student monk, and his attendant Rénjì (仁濟) arrived.
I then received a detailed letter from Upāsaka (Shàngrén) Zài (載), dated the eighteenth day of the twelfth month of Huìchāng (會昌) first year, stating:
The Japanese Ambassador to Tang China (Rìběn Rùtáng Dàshǐ Xiànggōng)
arrived in the capital of his home country. The Senior Clerk (Zhǎngpànguān) who died was named Dé Yīzhōu Jiè (得伊豫介),
the Recorder (Lùshì) was named Dé Zuǒshǎoshǐ (得左少史),
and the Clerk Gāo (Gāo Lùshì) was the Grand Administrator (Dàzǎi Diǎn).
Emperor Chúnhé (Chúnhé Huángdì)
passed away in the seventh month of last year.
The second ship drifted to the land of naked people (Luǒrén Guó).
The ship was wrecked,
and all personnel and goods were damaged.
By chance, about thirty people survived.
They broke up the large ship
to build a small boat,
and managed to reach their home country.
Also, Liú Shènyán (劉慎言), a Silla (Xīnluó) interpreter from Chǔzhōu (楚州),
sent a letter via Rénjì (仁濟) on the first day of the second month of this year, stating:
“The tribute envoy has been sent.
The helmsmen and sailors
returned to your country in the autumn of the year before last.
Ācháolí (Ācháolí) Xuánjì (玄濟)
attached a letter
and twenty-four small taels of gold dust,
which are now at my humble abode.
Reverend Huì'è (Huì'è Héshàng) arrived at Chǔzhōu (楚州) by ship.
He has already toured Wǔtái Shān (五臺山).
He plans to return to his homeland this spring.
Shènyán (慎言) has already arranged
for people and a ship.
As for Reverend È (È Héshàng), he temporarily stayed in Tiāntái (天台) last autumn.
In winter, I received a letter stating
that he planned to catch the ship of Lǐ Líndé (李隣德) Sìláng (四郎)
and return to his country via Míngzhōu (明州).
All of Reverend È's (È Héshàng) money, clothes, and disciples
are in Chǔzhōu (楚州).
Also, since people and a ship are already prepared, I cannot but invite him.”
From this, Upāsaka (Shàngrén) Zài's (載) detailed message was sent:
Monk Xuánjì (玄濟)
brought twenty-four small taels of gold,
along with letters from various people, etc.,
and entrusted them to Táo Shí'èr Bù (陶十二部) to return to Tang.
These items are now at Liú Shènyán's (劉慎言) residence.
On the twenty-fifth day, an official document inquired
about the professional skills of foreign monks.
Circulated notice to the Yánghuà Group (Yánghuà Tuán):
“To all monasteries in this group
where there are foreign monks, etc.:
Regarding the official document inquiring about
which country they came from,
the month and year of their arrival in the city,
their current monastery,
their age,
and what professional skills they possess,
a detailed list of names must be submitted.
It is necessary to circulate this notice to the group.
You are urged to promptly prepare a report and submit it.
There must be no delay.”
Notice dated the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of Huìchāng (會昌) second year.
Yāyá Zhīxún (押衙知巡) Hé
Zīshèng Sì's Japanese monks Yuánrén's disciples, monks Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo.
A notice was served to investigate:
"From which country do you come?
And what year and month did you arrive in the capital?
Also, in which temple do you reside?
And how old are you?
What skills and professions do you possess?"
Regarding Yuánrén and others:
"To copy incomplete Sūtras and commentaries
for transmission to our native country,
we came in the seventh month of the third year of Kāichéng
with the Japanese tributary envoys.
We arrived in Yángzhōu.
On the twenty-third day of the eighth month of the fifth year of Kāichéng,
we arrived in the capital.
We presented an envoy's牒 (dié)
and were temporarily allowed to reside in Zīshèng Sì to study.
We have respectfully provided the information as above.
Respectfully submitted."
"The attached statement is as above."
"Respectfully submitted."
The twenty-sixth day of the fifth month of the second year of Huìchāng. Respectfully submitted by Japanese monk Yuánrén and others.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, we began
to relearn Siddhaṃ
from Tiānzhú Sānzàng Bǎoyuè at Qīnglóng Sì.
We received the correct pronunciation directly from his mouth.
On the twenty-ninth day, there was an Imperial Edict
suspending the twenty Monks of Great Virtue from each of the Two Streets who served in the Inner Court.
On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
on the current Emperor's Déyáng Day,
an imperial decree ordered a vegetarian feast within the palace.
Monks of Great Virtue from the Two Streets debated with Daoist priests
before the Emperor.
Two Daoist priests were granted purple robes,
but the Buddhist monks were not permitted to wear purple.
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month,
the retained student monk's attendant, Rénjì, returned to Tiāntái.
Wéizhèng was dispatched to accompany him to Chǔzhōu
to retrieve letters from his native country.
On the night of the sixteenth day of the eighth month, there was a lunar eclipse.
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month,
Wéizhèng returned from Chǔzhōu
to the Upper Capital.
He obtained two letters from the great country,
one letter from Léngyán Yuàn,
and one letter from the esteemed Gāo.
Four knives.
He was supposed to deliver twenty-four small liǎng of gold in a pot,
but the Chǔzhōu interpreter Liú Shènyán
had already spent it all by the end of the previous month and received nothing.
He came empty-handed.
The interpreter reported,
"According to the order of Āchāryá Yuánzài,
it has already been spent."
The sealed letter box had already been opened.
On the ninth day of the tenth month, an Imperial Edict was issued,
stating that all monks and nuns in the realm who could perform fire rituals,
ritual purification, spells,
breath control,
desertion from the army,
had whip marks on their bodies,
or practiced various bird-script crafts,
or had committed lewd acts,
raised wives,
or did not cultivate monastic precepts,
were all to be compelled to return to lay life.
If monks or nuns
possessed money, goods, grain, land, or estates,
they were to be confiscated by the government.
If they cherished their wealth
and willingly returned to lay life,
they would also be allowed to return to lay life.
They would be incorporated into the corvée labor of the Two Taxes.
The Imperial Edict text is separate.
The Commissioners of Merits from the Two Streets in the capital posted notices to various temples,
forbidding monks and nuns from leaving
and keeping the temple gates closed.
Monk Xuánxuán
submitted a memorial stating he would personally forge sword-wheels
and lead troops to attack the Huíhú Kingdom.
An Imperial Edict ordered that monk to try forging sword-wheels,
but he failed.
Also, according to the memorial presented by Chancellor Lǐ Shēn,
this provision was initiated because
monk Xuánxuán
was deceiving and controlling the wealth of monks and nuns.
According to the Imperial Edict and the memorial, the entire realm, including the Secretariats of various prefectures, issued directives.
In the capital, General Qíū Jūnróng resisted the Imperial Edict
and was unwilling to enforce the memorial's provisions.
Because the Imperial Edict's intention was not to permit it,
he was tentatively allowed to request a temporary suspension for one hundred days.
Notices were posted to various temples
to prevent monks and nuns from leaving the temples.
The Commissioner of Merits of the Left Street reported,
"According to the Imperial Edict and the memorial,
among monks and nuns,
excluding those who are already old and infirm
and those with precise monastic discipline,
those who cherished their wealth
and willingly returned to lay life numbered 1,232 (nuns and monks combined)."
The Commissioner of Merits of the Right Street reported,
"According to the Imperial Edict and the memorial,
among monks and nuns,
excluding those who are already old and infirm
and those with precise monastic discipline,
those who cherished their wealth and willingly returned to lay life (monks and nuns combined)
numbered 2,259."
An Imperial Edict was issued: "The Commissioner of Merits of the Right Street reported, according to the Imperial Edict and memorial of the seventh
and sixteenth days of the tenth month of last year,
regarding monks and nuns ordered to return to lay life,
those who, out of love for their wealth, willingly returned to lay life
shall each be entrusted to their native prefecture
and registered as two-tax households.
In the future, in all circuits,
if such cases arise,
they shall all be handled according to this precedent.
Regarding the slaves and maidservants they possessed,
monks are allowed to keep one male slave,
and nuns are allowed to keep two maidservants.
The rest shall be returned to their original families.
If they have no family, the government shall sell them.
Their remaining assets, apart from their robes and begging bowls, shall be confiscated
pending further Imperial Edict.
If the slaves and maidservants retained by monks and nuns
possess martial arts
or are skilled in various medicines or arts,
they shall all not be allowed to be retained.
It is forbidden to shave heads or privately ordain.
If there are any violations,
the monastic administrators
shall report them to the authorities.
As for other assets, money, etc.,
each Commissioner of Merits shall personally memorialize and report."
The first day of the first month of the third year of Huìchāng, cyclical year Guǐhài.
On the seventeenth day,
the Commissioner of Merits posted notices to various temples:
monks and nuns included in the memorial's provisions
were all ordered to return to lay life.
In this Zīshèng Sì, 37 people.
On the morning of the eighteenth day,
the return to lay life was completed. On the Left Street, a total of
1,232 monks and nuns returned to lay life.
On the Right Street, a total of
2,259 monks and nuns returned to lay life.
On the twenty-seventh day,
the General had a notice
summoning foreign monks from temples along the streets.
On the morning of the twenty-eighth day, they entered the army barracks.
Five people, including Tiānzhú Sānzàng Bǎoyuè from Qīnglóng Sì,
one person, Tiānzhú Sānzàng Nántuó from Xīngshàn Sì,
one monk from the Kingdom of Siha (Shīzi) from Cí'ēn Sì,
three Japanese monks from Zīshèng Sì,
Sīxī monks from various temples, etc.
There were also monks from the Kingdom of Kucha (Gūcí),
whose names are not recorded.
In total, 21 people
gathered at the Left Shéncè Army.
They drank tea in the General's headquarters
and later met the General.
The General personally consoled and comforted them.
On that day, they all returned to their respective temples.
On the twenty-ninth day, a Sīxī merchant arrived from Chǔzhōu.
He brought one letter from the Chǔzhōu interpreter Liú Shènyán
and one letter from Āchāryá Shùnchāng.
On the first day of the second month,
an envoy's牒 (dié) stated:
"Monks and nuns who have already returned to lay life
are strictly forbidden from entering temples
or stopping there.
Also, monks and nuns from outside the capital
are not permitted to reside in the capital or enter garrisons."
On the twenty-fifth day of the second month,
the Princess who married a barbarian entered the capital.
All officials and three thousand soldiers and horses
went outside the city
to welcome her through Tōnghuà Mén and into the inner palace for an audience.
An Imperial Edict ordered her to be housed in the Southern Inner Court.
This was Princess Dàhé.
The Dàhé Emperor
had married her to the Huíhú King
to make peace with the Huíhú Kingdom.
Now, because that king had passed away,
and rebellions had broken out,
the Princess fled back to her native country.
The Huíhú people who came with the Princess
were all forbidden from entering the city.
The Huíhú Prince who accompanied the Princess
was killed by the Princess herself en route.
In mid-fourth month,
an Imperial Edict was issued:
"Today, all Manichaean teachers in the realm are to be killed. Their heads are to be shaved, and they are to be dressed in monastic robes, made to resemble Buddhist monks, and then killed."
The Manichaean teachers
were revered by the Huíhú.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month,
an envoy's notice was posted to investigate the origins of foreign monks in various temples.
A notice from the巡院 (xúnyuàn) was posted to the Pútítuán:
"All foreign monks, etc., in various temples..."
This dispatch from the Imperial Envoy requires your
investigation: Where did you come from?
When did you arrive in the city?
Also, what are the years and months you have resided in the temple?
And how old are you?
What skills or professions do you practice?
Each must be fully detailed by name and position and reported.
No delays are permitted.
The matter requires a detailed report to be submitted quickly.
The report will serve as proof.
Report to the envoy.
Let the report serve as proof.
The 25th day of the 5th month.
Xíng Yāyá Zhīxún Hé (Acting Commissioner of the Prefecture, Investigating Officer Hé).
Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
Disciple monk Wéizhèng.
Monk Wéixiǎo.
The above Yuánrén and others,
for the sake of seeking Buddhist teachings,
traveled across the sea with the tribute mission.
On the 23rd day of the 8th month of the 5th year of Kāichéng (840 CE),
by order of the Imperial Envoy,
we were temporarily lodged at Zīshèng Sì.
We respectfully submit the aforementioned details.
Respectfully submitted.
The attached report is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
The 26th day of the 5th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE) – Respectfully submitted by Yuánrén, monk from Japan seeking the Dharma.
The 3rd day of the 6th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE).
Jūnróng (General of the Imperial Guards) resigned from office and returned home.
Previously, five or six times,
he had submitted memorials requesting to retire to his home.
An imperial edict did not permit it.
He resubmitted memorials requesting it.
In the 5th month, there was an imperial edict permitting him to return home.
He then moved his furniture.
On the 3rd day,
Jūnróng resigned from office and returned home.
An imperial edict appointed a new Zhōngwèi (Palace Commissioner).

Yáng Qīnyì, Inspector-General of the Palace, Grandee, was appointed Left Commander of the Shéncè (Divine Strategy) Army and Commissioner of Merit for the Left Street, and immediately assumed office on that day.
On the 11th day, the present emperor's Déyáng Day (birthday).
A vegetarian feast was held in the palace.
Great Virtues (eminent monks) from both streets and Daoist priests
debated the Dharma before the emperor.
Each street was to have twelve Great Virtues participate.
The Commissioner of Merit posted notices to the monasteries,
ordering them to select Great Virtues.
Seven from each street
were to enter the palace according to old custom.
The Great Virtues debated with the Daoist priests.
Two Daoist priests
were granted purple robes by imperial edict.
However, none of the Great Virtues were allowed to wear purple.
Also, fifteen days before Déyáng Day,
the various departments within the inner palace went to the various temples
to hold vegetarian feasts and offer longevity blessings.
Wéi Zōngqīng, Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting,
compiled a twenty-scroll commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra and presented it.
The present emperor, after perusing it,
burned the sūtra commentary.
He issued an imperial edict to the Zhōngshū Ménxià (Chancellery and Secretariat)
to search for and burn the draft copies at his residence. The text of the edict is as follows:
Edict:
Wéi Zōngqīng, Silver-Blue Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, Acting Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting,
Pillar of the State, Founding Male of Huāyīn County with an enfeoffment of three hundred households,
is listed among the honored officials.
He should adhere to Confucian scholarship.
Yet he is immersed in perverse doctrines,
thereby fanning evil winds.
He has initiated a deceptive path,
completely deviating from the essence of the classics and ancient texts.
How profound is the decay within the ranks of officialdom!
Moreover, words that are not from the Sage
should still be prohibited and rejected.
How can foreign teachings
be allowed to spread?
Although one might wish to tolerate them,
it would harm public morals.
He should be demoted.
However, out of clemency, he is permitted to serve as Governor of Chéngdū Fǔ.
He is to depart by post-horse.
Wéi Zōngqīng, Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting,
presented the twenty-scroll commentary on the Buddhist Nirvāṇa Sūtra, titled "Three Virtues,"
and an imperial edict [referred to] the twenty-scroll "Mirror of the Great Perfect I-character."
We have already carefully reviewed them.
Buddha was originally a person from the Western Regions,
whose teachings promoted the doctrine of non-birth.
Confucius was a sage of the Central Kingdom,
whose scriptures spoke of beneficial words.
Yet Wéi Zōngqīng, a Confucian scholar
and a prominent figure among the gentry,
could not expound on Confucius and Mozi,
but instead blindly believed in Buddhism.
He presumptuously compiled barbarian books
and casually presented them.
Moreover, the common people of China
have long been tainted by this influence.
It is truly proper to jointly curb this delusion,
making them return to simplicity.
Yet he gathers demonic falsehoods
to further mislead foolish people.
Occupying a position in the court, how can he not be ashamed?
The sūtra he presented has already been burned within the palace.
The draft copies are hereby entrusted to the Zhōngshū Ménxià [Chancellery and Secretariat]
to search for and burn,
and they must not be circulated outside.
Issued on the 13th day of the 6th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE).
On the 23rd day, Jūnróng Qiú died.
An imperial edict ordered the sending of mourning clothes.
On the 25th day, an imperial edict ordered the execution of Jūnróng Qiú,
the Kongmu Official,
Zhèng Zhōngchéng,
Zhāng Duāngōng, and four others,
as well as their male and female servants and slaves,
all to be killed and their families destroyed.
On the 27th day, at the third watch of the night,
a fire broke out in the East Market.
It burned twelve rows of shops west of the Cáomén gate of the East Market,
over four thousand households.
Official and private money and goods,
gold, silver, silk, medicine, etc.,
were all completely burned.
On the 28th day, at the third watch,
a fire broke out inside the palace, burning Shénnóng Sì.
On the 29th day, a fire broke out outside Chánglè Mén,
burning the hayfield.
Previously, there was an imperial edict
to burn Buddhist sūtras in the palace,
and to bury statues of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Deva Kings.
Afterward, two places caught fire.
Then, the East Market also had several fires over two nights.
Japanese monk Yuánrén,
disciples monk Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo,
and lay practitioner Dīng Xióngwàn.
Excluding these four persons in the room,
there are no other visiting monks, novices, or lay guests.
There is a dispatch from the temple authorities,
stating:
"According to the official dispatch from the Imperial Envoy's office,
it is strictly forbidden to allow any outsiders, novices, or lay guests to stay.
If anyone is found later
to be accused of harboring such persons in their room,
severe punishment will be sought.
We respectfully request your decision."
The attached report is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
The 2nd day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE) – Submitted by Yuánrén, monk from Japan.
Disciple monk Wéixiǎo has been ill since the 1st day of the 12th month of last year,
until the 7th month of this year.
A total of eight months of illness.
The 24th day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE).
Late at the second watch of the night,
he passed away.
Yuánrén, monk from Japan, disciple monk Wéixiǎo.
The above disciple Wéixiǎo suffered from a long illness.
He passed away late at the second watch of last night.
We respectfully submit this report to inform you and request your decision.
The attached report is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
The 25th day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE) – Submitted by Yuánrén, monk from Japan.
Death of disciple monk Wéixiǎo, a monk from Japan.
Regarding the above disciple monk Wéixiǎo,
apart from his personal clothing and belongings in his room,
there are no other monies, valuables, bolts of cloth, or measures of grain.
If anyone should later accuse us, claiming that the deceased monk's room contains other monies or valuables,
his teacher, monk Yuánrén,
and fellow disciple monk Wéizhèng,
request to be subject to punishment. We respectfully state the above.
We humbly request your decision.
The attached report is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
The 25th day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE) – Respectfully submitted by Yuánrén, monk from Japan.
Deceased disciple monk Wéixiǎo, a monk from Japan.
The above disciple monk Wéixiǎo has passed away.
We have no money to purchase land.
We humbly beg the compassionate Sangha Gāṇavī Kasa (Head Monks)
to grant us a burial plot for interment.
We respectfully state the above.
We humbly request your decision. The attached report is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
The 25th day of the 7th month of the 3rd year of Huìchāng (843 CE) – Respectfully submitted by Yuánrén, monk from Japan.
The Gāṇavī granted a burial plot.
On the 27th day, he was interred outside Chūnmíng Mén,
east of Zhènguó Sì,
on the land at the north corner of the tile kiln of Zīshèng Sì.
On the 29th, a memorial service was held at the tomb.
The monk Huìjiàn from the same monastery,
and the monk Zōngxìn
were specifically in charge of the funeral arrangements.
Monk Huái'ān of the Jìngtǔyuàn
provided offerings for the funeral procession.
The monks in the funeral procession included Sīliáo,
Jìngzhōng,
Huáiyuē,
Huìjiàn,
and Zōngxìn.
The great virtuous master Zhīxuán Fǎshī, who served as the Daǐgōngfèng Sānjiào Jiǎnglùn within this temple,
sent his fellow disciple monk Kěcóng to attend the funeral.
More than ten monks and laypeople in total accompanied the funeral procession out of the city.
Before the funeral at the tomb, seven monks were invited.
They chanted the names and ten nian mantras.
On the 13th day of the 8th month,
in order to return to the homeland,
I appealed to Lǐ Yuánzuǒ, the Yāyá of the Zuǒ Shéncèjūn.
He was the Qīnshì Yāyá of the Zuǒ Jūnzhōngwèi.
He sincerely respected Buddhist dharma
and had a profound spiritual inclination.
He was originally from Xīnlúo.
His residence was in the Yǒngchāngfāng,
entering the North Gate,
turning west, at the south wall of the first lane.
It was behind the Hùguósì, at the northwest corner of its back wall.
I met him at his residence.
He promised to arrange a meeting.
On the 15th, a three-week fasting ritual was held for Wéixiǎo.
That night, there was a lunar eclipse.
On the 29th, a five-week fasting ritual was held.
On the 13th day of the 9th month,
a seven-week fasting ritual was held.
The Fùmǎ Zhuó Cóng
was appointed Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán.
Lǐ Shēn, who was also Pàn Tiānxià Yán Tiěshǐ, Huáinán Jiédùshǐ, and Púyè,
received an imperial edict to be summoned to the capital to become a chancellor.
Liú Cóngjiǎn, the Jiédùshǐ of Héběi Lùfǔ, rebelled.
An imperial edict was issued to all prefectures
to gather five myriad troops and horses
to prevent the Lùfǔ from entering their borders.
They remained at the border, facing and guarding each other.
The army's daily expenses amounted to 200,000 strings of cash.
The transportation from various circuits was insufficient,
so provisions were continuously supplied
from the imperial treasury within the capital.
The Lùfǔ Liúhòuyuàn was in the Píngkāngfāng on the left street of the capital.
Jiāngsūn, the Yāyá of Lùfǔ,
was in the院, overseeing affairs of that circuit.
An imperial edict ordered his capture.
He escaped, and his whereabouts are unknown.
Searches in various places failed to apprehend him.
Only his wife, children, and others were captured.
They were executed, and their family was destroyed.
Someone reported that
Jiāngsūn, the Lùfǔ Liúhòu Yāyá, had shaved his head
and was now hiding among the city's monks.
An imperial edict was then issued to the Liǎngjiē Gōngdéshǐ to investigate the monks in the city.
All those without official documents were forcibly returned to lay life and sent back to their native places.
The same rule applied to prefectures of all circuits.
Monks residing in nearby temples
whose origins were unclear were all arrested and sent to Jīngzhàofǔ.
Over three hundred newly tonsured monks were beaten to death in the府.
Those who had fled and hidden
dared not walk in the streets.
The troops and horses of the Huíhúgúo suffered a great defeat.
A report was immediately submitted from their original circuit.
The troops from various prefectures had all returned to their original circuits.
On the 3rd day of the 11th month,
a hundred-day fasting ritual was held for Wéixiǎo.
In the 12th month, I received a letter from Liú Shènyán, a Xīnlúo translator from Chǔzhōu. It said:
“The Bhikṣu Yuánzài, a student at Tiāntáishān, states
that he sent a memorial and two disciples,
ordering them to return to Rìběngúo.
These disciples
came to Shènyán to seek a ship.
Shènyán
arranged a ship for them
and sent people to dispatch them.”
Those who departed in the 9th month of this year
— in the 2nd month of Huìchāng Sìnián, which was the Jiǎzǐ year —
Pān, the Yāyá of Yuèzhōu Jūnshì,
came to deliver medicine on an embassy.
He brought a letter from Bhikṣu Yuánzài.
The letter said:
“Because clothing and provisions have been exhausted,
I am sending two disciples, Rěnhǎo and others,
to our home country
to request clothing and provisions.”
Yāyá Pān said:
“Master Zài
wished to enter the city and obtained a document from Yuèzhōu.
He entrusted it to me
to submit to the Zhōngshūménxià.
I have recently been waiting for an opportune moment
to enter the Zhōngshū and deliver the document.
The chancellor rejected it,
not allowing it to be presented to the emperor.
Therefore, the usual human affairs could not be accomplished.”
In the 3rd month, an imperial edict was issued:
“I wish to travel to Dōngjīng.
And it is also made clear to all officials that if any courtier remonstrates, their person and family shall be exterminated.”
An edict forbade the worship of the Buddha's tooth.
Another imperial edict stated:
“At Wǔtáishān in Dàizhōu,
and at Pǔguāngwángsì in Sìzhōu,
Wǔtái in Zhōngnánshān,
and Fǎménsì in Fèngxiángfǔ,
there are Buddha's finger bones in the temples.
All offerings and pilgrimages are forbidden.
If anyone sends a single coin,
they shall receive twenty strokes of the back-staff.
If any monks or nuns
receive a single coin at the aforementioned places,
they shall receive twenty strokes of the back-staff.
In all prefectures and counties,
if anyone provides offerings,
they shall be captured on the spot
and receive twenty strokes of the back-staff.
Because of this, people ceased to visit these four sacred sites.
With no one sending offerings, monks in those places were investigated according to the edict.
Those without official permits
were beaten to death on the spot.
Their names were recorded and reported to the emperor.
It was feared that the Lùfǔ Liúhòu Yāyá might be hiding there as a monk.”
Chancellors Lǐ Shēn and Lǐ Déyù memorialized to stop the three long months of Daoist teachings.
The three Yuán months were newly established:
the first month as Shàngyuán,
the sixth month as Zhōngyuán,
and the tenth month as Xiàyuán.
The constant practice in Tánggúo during the three long months
was to forbid the taking of life.
But the current emperor was not like this.
To destroy the Lùfǔ, an edict summoned eighty-one Daoist priests.
Also within the palace,
a Jiǔtiān Dáochǎng was ordered to be built in the open air.
Eighty beds were stacked high, arranged splendidly.
At twelve o'clock, rituals were performed to sacrifice to Tiānzūn.
Dried meat, wine, and meat
were used to sacrifice to Huǒluótiān.
It began on the first day of the fourth month.
It continued until the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Its duration was fixed. This *dàochǎng*
was not within a building;
rituals were performed in an open courtyard.
When it was clear, the sun beat down on them; when it rained, their bodies were soaked.
Among the eighty-one people, many fell ill.
The current Emperor *piānxìn Dàojiào* (偏信道教).
Monks envied Buddhist Dharma.
He disliked seeing monks.
He did not wish to hear about the Three Jewels (*Sānbǎo* 三寶).
The *dàochǎng* in the *Chángshēng Diàn* (長生殿),
from ancient times,
had housed Buddhist statues and scriptures.
Three or seven monks who chanted were selected from various temples on the two streets.
They were assigned in rotation.
They chanted daily,
day and night without interruption.
The current Emperor immediately ordered the burning of scriptures
and the destruction of Buddhist statues.
The monastic communities were expelled and returned to their respective temples.
In the *dàochǎng*, statues of *Tiānzūn* (天尊) and *Lǎo Jūn* (老君) were placed.
Daoists were ordered to recite Daoist scriptures
and cultivate Daoist arts.
According to national custom, every year on the Emperor's birthday,
venerable *dàdé* (大德) monks from the two streets who lectured and debated,
as well as Daoists, were invited
to set up vegetarian meals and offer incense within the palace.
Monks were invited to discuss scriptures.
Buddhism and Daoism debated their doctrines.
This year, only Daoists were invited,
not monks.
Looking at his demeanor,
it seems that from now on,
no monks will be allowed into the palace.
A Daoist memorialized, saying:
“Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
‘When the Lǐ (李) clan has eighteen sons,
their flourishing destiny will end.
Then a black-robed Son of Heaven will govern the country.’
We, your subjects,
humbly consider
that ‘black-robed’
refers to monks.”
The Emperor accepted these words,
and therefore developed a hatred and suspicion towards monks and nuns, meaning:
“The eighteen sons of the Lǐ (李) character refer to the current Emperor, who is the eighteenth generation. Perhaps the Lǐ (李) family's destiny will end,
and then a black-robed one will usurp the throne?”
The *Gōngdé Shǐ* (功德使) issued a proclamation to all temples:
“According to the imperial edict, monks and nuns are not allowed to walk in the streets and violate the sound of the bell.
If any go out,
they must return to their respective places before the bells of the various temples sound.
Each returns to their original dwelling.
Furthermore, they are not allowed to lodge at other temples.
If any monk or nun walks in the streets violating the sound of the bell,
or lodges at another temple overnight,
they will be punished for disobeying the imperial edict.”
Previously, they were not allowed out of the temple after noon;
now they are not allowed to violate the sound of the bell.
In the second month, the Emperor visited the *Jīnxiān Guān* (金仙觀) on the right street.
This was a nunnery, and there were Daoist nuns in the nunnery.
They were very beautiful.
The Emperor summoned them and took a liking to them.
An imperial edict bestowed a thousand bolts of silk.
Then, he summoned the palace eunuchs
to order the renovation of the nunnery.
It was connected to the inner palace.
The *Jīnxiān Lóu* (金仙樓) was specially built.
The nunnery was originally dilapidated.
He ordered it to be renovated and made magnificent. The Emperor frequently visited.
Later, he visited the *Xīngtáng Guān* (興唐觀) on the left street.
This was a Daoist temple.
He also bestowed a thousand bolts of silk.
He specifically ordered its renovation.
Bronze statues of sacred images were cast.
These sacred images were to be made solemn and extraordinarily beautiful, surpassing all temples in the city.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, offerings were made.
Various temples made flower waxes,
flower cakes,
artificial flower and fruit trees, etc.
Each competed in ingenuity and beauty.
Normally, all these were set up
in front of the Buddha halls as offerings.
The entire city toured the temples and rejoiced.
It was a grand occasion.
This year, the offerings set up by various temples
surpassed those of previous years.
An imperial edict ordered all flowers, medicines, and other offerings from the Buddha halls of various temples
to be moved to the *Xīngtáng Guān* (興唐觀)
to sacrifice to *Tiānzūn* (天尊).
On the fifteenth day, the Emperor visited the *Guān* (觀) and summoned the common people to watch.
The common people cursed, saying:
“Taking Buddha's offerings to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits—who would want to watch?”
The Emperor was surprised that the common people did not come.
The various temples, having their offerings seized,
were in great distress.
The *Dǎlù Fǔbīng* (打路府兵)
were not allowed to enter other territories.
But at the border,
there were frequent imperial edicts urging them, wondering why there was no news.
Although soldiers had been conscripted for a long time,
there was no news of any punitive expeditions.
Frightened by the soldiers, they captured herdsmen and farmers from the border
and sent them to the capital.
They falsely claimed to have captured rebels.
An imperial edict bestowed a sealed sword.
They were beheaded in three sections in the streets.
Soldiers from both armies surrounded and killed them.
Such deliveries continued uninterrupted.
The soldiers were ceaseless.
Often, corpses lay full in the streets,
and blood flowed, wetting the earth into mud.
Spectators filled the roads.
The Emperor came to watch from time to time.
Flags and spears crisscrossed in disorder. It was said
that those brought in
were not Tang rebels,
but merely herdsmen and farmers from the border
who were wrongly captured.
The national army
originally did not enter other territories. Fearing that the King would be upset that there was no news,
they wrongly captured innocent people
and sent them to the capital.
The brave soldiers from both armies,
every time they beheaded someone,
cut out their eye flesh and ate it.
People in all wards said:
“This year, the people of *Cháng'ān* (長安) are eating people.”
An imperial edict recalled the *Huáinán Jiédùshǐ* (淮南節度使), *Dù Fùmǎ* (杜附馬), to the capital.
The Chancellor, Lǐ Shēn (李紳),
volunteered to become the *Huáinán* (淮南) envoy.
According to the edict, *Jiédùshǐ Dù Fùmǎ* (節度使杜附馬) was sent to the capital.
On the day he was granted an audience, he was appointed Chancellor.
He also oversaw the Salt and Iron Monopoly and Fiscal Department. All officials were surprised.
Since ancient times,
there had never been a precedent for an Imperial Son-in-Law (*Fùmǎ* 附馬) to be appointed Chancellor.
According to national custom, Chancellors were granted the title of *Píngzhāng Shì* (平章事).
Lǐ Déyù (李德裕) memorialized, saying:
“An Imperial Son-in-Law appointed Chancellor
should not ride in the imperial carriage.”
The Emperor's intention was lenient.
There was no imperial edict yet,
so the *Fùmǎ* (附馬) was still not allowed the carriage.
The *Dǎlù Fǔbīng* (打路府兵) troops
used two hundred thousand *guàn* (貫) of cash daily.
Various prefectures could not transport enough.
Also, the official treasury in the capital was almost depleted.
An edict was issued to allocate outstanding funds to various departments,
according to the rank of the official,
to collect varying amounts of money
to supplement the provisions of the *Dǎlù Fǔbīng* (打路府兵).
Officials in various circuits and prefectures
were all subject to this rule.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to destroy all mountain hermitages (*shānfáng* 山房) and *āraṇya* (蘭若)
(Buddhist temples), common Buddha halls,
charitable wells,
and village refectories (*zhāitáng* 齋堂) in the empire that were less than two hundred *jiān* (間)
and not officially registered as temples.
Their monks and nuns were all compelled to return to secular life
and assigned to village labor.
Detailed reports of their demolition were to be submitted.
Moreover, in the city of *Cháng'ān* (長安),
there were over three hundred Buddha halls in the wards, with Buddhist statues and scripture repositories, etc.
They were magnificently adorned according to the Dharma.
All were works of famous artisans.
One Buddha hall compound
could rival a large temple in an outer prefecture.
According to the edict, all were abolished.
The total number of Buddha hall compounds throughout all circuits and the empire
is unknown.
All *Zūnshèng* (尊勝) stone pillars (*shí chuáng* 石幢) and
monks' stupas (*sēng mùtǎ* 僧墓塔) in the empire
were ordered to be destroyed by imperial edict.
An edict summoned scholars from the *Guózǐ Jiān* (國子監)
and all successful *jìnshì* (進士) in the empire,
those who were learned,
to enter Daoism.
Not a single person joined their Daoist order.
This year,
whenever it rained for a short while,
the *Gōngdé Shǐ* (功德使),
following an imperial edict, issued proclamations to various temples and Daoist temples,
ordering them to chant scriptures to pray for rain.
When rain was successfully brought,
Daoists alone received generous rewards.
Monks and nuns were left neglected and without any tasks.
The people in the city sighed, saying:
“When praying for rain, they trouble the monastic teachers;
when distributing rewards, they favor only the Daoists.”
In the eighth month, the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) passed away.
Empress Guō Shì (Guō Shì Tàihé Huánghòu).
Because the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) had a Daoist heart,
she believed in the Buddhist Dharma.
Whenever she submitted memorials regarding monks and nuns,
she always offered remonstrances.
The Emperor (Huángdì) ordered medicated wine to be given, and she was poisoned to death.
Also, Empress Xiāo Shì (Xiāo Shì) of Yìyáng Palace (Yìyáng Diàn),
who was the present Emperor's (Jīnshàng) mother, was very beautiful.
The present Emperor (Jīnshàng) summoned and accepted her as a consort (fēi).
But the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) did not obey the command.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) took a bow and shot her to death.
The arrow pierced her chest, and she died.
Three thousand soldiers from the Tàiyuán Prefecture (Dàyuán Fǔ)
had been stationed for three years guarding and apprehending in the Huíhú territory.
This year, they fought the Huíhú, defeated them, and returned.
Upon reaching the prefecture, not many days had passed.
They had not yet seen their relatives.
The Jíedùshǐ immediately dispatched them again.
They were sent to Lù Fǔ.
The soldiers (jūnjiàn) repeatedly protested, saying,
"For three years we fought the Huíhú,
toiling and exhausting ourselves.
Now we have reached our hometown,
but have not yet seen our relatives, parents, etc.
We humbly request
a difference in the deployment of troops."
The Jíedùshǐ refused.
Consequently, all three thousand men resented it.
They fought fiercely around the city.
The Jíedùshǐ heard the report
and had them arrested and sent to the capital (Jīngchéng).
An imperial envoy (chìshǐ) and soldiers
greeted them and brought them to be questioned.
These men spoke of their achievements in fighting the Huíhú,
and that they should not be killed.
The full details of the matter were recorded and reported to the throne.
An imperial edict (chì) refused to follow the report.
An imperial edict (chì) granted an encased saber,
ordering them to be cut into three pieces.
They were executed at the pile of heads in the north street of the East Market (Dōngshì).
The brave men (jiàn'ér) brought from Lù Fǔ
were always executed at this place.
In the ninth month, Lù Fǔ suffered a great defeat.
Moreover, the Ỳāyá and great generals from that place were captured
and sent to the capital (Jīngchéng).
They were beheaded six or seven times.
Later, the head of the rebel leader Liú Cóngjiǎn (Liú Cóngjiǎn) was chopped off and brought.
It was impaled on the points of three spears.
The staffs were over three zhàng high.
A name was written at the top.
First, it was paraded around the two markets.
Then it entered the Inner Palace (Nèilǐ).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) sat on the Yíntái Gate Tower (Yíntái Ménlóu).
He looked and spoke loudly, saying,
"Zhàoyí has already been broken.
What remains to be eliminated now
are all the temples and monasteries (sìshè) in the realm,
and the memorials regarding monks and nuns have not yet been concluded.
Do you, gentlemen, know this?"
Tens of days later,
in accordance with the imperial edict (chì), the assets, money, valuables, jade pendants, furniture, etc. of the Liú (Liú) family of Lù Fǔ were confiscated.
Each time, seven or eight carriages,
gold-adorned vehicles, transported them.
They were sent to the city
and delivered to the Imperial Treasury (Nèikù).
The son of Qíu Jūnrōng (Qíu Jūnrōng), the Chángshì, who was in charge of the Inner Province (Nèishěng Shì),
got drunk and went mad.
He mistakenly offended the Dragon Visage (Lóngyán).
He reported, saying,
"Although the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) is so noble,
he was enthroned by my father."
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) was enraged.
He was immediately beaten to death.
An imperial edict (chì) ordered his wife and daughters
to be exiled.
Their hair was shaved, and they were ordered to guard the imperial tombs.
Moreover, the imperial eunuchs (zhōngguān) were ordered to confiscate his family's possessions: money, rare treasures, ivory filling the house,
pearls, jade, gold, silver, etc.
All filled the treasury.
The money and bolts of silk were countless.
Thirty carriages daily
transported them into the Imperial Treasury (Nèikù).
Within a month,
the transport was not finished, and there were other jade pendants,
and strange and rare objects,
innumerable.
The Emperor (Huángdì) went to the Imperial Treasury (Nèikù) to see.
He clapped his hands in wonder, saying,
"My treasury has never had such things!"
All the high-ranking and low-ranking officials bowed their heads and remained silent.
The Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn (Zhào Guīzhēn) and others reported, saying,
"Buddha was born in the Western Barbarians (Xīróng).
His teachings speak of non-birth.
Indeed, non-birth
is merely death.
He transforms people to return to Nirvana.
Nirvana is death.
He extensively discusses impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
This is truly strange and demonic.
It does not involve the principle of non-action (wúwéi) and longevity.
The Grand Supreme Venerable Sovereign (Tàishàng Lǎojūn),
upon hearing of his birth in the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó), established the Dao in the realm of Tàiluó.
He is free and unfettered, acts through non-action, and is natural.
He transforms and refines divine elixirs.
By consuming them, one achieves longevity.
He widely established divine abodes,
benefiting without limits.
We request that within the forbidden palace (nèijìn),
an immortal platform (xiāntái) be built,
for refining the body and ascending to the clouds,
and for freely roaming the nine heavens.
May the holy longevity be blessed forever with the joy of eternal life."
The Emperor (Huángdì) approved the report and issued an imperial edict (chì) ordering the two armies to build an immortal platform (xiāntái) within the Inner Palace (Nèilǐ).
It was to be one hundred fifty chi high.
Construction began in the tenth month.
Daily, three thousand soldiers (jūnjiàn) from the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies (Zuǒyòu Shéncè Jūn) transported earth for its construction.
The Emperor (Huángdì) was eager for it to be completed soon.
Daily there were imperial edicts (chì) to urge on the construction.
The two armies' Dū Yúhóu
inspected with sticks.
The Emperor (Huángdì), upon seeing this during an inspection,
asked the inner official (nèi zhǎngguān),
"Who is that person holding the stick?"
The official reported, saying,
"It is the Hùjūn Dū Yúhóu,
overseeing the construction of the platform."
The Emperor (Huángdì) declared,
"You need not oversee it with a stick.
You must personally carry earth."
He was then made to carry earth.
Later, the Emperor (Huángdì) again visited the construction site.
The Emperor (Huángdì) himself took a bow and, for no reason, shot one Yúhóu to death.
This was the height of tyranny.
Since last year,
preaching in the two streets has ceased.
Since his ascension to the throne,
he has been fond of going out on imperial tours.
Apart from the four seasons and eight festivals, he would go out every one or two days.
Each time he traveled, he ordered the various temples
to prepare beds and mats,
felt blankets,
and flower canopies to build towers.
They laid out bowls, plates, tables, chairs, etc.
Each time he traveled,
each temple spent four or five hundred strings of cash.
If not finished,
an imperial edict (chì) ordered demolition.
Small temples throughout the realm had their Buddhist scriptures and statues moved into larger temples.
