Bells were sent to Daoist temples (guàn).
Monks and nuns of those demolished temples who had coarse conduct and did not adhere to the precepts,
regardless of age,
were all forced to return to secular life,
and sent back to their native places
to serve in local labor.
Those who were old and had adhered to the precepts
were assigned to large temples.
Even if they had adhered to the precepts,
if they were young,
they were all forced to return to secular life
and sent back to their native places.
Thirty-three small temples within the city were demolished.
Monks and nuns were disciplined
strictly according to the imperial edict (chìwén).
In the eleventh month, an imperial edict (chì) was issued, saying,
"Because Zhàoyí
and the bandits have been defeated,
I will, in the first month of next year,
again perform the Southern Sacrifice (Nánjiāo).
Moreover, all officials (bǎiliáo) are ordered
to inform various departments
to make arrangements early."
All government offices (bǎisī) followed the imperial edict (chì).
They repaired bridges, roads, streets,
preventing passage for people, horses, carriages, and oxen.
The Altar of Heaven (Jiāotán) in the southern suburb of the city
was specially renovated.
Flower canopies were erected and spread around the four sides of the altar.
Towers, pavilions, and city camps
were all made in the style of the Inner Palace (Nèilǐ) within the city.
All government offices (bǎisī) toiled tirelessly.
On the third day of the first month of the 'yǐchǒu' year, the fifth year of Huìchāng.
The sacrifice at the southern suburb was performed.
The ceremonial procession was majestic.
Exactly like the first year.
Monks and nuns were not permitted to watch.
Moreover, there were old regulations
prohibiting monks and nuns from leaving their temples after noon,
and from violating the fasting rules
or staying overnight at another temple.
Therefore, monks were not permitted to watch the southern suburb sacrifice.
The construction of the Immortal's Platform was nearing completion.
An imperial order commanded Daoist priests to refine elixirs of immortality.
The chief Daoist priest, Zhào Guīzhēn, reported, saying:
"There is a kind of immortal medicine;
this country completely lacks it.
But in the Tǔfān Kingdom,
this medicine exists.
Your servant requests to go personally to Tǔfān
to collect this medicine."
The two Palace Commissioners refused,
and then memorialized, saying:
"It would be acceptable to dispatch another person to go.
However, Zhào Guīzhēn, being a master in the pursuit of immortality,
should not go personally."
An imperial edict followed the Palace Commissioners' memorial,
and did not permit him to go.
There was an imperial edict asking:
"What medicines are used for seeking immortality?
List the items and report them."
The Daoist priests reported a list of medicine names:
Ten catties of plum skins,
ten catties of peach fuzz,
ten catties of raw chicken membrane,
ten catties of turtle hair,
ten catties of rabbit horns, etc.
An imperial order commanded them to search for these at pharmacies in the markets.
All claimed they were unavailable.
Consequently, the person responsible for the report was beaten.
His distress was endless.
So he sought them in various places,
but they could also not be obtained.
Prior to the Hánshí Festival,
it had always been customary to grant seven days of leave.
The three thousand government laborers working on the platform every day were not granted leave during the Hánshí Festival.
Full of resentment, they laid down their tools.
All three thousand men simultaneously murmured their discontent.
The Emperor was startled and afraid.
He granted each person three bolts of silk
and granted three days of leave.
On the third day of the third month.
The construction of the platform was completed.
The Xiāntái was presented.
The sovereign ascended the platform.
The two Commanders-in-chief of the armies,
all the high officials,
Dàoshì, and others
followed the Huángdì up.
The two Commanders-in-chief of the armies said to Zhào Guīzhēn,
"Today the Xiāntái has been presented.
We wonder if you gentlemen have managed to find immortals."
Zhào Guīzhēn lowered his head and said nothing.
It is said that
the Xiāntái was one hundred and fifty *chǐ* high.
Its top was round,
level with the foundation of a seven-bay hall.
Above it rose a five-peak tower.
People inside and outside
could all distantly see the solitary mountain towering high,
resembling the winding rocks of Zhōngnán Shān,
forming four mountain cliffs.
There were grottoes and winding paths,
carved and adorned with exquisite skill.
Pine and cypress and strange trees were planted.
It was delightful and pleasing to the eye.
Then an imperial edict was issued,
ordering seven Dàoshì
to perform immortal flight exercises on the platform to seek immortality.
Another edict was sent down to all temples throughout the realm,
forbidding them to establish manors or farms.
It also ordered an inspection of all temples throughout the realm,
regarding the number of slaves and maidservants, as well as money, valuables, *hú*, *dǒu*, and bolts of silk.
Everything was to be truthfully recorded in detail
and reported to the throne.
The temples in the city
were subject to inspection by the two Commanders-in-chief of the armies.
The temples in all prefectures and subprefectures were entrusted to the Zhōngshū Ménxià for inspection.
Furthermore, the slaves and maidservants in the city temples were divided into three categories.
Those with skills were to be taken into the army.
Those without skills, but young and strong, were to be sold.
The old and weak were to be assigned as palace slaves and maidservants.
The sorrowful cries of fathers to the south and sons to the north
were heard at this time.
The Gōngdéshǐ posted notices at all temples:
five slaves and maidservants formed one *bǎo*.
If one person escaped from a *bǎo*,
a fine of two thousand *guàn* of cash would be imposed.
All the money and valuables of the temples,
along with the ransom money from sold slaves and maidservants,
were all to be confiscated by the government,
intended to supplement the salaries and stipends of the hundred officials.
Another edict ordered all temples throughout the realm
that monks and nuns aged forty and below
were all to be compelled to return to lay life
and sent back to their native places.
The sovereign again ascended the Xiāntái.
An edict ordered the musicians
to push down the Commander-in-chief of the Left Army.
The musicians refused to push him.
An edict asked, "I commanded you to push him!
Why do you not obey?"
The musicians reported, "
The Commander-in-chief is a high minister of the state.
We dare not push him down."
The Tiānzǐ angrily had them flogged twenty strokes on the back.
On the platform, he sternly said to the Dàoshì,
"I have ascended the platform twice,
yet none of you has ascended to immortality. What is the meaning of this?"
The Dàoshì reported,
"The reason is that Buddhism in the country
coexists with Daoism,
and its influence is growing stronger,
hindering the path to immortality.
Therefore, we cannot ascend to immortality."
The sovereign declared to the Gōngdéshǐ of the two streets,
"Do you know?
If this is the case, I want no more teachers of any kind!"
A few days later, an edict was issued:
all monks and nuns throughout the realm
aged fifty and below
were all to be compelled to return to lay life
and sent back to their native places.
Later, another edict stated:
all monks and nuns throughout the realm
aged fifty and above,
if they did not possess a Cíbù diploma,
were all to be compelled to return to lay life
and sent back to their native places.
Those who possessed a Cíbù diploma
were to be entrusted to their respective prefectures and counties for verification.
If there were discrepancies,
they were all to be compelled to return to lay life
and sent back to their native places.
Monks and nuns in the city
were entrusted to the Gōngdéshǐ.
In accordance with this regulation, those with diplomas were to be processed.
The Zhōngshū Ménxià issued edicts to all circuits accordingly.
For monks and nuns in the city,
the Gōngdéshǐ's processing of diplomas
was very strict and urgent.
First, the number of monks and nuns without Cíbù diplomas was to be ascertained,
recorded in detail, and submitted to the throne.
Then, notices were posted at all temples,
listing all household items to be transferred.
Those with Cíbù diplomas
were all to be gathered and taken into the army for verification.
If there was even a slight smudge or stain on the Cíbù diploma, or if the birth year differed from the Gōngdé case records,
those with discrepancies
were all counted among those returning to lay life.
Those without discrepancies
were then recorded in the army archives and not released.
Thus, all monks and nuns in the temples ended up without official certificates.
Everyone said,
"Not returning the official certificates
is a sign of the intention not to spare monks and nuns.
Confiscating the temples' slaves, money, and valuables
is a sign of the destruction of temples."
The Huángdì declared,
"The pit of the *bān shì* is extremely deep,
making people fearful and uneasy.
I wish to fill it.
On the day of the sacrifice to the platform,
I will feign to hold a vegetarian feast to celebrate the platform.
All monks and nuns from the two streets will be summoned to the Left Army camp, and their heads will be cut off to fill the pit."
Jiǎn Shū and Bǔ Mì secretly reported,
"Monks and nuns are originally the common people of the state.
If they are compelled to return to lay life and support themselves,
it will be beneficial to the state.
Please do not summon them in.
Please order the relevant authorities
to compel them all to return to lay life
and send them back to their native places,
to be assigned to local labor."
The Huángdì nodded.
After a long while, he said,
"Act according to the report."
The monks and nuns of the various temples
also heard of this matter,
and their souls were lost,
not knowing where to go.
Yuánrén submitted a petition expressing his desire to return to lay life and return to his home country. The Gōngdéshǐ received the petition.
There was no immediate decision.
However, decrees frequently came to ensure their safety.
The Gōngdéshǐ posted notices to all temples,
stating, in accordance with the imperial edict and regulations,
that monks and nuns were not permitted to leave the temples.
It was necessary to assign five or six household members
to guard the temple gates,
and under no circumstances were monks and nuns to be allowed to leave the temple.
If anyone violated this,
the *gāngwéi*, the three elders, and the *diǎnzhí*,
along with the gatekeepers,
would each receive twenty strokes of the back-staff.
Monks and nuns who left the temple
would be executed on the spot.
The Zuǒyòu Shéncèjūn
were the Tiānzǐ's bodyguard army.
Each year there were one hundred thousand troops.
From ancient times, kings
frequently faced difficulties with rebellious ministers.
Therefore, this army was established.
Since then, no one has dared to seize the national position.
Imperial edicts bestowed seals.
Whenever a Commander-in-chief first took office,
in accordance with the edict, troops and horses were dispatched to welcome the seal.
They conducted their affairs independently
and were not subordinate to the Southern Bureau.
In the fourth month of this year,
there was an imperial edict
demanding the seals of the two armies.
The Zhōngwèi refused to surrender the seals.
There was a repeated imperial edict demanding them again and again.
The edict’s intention was to demand the seals of the Hùjūn.
These were to be handed over to the Zhōngshū Ménxià,
who would jointly manage the affairs of the two armies.
All matters were to be deliberated and resolved by them.
The Zuǒjūn Zhōngwèi
immediately agreed to surrender the seals.
However, the Yòujūn Zhōngwèi
refused to surrender the seals.
He then reported, saying:
“On the day of receiving the seals,
soldiers and horses should be dispatched to welcome them.
On the day of surrendering and welcoming [the seals],
soldiers and horses must also be mobilized to surrender them.”
The Zhōngwèi’s intention was,
if the emperor permitted this,
he would use this as an opportunity to mobilize troops and stir up trouble.
Then, the relevant officials were instructed
to secretly arrange troops.
The sovereign, fearing this, temporarily conceded
and did not demand them.
It is heard that
the Gōngdé Shǐ proposed in a memorial to secularize monks and nuns.
The discussion proceeded in stages.
First, all those aged thirty and below were ordered to return to secular life.
Next, all those aged fifty and above were ordered to return to secular life.
Next, all those aged fifty and above without a Cíbù diploma were ordered to return to secular life.
The third stage was to review and verify Cíbù diplomas.
Those found to be fraudulent were to return to secular life.
Finally, those with genuine Cíbù diplomas without discrepancies
were all ordered to return to secular life.
Thus, monks and nuns would be eliminated.
This deliberation
was widely adopted throughout the empire.
In accordance with the imperial edict, starting from the first day of the fourth month,
all monks and nuns aged forty and below were compelled to return to secular life,
returning to their native places.
Three hundred monks were secularized daily.
On the fifteenth day, all monks and nuns aged forty and below were finally secularized.
Starting from the sixteenth day,
monks and nuns aged fifty and below were secularized.
This continued until the tenth day of the fifth month, when it was completed.
Starting from the eleventh day,
monks and nuns aged fifty and above
who did not possess a Cíbù diploma were secularized.
Since the previous year,
monks and nuns whose diplomas were reviewed, namely those with crude conduct not adhering to their original teachings, were all compelled to return to secular life,
returning to their native places.
This year, there was no distinction made between those with lofty conduct and crude conduct, nor were eminent monks, great virtues, or imperial chaplains examined.
As soon as their turn came,
they were ordered to return to secular life.
There were frequent imperial inquiries about how many had already returned to secular life
and how many had not yet returned.
The numbers were urged forward.
Foreign monks
were not yet included in the regulations.
The Gōngdé Shǐ
separately reported and sought a decision, and there was an imperial edict stating:
“As for foreigners,
if they do not possess Cíbù diplomas,
they shall also be compelled to return to secular life and return to their home countries.”
Nánduó (Nanda), the Sāncáng from the Western Regions and Northern Tiānzhú,
was at the Dàxīngshàn Sì.
Bǎoyuè, the Sāncáng from Southern Tiānzhú,
along with his four disciples,
at Zhōngtiān,
had achieved proficiency and thoroughly understood the Great Dhāraṇī Dharma.
Their monastic discipline was strict and meticulous,
and they had extensive knowledge of sūtras and treatises.
They were at Qīnglóng Sì.
None of them possessed a Táng dynasty Cíbù diploma.
Many monks from the kingdom of Xīnxīluó
also did not possess Cíbù diplomas.
The Japanese monk Yuánrén
and Wéizhèng also did not possess Táng dynasty Cíbù diplomas.
The Gōngdé Shǐ, in accordance with the imperial edict,
assigned them to the category of those to be secularized.
Furthermore, a notice was posted to all monasteries, stating:
“If any monk or nun
disobeys the order to return to secular life,
they shall be charged with the crime of violating the imperial edict,
and shall be immediately executed.”
Upon hearing this news, I packed my documents,
the sūtras and treatises I had copied,
the teachings and methods of practice,
Maṇḍalas, etc.
All were packed.
The documents and clothing together filled four baskets, so I bought three donkeys
to await further instructions.
My heart was not troubled by returning to secular life;
I only worried that the sacred texts I had copied
could not be carried with me.
Also, the edict strictly suppressed Buddhism.
I feared that along the way, various prefectures and counties
might inspect them and, if verified, charge me with the crime of violating the imperial edict.
On the thirteenth, an envoy arrived with a notice.
Thirty-nine monks
of this monastery
who did not have Cíbù diplomas
included two Japanese monks, namely the previously secularized monk Línzōng
and Xìnguān. We discussed their wishes and agreed to them.
I escorted them to Biànzhōu.
The city is one thousand four hundred *lǐ* from the capital.
Seeing their earnestness,
I did not obstruct their wishes.
The Sāngāng and Sānlǎo, etc.,
came to express their concern, saying:
“You have journeyed across borders to seek the Dharma, and now you encounter this royal calamity; you should not avoid changing your attire.
From ancient times to the present,
those who seek the Dharma have frequently encountered obstacles. Please make arrangements.”
I replied: “If not for this difficulty,
there would be no reason to return to my country.
I am simply glad to be able to bring the sacred teachings back to my home country.
This aligns with my original vow.”
The Dūwéinà, monk Fǎyù,
donated a sandalwood shrine image
to be taken back to my country for worship.
In the evening,
after bidding farewell to the monks of the monastery,
I donned secular clothes.
On the morning of the fourteenth,
I entered Jīngzhàofǔ
to request official credentials,
fearing that without official certification, it would be difficult on the road.
Seven Sāncáng from the Western Regions, etc.,
were also at the prefecture
requesting official credentials.
The prefectural office issued two travel passes,
instructing that along the way, people should be dispatched to relay them.
However, since the first year of Huìchāng, I had repeatedly submitted petitions through the Gōngdé Shǐ to return to my home country,
numbering over a hundred times.
I had also been associated with several influential individuals,
using resources for arrangements,
but still could not leave.
Now, due to the difficulty of monks and nuns returning to secular life,
I am finally able to return to my country.
I am both sad and joyful.
Lǐ Yuánzuǒ, the Yāyá of the Zuǒshéncèjūn, Yínqīng Guānglùdàfū, Jiǎnjiào Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, Diànzhōng Jiāncásìyùshǐ, Shàngzhùguó,
had been approached regarding my return to my home country.
We had known each other for nearly two years,
and our friendship was very close.
Any shortcomings in my resources as a guest
he was able to fully assist with.
Since the Gōngdé Shǐ lacked compassion,
I consulted him about returning to my country,
but my request was not granted.
While I was in the prefecture,
he also provided food, blankets, etc.,
assisting me with great kindness.
On the fifteenth, I departed from the government office.
Arrived at Wànnián Xiàn.
A messenger from the Fǔ household
escorted me to Dàlǐ Qīng, Zhōngsàn Dàfū, bestowed with the purple-gold fish bag, Yáng Jìngzhī.
He had previously served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He sent a special envoy to inquire
on what day I would leave the city,
and by what road I would travel.
He also bestowed a string of compressed tea.
I drafted a memorial in the county
to express my gratitude.
The Nèi Gòngfèng, Tánlùn Dàdé, who returned to his hometown last year,
and of whom I had received no news,
now secretly came, covering his head,
and hiding in Yáng Qīng's residence. He sent his young servant Qīngliáng with a letter.
The letter contained words of a secret farewell,
which were extremely tragic.
Yúnqī, the presiding monk of the Vimalakīrti Sutra lectures at our temple,
and Língzhuāng, the presiding monk of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra lectures,
who had both been laymen forty years ago and below,
now came, covering their heads and wearing lay clothes.
We met in the county.
Lǐ Shìyù, with his nephew Yú Shísānláng,
came together to inquire about me.
One of them took care of the luggage coming and going,
and helped buy felt hats, etc.
They also entered the temple to check documents, baskets, donkeys, etc.
Presiding monk Yúnqī
also took care of the baskets and donkeys,
arranging them together.
Fearing that they could not be carried along,
we left the city in the evening.
The county office sent a messenger
to relay the escort and provide care to the next county.
We were eighty or ninety *lǐ* from the city.
Lǐ Shìyù
and presiding monk Yúnqī escorted me together
to outside Chūnmíng Mén.
We ate biscuits.
Yáng Qīng sent a messenger with a letter saying:
“Your disciple has five memorials,
along with personal letters to be delivered to old acquaintances, officials in the prefectures and counties along the road ahead.
Just by presenting these letters, you will certainly benefit.”
Zhīfāng Lángzhōng, bestowed with the scarlet fish bag, Yáng Lǔshì,
who had previously attended to me when I was at the temple,
inquired about me with great sincerity.
He had also visited the temple several times to check.
He had previously donated silk, coarse cloth shirts, trousers, etc.
Now he sent his young master with a letter,
and delivered two bolts of road silk (Měngdǐng tea),
two *jīn* of biscuits,
a string of compressed biscuits,
and two *guàn* of cash.
He entrusted two sealed letters for the road ahead.
There was also a personal note.
The lay patron Yáng sent a messenger
with one bolt of silk,
one bolt of coarse cloth,
and one thousand cash
to be used on the road.
As for the other escorts,
I cannot list them all.
They all bowed in farewell outside Chūnmíng Mén, saying:
“We must part here.”
Yáng Qīng's envoy
and Lǐ Shìyù
were unwilling to return,
and escorted me to Chánglè Pōtóu,
five *lǐ* from the city.
We stayed together for one night in an inn, conversing.
Lǐ Shìyù
sent farewell gifts:
ten bolts of thin Wú silk,
one piece of sandalwood,
two types of sandalwood shrine images, and one porcelain bottle of incense,
one five-pronged silver vajra,
two felt hats,
one scroll of the Diamond Sutra with silver characters,
one pair of soft shoes,
and two *guàn* of cash.
The exact quantities are on a separate sheet.
He expressed his reluctance to part with such sincerity,
saying: “Your disciple has been fortunate through many lives
to meet the venerable master who traveled far to seek the Buddha's teachings.
Several years of offerings
still leave my heart unsatisfied.
Throughout my life, I do not wish to leave the venerable master's side.
Now the venerable master has encountered royal misfortune
and must return to your native country.
Your disciple believes it will be difficult to see you again in this life.
In the future, in the Pure Land of all Buddhas,
may it still be like today,
with me as a disciple to the venerable master.
When the venerable master attains Buddhahood,
please do not forget your disciple.”
He also said: “Please leave the patched monastic robe
worn by the venerable master with your disciple.
I will take it home
and offer incense to it for the rest of my life.”
Since he said this,
I gave it to him.
Nephew Shísānláng also formed an extremely deep connection.
On the morning of the sixteenth,
we bade farewell and set off.
Nineteen Táng monks traveled together.
In the evening,
we arrived at Zhàoyìng Xiàn to lodge.
Among the traveling companions,
there was a monk twenty years old,
from Cháng'ān Chéng.
His parents, brothers, and sisters are still alive.
He entered Buddhism in his youth
at Dà Jiànfú Sì,
serving a Sīllá monk as his master.
Due to the monastic misfortune,
he inherited the Sīllá monk's name and was allowed to reside in the temple.
The government, based on his official credentials,
was relaying him to Sīllá Guó.
While in the capital,
he tried every means to appeal, but could not avoid being sent away.
His relatives wept
as they bade farewell in the street.
He was then relayed to Zhàoyìng Xiàn.
We lodged together. At the fifth watch, we departed.
That monk secretly ran away and escaped.
None of the traveling companions noticed.
Upon reaching the county and daylight, we immediately knew.
Among the three household servants,
two went in separate directions to search.
They searched all day but did not find him.
I imagine he had already returned to his family home in the city and was hiding.
The county office reported to the Fǔ to search for him.
On the twenty-second, we passed Tóngguān.
This is the throat of the capital city.
Wèinán Xiàn,
Huāyīn Xiàn,
Yǒngníng Xiàn –
all had letters from Yáng Qīng.
All were presented.
On the first day of the sixth month,
we arrived at Cuī Tàifù's residence in Dōngdū.
I delivered Yáng Qīng's letter.
The Tàifù sent a special envoy
to convey his regards and well-wishes.
He bestowed one bolt of silk.
On the 9th, I arrived at the residence of the Cìshǐ Lǐ Shèrén in Zhèngzhōu.
There was a letter from Yáng Qīng.
At the residence of Rèn Pànguān, there was also a letter from Yáng Qīng.
I brought the letters into the prefecture.
I saw the Cìshǐ and Pànguān.
They were both safe and sound and very cordial.
The Zhōuzhǎnglì, Diànzhōng Jiānchá Shìyùshǐ, bestowed with a purple-gold fish bag, Xīn Jiǔyù.
He had served in Cháng'ān for a long time.
His meals were free.
His affection was very cordial.
Last year, he was appointed as the Zhèngzhōu Zhǎnglì.
Now we meet in the prefecture.
Joy and sorrow mingled.
His concern was extremely profound.
He immediately called for me to stay at his residence.
And rest during the midday break.
The Cìshǐ gave two bolts of silk.
Everyone said,
"This place is on the great road between the two capitals.
It's a place where many guests come and go.
People act without discretion.
If it weren't for a high official,
or an ordinary dignitary who is extremely cordial,
one would receive one or two bolts.
That Héshang received two bolts.
This shows the Cìshǐ's deep respect."
Rèn Pànguān gave one bolt of patterned silk.
When Zhǎnglì Xīn saw me,
he immediately instructed it to be cut into a coarse robe.
After the meal, I left the prefecture.
And returned to my lodging.
Zhǎnglì Xīn sent a special messenger.
Who brought a bolt of silk.
One pair of socks.
A sweat-shirt and a coarse robe.
And a letter.
The letter said,
"I will come to bid farewell later.
Please wait a moment."
Because the county had already sent people to conduct the unfortunate inspection,
I couldn't wait and had to depart.
Fifteen *lǐ* later, I turned my head and looked west.
I saw Zhǎnglì Xīn riding his horse, catching up.
Three pairs of government officials
ran to block the road.
So, in an earthen shop, we ate together and talked for a long time.
He said as we parted,
"The Buddhist Dharma in this country is indeed non-existent.
Buddhism flows eastward.
As has been said since ancient times.
I wish Hèshang to strive hard.
To establish and spread the Buddhist Dharma in his own country soon.
Your disciple has been fortunate to pay respects for a long time.
Today we part.
It will probably be difficult to meet again in this life.
When Hèshang attains Buddhahood,
I pray you will not abandon your disciple."
On the 13th, I arrived at the residence of Jiédù Fùshǐ Péi Lángzhōng in Biànzhōu.
There was a letter from Yáng Lángzhōng.
At the residence of Zhú Bīngmǎshǐ, there was a letter from Yáng Qīng.
Both were delivered.
Péi Lángzhōng was very cordial in his inquiries.
He immediately dispatched one official
to handle the transportation and send-off.
The Bīngmǎshǐ was not in the prefecture.
So I couldn't meet him.
Péi Lángzhōng hired a boat.
Which went directly to the anchorage west of Chénliú Xiàn.
Waiting for the county's official dispatch.
It had not arrived.
Because it was a boat carrying both official and private goods,
it couldn't wait.
So it departed earlier for the Biànhé.
Along the way, at each county,
I had no choice but to hire a boat myself.
From Biànzhōu onwards, along the river.
The people along the way
were urgent, malicious, and unkind.
Like the swift and turbid current of the Biànhé water they drank.
The capital's dispatch did not mention travel provisions.
I had to carry my own food on the journey.
On the 22nd, I arrived at Xīzhōu.
The prefecture was under the Xú Jiédù Fǔ.
Pǔguāngwáng Sì in Sìzhōu.
Was a renowned place throughout the land.
Now, its manors, gardens, money, goods, and slaves
were all confiscated by the government.
The temple was desolate.
No one came or went.
The prefecture, according to the imperial edict,
intended to destroy it.
On the 23rd, I crossed the Huái River and arrived at Xùyí Xiàn.
It was two hundred *lǐ* east of Chǔzhōu.
My original intention was to go from here to Chǔzhōu.
To find a boat to cross the sea.
But the county government insisted on sending me towards Yángzhōu.
I submitted a petition and explained the situation.
The county magistrate did not agree.
I had no choice but to go to Yángzhōu.
From Xùyí Xiàn to Yángzhōu.
There were nine courier stations with no water route.
Documents were carried by basket on donkeys.
Hired at each station.
On the way, I saw Péi Shèrén.
He had served as the Cìshǐ of Hǎizhōu.
And was recalled this spring.
Demoted to be the Zhǎnglì of Táizhōu.
There was also a Hànlín Bóshì.
Demoted to be a Sīmǎ in an outer prefecture.
When we met, he said,
"On the 29th of the fifth month.
I left Cháng'ān.
When I was in the city.
All the monks and nuns in the city had already been defrocked.
According to the imperial edict.
Each temple was to retain three *sāngāng*.
To inspect money and goods.
After the government collects the temple's money and goods,
they are then to be defrocked."
Temples were currently being demolished.
Zhāngjìng,
Qīnglóng,
and Ānguó three temples.
Were entirely converted into imperial gardens.
On the 28th.
I arrived at Yángzhōu and saw the monks and nuns in the city wrapping their heads.
And being sent back to their native places.
The gold, money, goods, manors, and bells of the temples were to be destroyed.
And confiscated by the government.
A recent imperial edict stated in a dispatch that all bronze Buddhas.
And iron Buddhas throughout the land were to be shattered.
Weighed.
And handed over to the Yántiě Sī for management.
With a detailed record to be submitted to the throne.
Hóngdū Xiàn dispatched someone.
To send me to Jiāngyáng Xiàn.
I requested the use of materials to go to Chǔzhōu Xiàn.
And then was sent towards Chǔzhōu.
Passing through Gāoyóu
and Bǎoyìng two counties.
On the third day of the seventh month,
we reached Chǔzhōu.
First, we entered the Xīnluó Fāng.
We met the Zǒngguǎn of the prefecture, Xūe, who was also a Shíjiàng.
The Sīnluó interpreter was Liú Shènyán.
We exchanged greetings and inquiries with great warmth.
The documents and cages
were placed on the boat at the interpreter's residence.
Then we entered Shānyáng Xiàn.
We presented a memorial, fully explaining our original intention.
The tribute envoys from the country of Rìběn
all depart from here by boat
to cross the sea and return to their country.
Yuánrén and others,
upon arriving here, wish to return to their country and request to cross the sea from here.
The county government did not agree.
They said,
"This prefecture is not the farthest point by sea.
It is by imperial decree that you are to be passed on
and not allowed to stay.
The matter requires you to be passed on to Dēngzhōu, the farthest point
from where you may embark and return to your country."
The Xīnluó interpreter, Liú Shènyán,
had been using funds since arriving at the county.
He consulted about a wooden table.
He immediately discussed it with the county magistrate, who agreed.
Then he said,
"This place is governed by law.
Moreover, it is within the jurisdiction of Prime Minister Lǐ Shēn.
Those who are to be passed on by imperial decree
cannot stay for two days.
That would be a crime of disobeying the imperial decree."
The county government would not listen to reason.
Ambassador Xūe
and Interpreter Liú
went to the prefecture again to consult.
Again, they were refused.
Within two days,
all efforts failed.
It was decided that we must be passed on.
The Shānyáng Xiàn government,
unable to bear Interpreter Liú's earnest plea,
and having no other plan,
said,
"If the monk wishes to go south,
we will pass you on to the south.
If he wishes to go north,
we will pass you on to the north.
But if you want to stop here to find a boat,
the county government is powerless to assist."
Having exhausted all arguments,
we requested to proceed to Dēngzhōu.
Dēngzhōu is the farthest point in the northeast of the Táng country.
It is over one thousand one hundred *lǐ* from Chǔzhōu.
The county issued a document and dispatched officials to escort us to Dēngzhōu.
Ambassador Xūe
and Interpreter Liú
wished to keep us at the Xīnluó Fāng
and send us off from there to return to our country.
However, because the county would not agree,
they were unable to detain us.
At dawn on the fifth day,
I went with my household servants to Interpreter Liú's residence.
The interpreter gave the household servants three hundred *wén*.
He privately arranged, saying,
"When the monks and others are truly hot
from their long journey,
they will be visibly exhausted.
Shènyán
wishes to accommodate them at his residence
so they can rest for two or three days.
You gentlemen should return to your original posts for now.
Come early on the eighth day."
The household servants accepted the instruction and returned home.
The ambassador
and the interpreter
exerted themselves greatly to prepare for departure.
I saw that the road from Chǔzhōu to Dēngzhōu
was entirely mountainous slopes and wilderness.
The grass and trees were tall and dense,
and mosquitoes and gnats were like rain.
All day we crossed mountains and traversed fields.
Villages were far apart.
We rarely saw houses.
The people's dispositions were rough and wicked.
After traveling seventy or eighty *lǐ*,
there would only be one or two houses,
which made people fearful.
If we were to carry the document cages with us on the journey,
we were afraid that the items might be damaged or lost due to people's alarm.
Now, furthermore, the imperial decree has prohibited Buddhism,
strictly forbidding it. In the northern prefectures and counties, people are rough and wicked.
If they see Buddhist images carried on one's person,
they will certainly cause trouble,
and it will be a crime of disobeying the imperial decree.
Therefore, I discussed with the interpreter
the sacred teachings and merit scrolls brought from the capital,
as well as monk's robes, etc.
In total, four cages.
We provisionally left them at the interpreter's residence.
I entrusted them to the interpreter,
instructing him to guard them.
I earnestly urged him, saying,
"If we arrive at Dēngzhōu and are allowed to stay,
I will send a letter requesting them.
Until then, please guard them carefully.
Do not let anything be lost."
The interpreter accepted the instruction and began arranging the luggage.
Ambassador Xūe provided three *liǎng* of socks.
Interpreter Liú provided nine *pǐ* of silk
and ten Xīnluó knives,
and five *liǎng* of socks.
Other supplies were considerable.
The people in Huáinán Dào and Chǔzhōu county were treacherous and wicked.
It was very difficult to manage them.
Someone reported to the interpreter that
two boats, also from Rìběn,
had arrived and docked at the Jiāngnán Chángzhōu border.
This was over three thousand *lǐ* from here.
It was planned to sell the boats and hire other Táng boats
to transport goods.
This was probably the boats that sent Dàshī Yuánzài's disciples in Huìchāng year three
and were ordered to return.
Now, we plan to dispatch someone to investigate.
Also, Dàshī Huì'è from Rìběn,
in Huìchāng year two,
went to worship at Wǔtái Shān to seek offerings for Wǔtái.
He boarded Lǐ Lín Dé's boat
and returned to his country.
Year after year, he brought offerings.
Now, due to the national difficulty, he has returned to secular life.
He is currently in Chǔzhōu.
He specifically asked for news of Superior Yuánzài.
No one knew to inform him.
We departed on the eighth day.
Interpreter Liú
had a letter to be sent to Dēngzhōu.
Along the way, the villagers
were entreated to provide safety and care,
and to act as hosts.
We boarded a boat and entered the Huái River.
On the ninth day, during the fasting period.
Arrived at Liánshuǐ Xiàn.
The county is administered by Sìzhōu.
Due to a letter from the interpreter in Chǔzhōu to be delivered to a local in Liánshuǐ,
I was instructed to ensure its safe keeping,
and also to arrange for the matter of retaining the hook.
Still, upon arriving at the county,
I first entered Xīnluó Fāng.
The people of the district met me,
but were not warm-hearted.
When I approached the Zǒngguǎn and others,
it was difficult to gain recognition.
Everything was troublesome.
Cui Yūn (崔暈), the twelfth son of the corner (隅),
had once served as the Commander of Troops and Horses for Qīnghǎi Zhèn.
When he was in Chìshān Yuàn in Dēngzhōu,
we met once.
He then wrote his name and made an appointment, saying,
"When the Wèishàng (和上) returns to his country after seeking the Dharma,
it is essential to bring this name card to Liánshuǐ.
Yūn will use every means to send you off,
and together we shall go to Japan."
After this parting,
that person returned to Xīnluó again.
He encountered national difficulties
and fled to live in Liánshuǐ.
Seeing him now, I immediately recognized him, and our bond was not estranged.
He exerted all his strength to arrange for my stay.
After much difficulty in seeking recognition from the Guǎn and others, and considering the matter with deference,
I still prepared a petition to present to the Chángguān of the county.
I requested to anchor in the Xīnluó Fāng of that county
to find a boat to return to my country.
The Chángguān met me,
expressed pity and sympathy,
and summoned the Zhīchéngrén to give instructions.
He ordered them to arrange for food and drink,
and temporarily instructed them to bring me to see the Chángguān.
He asked,
"In Xīnluó Fāng,
have you ever had any acquaintances?"
I replied,
"Because when the Japanese envoy paying tribute to the court in the fourth year of Kāichéng departed from Chǔzhōu to return to his country,
people were drawn from Chǔzhōu and this county.
Therefore, I definitely have acquaintances."
The Chángguān gave instructions,
and the Zhīchéngrén said,
"Understood."
"When the Wèishàng arrives at Xīnluó Fāng,
if anyone recognizes him,
then immediately take a receipt from them.
If no one recognizes him,
then bring the Wèishàng back."
So, together with the envoy, I went to the district.
The Zǒngguǎn and others intended to take charge,
but another special official refused.
Therefore, no receipt was issued.
I returned to the county office.
The Chángguān issued a decree,
"Temporarily place him in Dàshàn Sì."
For three days,
I stayed there.
Cuī Shíèrláng (崔十二郎)
served as my host.
I obtained a county document and a courier
and set off towards the prefecture.
Cuī Shíèrláng
hired a boat,
arranged provisions for the journey, stacked vegetables, etc.
Everything was meticulously prepared.
Then we parted.
He said,
"This disciple wishes
to keep the Wèishàng here and send you off to your country from this place.
However, the people are unwilling,
and the official document has already been issued.
I am unable to exert myself enough,
and thus cannot fulfill my original wish.
After autumn, I intend to go to the Dēngzhōu area,
and hope to visit you then."
On the fifteenth day,
I arrived at Hǎizhōu.
I entered the county and presented a petition
to request a temporary stop.
"The Japanese envoy's ship arrived here.
From here, he will depart to return to his home country.
Yuánrén (圓仁) and others
accompanied the envoy to pay tribute to the court.
Now, we are returning to our home country.
Having been relayed stage by stage to this place,
this is the coast.
I humbly beg for a temporary stop in this prefecture,
where I can find my own boat
to return to my home country."
The Chángguān said,
"Recently, a Xīnluó monk
also came from Jīngzhàofǔ and requested to temporarily stop in this prefecture.
However, the Shǐjūn refused
and had him relayed onward.
For the Wèishàng to request to stop,
it will also likely be difficult.
However, the county office does not have the authority; the matter must go through the Shǐjūn via a petition."
On the sixteenth day,
I entered the prefecture and asked the Cìshǐ for permission to return to my country from Chángzhōu.
The Cìshǐ did not grant the request
and still decreed,
"In accordance with the imperial edict, relay him onward.
The prefectural office dares not detain him.
This is to inform you."
On the seventeenth day, I departed.
From Hǎizhōu northward, there was no waterway.
Although near the sea, the sea was not visible.
I spent the entire day crossing wild lands
and then entered the mountains.
On the eighteenth day, I arrived at Huáirén,
which is administered by Hǎizhōu.
The people were filial and obedient,
and treated guests with respect.
They interacted with ease.
The county office's intentions were also good.
On the twentieth day, I departed.
I traveled through mountains and wilds.
The grass and trees were tall and dense.
I rarely encountered people.
The entire day was spent ascending mountains and entering valleys,
treading through mud and water.
The hardship was extreme.
On the twenty-first day, I arrived at Jǔxiàn,
which is administered by Mìzhōu.
The people and county officials were rough and malicious.
On the twenty-sixth day, I arrived at Mìzhōu.
The people were fierce and malicious;
gentle ones were rare.
On the second day of the eighth month,
I arrived at Gāomì Xiàn.
The people were gentle and mild.
On the sixth day, I arrived at Jìmò Xiàn,
which is located in Láizhōu.
The people were filial and obedient.
They were able to keep guests safe.
On the tenth day, I arrived at Chāngyáng Xiàn,
administered by Láizhōu.
The people were good.
On the sixteenth day, arrived at Dēngzhōu.
Met Xiāo Duāngōng, who had newly arrived to take up his post.
There was also an imperial edict which stated:
"All gold and bronze Buddha statues throughout the realm
shall have their gold stripped by the prefectural and county offices, weighed, and submitted [to the court]."
From Hǎizhōu
all the way to Dēngzhōu,
the roads were impassable.
The wilderness roads were narrow,
covered by dense vegetation.
Every inch of the way was muddy,
and we frequently lost our way.
If there had been no locals to guide us,
not a single step could have been taken.
We went out of the wilderness into the mountains,
and out of the mountains into the wilderness.
The mountain slopes were steep, and the valleys deep and secluded.
The stream water was deep and cold;
those who crossed felt a bone-piercing pain.
When traveling in the mountains,
one would cross mountains a hundred times a day,
and ford rivers a hundred times.
When traveling in the wilderness,
the trees were dense and the grass deep.
It was hard to discern the faint path, only seeing the movement of the grass
did we know people had passed.
Mosquitoes and gnats were like rain,
and we could not swat them fast enough.
Under the grass was thick mud,
reaching to the knees or even the waist.
The prefectures and counties along the way
were merely like piles of earth in the wilderness.
The people of the mountain villages and counties
ate coarse and hard food.
They loved to eat salted vegetables with millet rice,
which was so rough it was hard to swallow.
Eating it caused chest pain.
It was a custom in mountain villages
never to cook soup.
For years, they only ate cold dishes.
For the most esteemed and important guests,
they would serve plain flatbreads and cold dishes as the finest meal.
Northward for 1,300 *lǐ*
it was all mountains and wilderness.
Although near the coast,
we had never seen the sea.
Only upon arriving at Dēngzhōu
did we finally see the sea.
Dēngzhōu
is the northeastern extremity of the Dàtáng empire.
It lies facing the northern sea,
and the prefecture was established by the sea.
The prefectural city is about one or two *lǐ* from the sea.
Although it is a frontier region in the north,
the regulations about monks and nuns demolishing temples and monastic dwellings,
prohibiting scriptures and destroying images,
and confiscating temple property
are no different from those in the Jīngchéng.
Moreover, to strip gold from Buddhas
and smash bronze and iron Buddhas,
weighing them by the *jīn* and *liǎng*—
how painful and helpless this is!
How many bronze, iron,
and gold Buddhas are there in the world?
There is no limit to their number.
According to the imperial edict, they are all to be destroyed and turned into dust.
The Pénglái Xiàn dossier was sent to Mùpíng Xiàn.
Proceeding southeast along the coast,
the rivers and wilderness were difficult to pass.
The mountain slopes were numerous and steep.
On the twenty-first day, arrived at Mùpíng Xiàn.
Received the county dossier.
Then proceeded southeast.
On the twenty-fourth day, arrived at Wéndēng Xiàn.
Crossing mountains and traversing wilderness,
our clothes were torn and completely worn out.
Upon entering the county, we met the County Magistrate,
and requested to go to the Xīnluó office in the eastern part of the county to seek assistance to prolong our humble lives,
find a boat ourselves,
and return to our homeland.
The officer approved our petition and issued a document,
sending us to the Xīnluó office.
It was seventy *lǐ* southeast of the county,
within Qīngníng Xiāng of Wéndēng Xiàn.
On the twenty-seventh day, arrived at the Xīnluó office.
The imperial edict designated Zhāng Yǒng, Marshal of the Pínglú Jūn Military Governor's Staff and concurrently Registrar of Dēngzhōu's various armies,
to manage the Xīnluó households within Wéndēng Xiàn. Upon reaching his residence,
we met and recognized each other with joy.
He inquired about our well-being with great solicitude.
Back in the fifth year of Kāichéng,
I had entered Wǔtái from this harbor.
At that time,
I had received assistance from this Dàshǐ Xīlì, who specialized in managing and dispatching official documents and certifications for prefectures and counties.
Now, I have returned here,
and he again treats me with solicitous care.
I immediately handed over the county document and fully explained my situation.
The Dàshǐ took possession of it and detained us (to offer lodging and assistance).
He promised to find a boat and send us back to our country.
He also said, delighted,
"Since you departed from here before,
until now,
we have received no news.
I thought in my heart that you had returned to your homeland long ago.
I never expected you to come here again.
To meet again is truly wonderful, truly wonderful!"
"My disciple and I,
have too much karmic connection.
There are no other urgent matters in my jurisdiction.
Please set your mind at ease and rest.
There is no need to worry or be anxious.
Until you return to your country,
I will willingly provide
your daily alms food
from my own means. Just eat your fill and sleep."
The Dàshǐ then drew up a report to the prefecture.
Received a document from Wéndēng Xiàn stating:
"The Japanese monks Yuánrén
and Wéizhèng, two persons,
were granted a long-term pass by the Jīngzhàofǔ,
to be transmitted to their home country according to imperial edict.
They have been transmitted to this county.
They requested to go to the Xīnluó office to seek assistance to prolong their humble lives.
They wish to return to their country when a ship bound for Rìběn Guó is available.
They are currently in the harbor."
Ten days later, received a prefectural document stating:
"These monks are to be entrusted to safe-keeping for now.
If there is a ship passing through to Rìběn Guó,
they may depart as they please."
Recently, there was an imperial edict
that all monastic robes of laicized monks and nuns throughout the realm
should be collected
and entirely burned by their respective prefectures and counties.
It was feared that gentry and influential persons
might hide [robes] in private homes
and secretly wear monastic attire.
Therefore, it was necessary to strictly increase collection
and burn them all.
It was reported that after the burning,
if any monk or nun were found carrying monastic robes
that were not permitted to be carried out,
during an inspection,
if such a package was found,
they would be dealt with according to the imperial edict.
All prefectures and counties,
according to the imperial edict,
in all wards and villages,
collected monks' and nuns' clothing,
brought them to the prefectures and counties,
and burned them all.
There was also an imperial edict ordering all temples and monasteries throughout the realm
to have their rare and precious ornaments,
pearls, jade, gold, and silver
collected by their respective prefectures and counties
and submitted [to the court].
Another imperial edict stated:
"All silver vessels, bells, *qìng* (stone chimes), cauldrons, pots, etc.,
used by monks and nuns in temples throughout the realm
are to be entrusted to the Yántiě Shǐ of various circuits
and stored in the official treasury.
This is to be recorded and reported [to the throne]."
There was an imperial edict prohibiting all single-wheeled carts throughout the realm.
Following this regulation, anyone found using a single-wheeled cart
