On the second day, one thousand scrolls were recited for Xiāngchūn Míngshén.
On the third day, one thousand scrolls were recited for Bāmàn Púsà.
The lecturer of Guānyīn Temple.
Assisted in every matter.
Two hundred *dùn* of white cotton were given as offerings to the monks reciting scriptures.
On the fourteenth day, in the afternoon, Nán Zhōngjiālì came.
Copied from the original manuscript of Sōngchán Yuàn, Fànshì Gǔ, Bǐyì Shān, on the thirteenth day of the second month of Wénhuà 2nd year.
Héyì Shān Jīnjīng Jiàosì Abbot Fǎyìn Dàsēngdū Chánghǎi.
On a day in the tenth month of Míngdé 2nd year, all four volumes were completed with great joy.
Fǎyìn Quán Dàsēngdū Xiánbǎo.

On the twenty-sixth day of the tenth month of Zhèngyīng 4th year, copied at Chánglè Sì Fāng, wiping old eyes; it is written after the original copy, and future generations should use it to collate with the original.
Fǎyìn Dàhéshàng Wèi Biànzhào Jīngāng Jiānyìn recorded this.
After copying and comparing, only notes on unclear matters were made.
The original was by the two monks, Sēngzhèng Xiànyuán.
Yuánrén,
known in Japan as Cíjiào Dàshī,
was a famous monk of the Tiāntái school.
He came to Huá during the reign of Emperor Wénzōng of Táng to study,
staying for ten years.
He returned to his country at the beginning of Emperor Xuānzōng’s Dàzhōng era.
He authored four volumes of *Rùtáng Qiúfǎ Xúnlǐjì*,
which is an important historical material on the Táng dynasty recorded by a foreigner.
This article briefly examines his life,
and uses his diary of his travels in Táng as the basis for this piece.
Shì Yuánrén, surnamed Rènsheng.
He was born in the 13th year of Emperor Huánwǔ's Enryaku era (the 10th year of Emperor Dézōng's Zhēnyuán era in Tang China,
794 CE) in Tūgā-gun, Shimotsuke.
He lost his father young,
and was intelligent by nature,
with a gentle and elegant demeanor.
At nine, his elder brother taught him classics and histories.
In Dàcí Temple in the same district, there was a monk named Guǎngzhì,
who was a third-generation disciple of the Tang monk Jiànzhēn.
His virtue and knowledge were profound,
and he took Yuánrén as his dharma heir.
Thus, Yuánrén devoted himself to the study of Buddhist scriptures.
At fifteen,
he ascended Mount Hiei in Kyōto to meet Grand Master Chuándiào Zuìchéng,
who taught him the profound wisdom of Zhǐguān Great Samādhi.
He clearly surpassed his peers.
When someone requested instruction on Zhǐguān,
Chuándiào would always have Rén lecture,
while he himself sat nearby to listen and verify,
making it a regular practice.
In the 4th year of Kōnin,
at the age of twenty,
he passed the official examination.
In the first month of the following year,
he received ordination and took the śrāmaṇera precepts.
In the 7th year, he received the full precepts at Tōdai-ji.
After Zuìchéng's passing,
he further diligent in his studies and practice,
establishing lecture halls in various places.
In the 3rd year of Emperor Nínmíng's Jōwa era, he received an imperial edict to travel to Tang China for further study.
In the 6th month of the 5th year,
he journeyed west across the sea with Fúyuán Chángsì, the 18th Japanese envoy to Tang China,
at the age of forty-five.
He traveled in Tang China for ten years before returning to Japan,
greatly propagating Buddhist dharma.
He received favor from Emperors Wéndé
and Qīnghé,
was honored as Grand Master Chuándēng,
appointed Tendai Zàozhǔ,
petitioned for the establishment of Zǒngchíyuan,
performed offerings for the emperor,
and imparted samādhi to his disciples.
He built the Chángxíng Hall
and greatly rectified the rules and guidelines of both exoteric and esoteric teachings.
He constructed the Wénshū Pavilion,
laying its foundation with soil and stones brought back from Mount Wǔtái.
While the Tendai school in Japan was founded by Zuìchéng,
it was Yuánrén who truly brought about its prosperity and great achievements.
On the 14th day of the first month of the 6th year of Emperor Qīnghé's Jōgan era,
he passed away at Enryaku-ji in Kyōto,
at the age of seventy-one.
The day before his passing, he imparted the secret seal anointing to his senior disciple Chángjì.
Yuánrén's demeanor was gentle and serene,
yet firm and inwardly restrained.
He wrote extensively.
According to Akahori-shi's compiled "Chronology of Japanese Literary Figures,"
his commentaries and private notes totaled ninety-four kinds,
in one hundred fifty-three volumes.
His "Commentary on the two scriptures of Adamantine Pinnacle and Susiddhi"
in seven volumes,
and "Treatise on Manifesting and Promoting the Great Precepts"
in eight volumes,
were all published by imperial decree.
His "Record of a Pilgrimage to Tang in Search of the Dharma"
is also renowned.
Commentators praised him, saying, "He crossed the vast ocean,
trod the sacred caves,
sought out the wisest and absorbed their teachings,
consulted great scholars and delved into their origins.
The profound Dharma of the Three Secrets,
he distinguished and truly transmitted;
the perfect and universally penetrating teaching of the One Vehicle,
he revitalized and left nothing out.
In the 8th month, an imperial edict commanded the offering of one thousand volumes of the Lotus Sūtra at Zǒngchíyuan,
and conferred the posthumous title, stating: 'The late Tendai Zàozhǔ Yuánrén,
whose compassionate heart is unfathomable,
and whose wings of wisdom soar high.
To reach Wǔtái and seek the truth,
was truly like staking his life;
to open the Three Secrets and propagate the teachings,
his achievement increased its splendor.
He turned the great Brahma wheel,
and issued the righteous lion's roar.
We, with Our humble person,
frequently received his compassionate gaze.
We regret the sudden separation of his protection and support,
and our thoughts of honoring him are endless.
It is fitting to bestow upon him the title Fǎyìn Dàhéshàng,
and also the posthumous name Cíjué Dàshī.'"
This is what was said.
Details are found in "Biography of Grand Master Cíjué,"
"Origins of the Transmission of Buddhist Dharma in the Three Kingdoms, Volume 3,"
"Gánkēng Shìshū, Volume 3,"
"Biographies of Eminent Japanese Monks, Volume 6,"
and "Huāfāng Yúhuī"
and other books.
In the 1st year of Emperor Nínmíng of Japan,
Counselor Fúyuán Chángsì was dispatched as an envoy to Tang China.
On the 2nd day of the 7th month of the following year, four ships departed together,
with Yuánrén accompanying them.
They encountered danger, and the ships were damaged,
all forced to turn back.
In the 7th month of the 4th year, they set out again,
but unfavorable winds prevented success.
By the 13th day of the 6th month of the 5th year,
they re-embarked from Hakata in Kyūshū, boarding the first and fourth ships;
this was their third attempt.
Rén's "Record of a Pilgrimage to Tang"
begins on this day.
On the 22nd day of the 6th month, they sailed into the ocean,
where the winds and waves were fierce,
and they endured many hardships.
On the 2nd day of the 7th month of Emperor Wénzōng's Kāichéng 3rd year,
they arrived at Hǎilíng County, Yángzhōu Prefecture, Huáinán Circuit.
The ambassador, with the approval of Lǐ Déyù, the Huáinán Jìedùshǐ, was permitted to enter Cháng'ān.
Yuánrén requested to make a pilgrimage to Tiāntái,
and remained in Yángzhōu awaiting imperial permission.
During this time, he studied Siddhāṃ with Zōngruì,
and obtained maṇḍalas of the Garbhakośa and Vajradhātu,
patterns for various venerated altars,
portraits of eminent monks, and twenty-one kinds of relics,
along with one hundred twenty-eight sets of sūtras, śāstras, commentaries, and annotations,
totaling one hundred ninety-eight volumes.
Later, he welcomed the ambassador in Chǔzhōu,
but his request for a pilgrimage to Tiāntái
was ultimately not granted.
Disappointed, he boarded the envoy's ship for the return journey.
The ship docked at Dōnghǎi County, Hǎizhōu.
Rén, accompanied by his disciples Wéizhèng
and Wéixiǎo,
and sailor Dīng Xióngwàn, pretexted their departure and secretly landed ashore.
They were discovered by the Hǎizhōu authorities
and inspected by the Cìshǐ.
Just then, the second ship of the Tang envoy arrived at the Hǎizhōu coast,
so they were escorted back to board that ship.
On the 18th day of the 4th month, they arrived at the coast of Moupíng County, Dēngzhōu.
The account in the first volume of the Pilgrimage Record ends here.
On the 7th day of the 6th month of Kāichéng 4th year,
the ship landed at Chìshān Pǔ in Wéndēng County, Dēngzhōu.
At Chìshān, there was the Fǎhuāyuan built by the Silla man Zhāng Bǎogāo,
with over thirty monks,
seven of whom were Japanese.
Yuánrén was moved by this news,
and bidding farewell to the ambassador again,
he landed and took refuge at Fǎhuāyuan,
staying there for over a year.
He made a request to Zhāng Yǒng, the Pínglú Jìedùshǐ and commander of all military affairs in Dēngzhōu.
Yǒng had previously visited Japan as an envoy
and admired Yuánrén's sincerity,
so he helped him.
Thus, Yuánrén received permission for a pilgrimage to Wǔtái.
Then, in the 4th month of Kāichéng 5th year, he traveled north from Dēngzhōu,
passing through Qīngzhōu,
Zīzhōu,
Qízhōu,
Dézhōu,
Bèizhōu,
Jìzhōu,
and Xíngtáng in Zhàozhōu,
heading northwest towards the Tàiháng Mountains.
On the 16th day of the 5th month, they reached the foot of Mount Qīngliáng.
The Pilgrimage Record states: "In the valleys of the mountain ranges,
the trees are upright and tall,
without a single crooked branch.
When entering the sacred land,
even seeing the lowliest person,
one dares not harbor contempt.
If one encounters a donkey or other animal,
one might feel suspicion,
fearing it could be a manifestation of Wénshū.
Everything one sees
evokes the thought that it is a manifestation of Wénshū.
The sacred and spiritual land
naturally inspires reverence in people."
Thus, his sincerity was profound.
The second volume of the diary ends here.
Yuánrén, on the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month, caught sight of Mount Wǔtái’s Central Terrace.
He prostrated himself and bowed from afar,
tears flowing unconsciously.
He then trekked to the northwest, east, and other terraces,
visiting sacred sites.
He met and paid respects to famous masters such as Xuánjiàn
and Zhìyuǎn,
presenting thirty points of doubt from the Enryaku-ji for clarification.
He copied secret texts of the Tiāntái school,
obtaining thirty-four works in thirty-seven volumes.
He stayed in the mountains for over fifty days.
On the first day of the seventh month,
he collected spiritual stones and soil from the lion's paw prints as mementos.
Bidding farewell to the sacred mountain,
he headed west towards Cháng'ān.
Passing through Xīnzhōu,
Tàiyuán,
and Hézhōng Fǔ,
he crossed the Yellow River at Lóngmén.
Traversing Cháoyì
and Lìzhōu,
he finally arrived at the Dà Táng capital, which had long occupied his dreams, on the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the fifth year of Kāichéng (830 CE).
He requested an audience with Qiú Shìliáng, the Commissioner of Meritorious Deeds for the Left Street,
and was ordered to reside at Zīshèng Sì.
At that time, Cháng'ān was teeming with famous monks,
competing in their brilliance.
Yuánrén studied the secret doctrines of the two mandalas (garbhadhātu and vajradhātu) from Reverend Yuánzhèng at the Fānjīng Yuàn of Dàxīngshàn Sì,
and from Reverend Yìzhēn at the Dōngtǎ Yuàn of Qīnglóng Sì.
He inquired about the Vajra Precepts from Fǎrùn at Qīnglóng Sì,
received the Garbhadhātu ritual from Fǎquán at Xuánfǎ Sì,
and inherited Zhǐguān from Zōngyǐng at Lǐquán Sì.
The ācāryas Wénwù from Dàxīngshàn Sì
and Yuánjiǎn from Dà'ānguó Sì
also provided inspiration.
He further re-learned Siddhaṃ from the Tripiṭaka Master Bǎoyuè from Southern India,
receiving correct pronunciation orally.
He obtained twenty-one items, including mandalas of the Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu,
altar designs for various deities,
and ritual implements.
He collected four hundred and twenty-three works of sūtras, śāstras, commentaries, and biographies,
totaling five hundred and fifty-nine volumes.
In the eighth month of the first year of Huìchāng (841 CE) of Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
Yuánrén had been in Táng for three years.
He had thoroughly comprehended the principles of the Three Vehicles,
and had instantly attained the gate of non-duality.
His wisdom surpassed others,
and his learning encompassed both inner and outer teachings.
He then submitted a memorial to the Commissioner of Meritorious Deeds requesting to return to his country,
but it was not granted.
Since Emperor Wǔzōng came to power,
the suppression of Buddhism and persecution of monks
grew increasingly severe.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of the third year of Huìchāng (843 CE),
a directive was issued to all monasteries to thoroughly investigate foreign monks.
Yuánrén submitted a detailed report.
The third scroll of his "Pilgrimage Record" ends here.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month of the third year of Huìchāng,
his disciple Wéixiǎo passed away.
He had been suffering from a chronic illness for seven months.
Yuánrén, in arranging the funeral, felt even more sorrow and decided to return quickly.
Emperor Wǔzōng's destruction of monasteries and expulsion of monks
reached its peak in the fifth year of Huìchāng (845 CE).
It was at this time that Yuánrén was also ordered to return to secular life,
thus gaining the opportunity to return to his home country.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, he departed Cháng'ān.
Believers such as Yáng Jìngzhī
and Lǐ Yuánzuǒ saw him off,
saying with great reluctance:
"Our country's teachings
will go east with the Venerable Monk!"
Yuánzuǒ requested his monk's robe,
reverently placing it on his head to console his feelings of separation.
Yuánrén grew his hair and changed into civilian attire,
passing through Zhèngzhōu,
Biànzhōu,
and Sìzhōu down to Wéiyáng.
He then exited Chǔzhōu
and Hǎizhōu,
traversing Mìzhōu
and Láizhōu to reach the Gōudàng Xīnlüo Suǒ in Wéndēng County,
where he waited for a convenient ship.
Although he received protection from Jìedùshǐ Zhāng Yǒng,
he repeatedly encountered hardships,
and ultimately found no opportunity for a return voyage.
Three years drifted by,
until the ninth month of the first year of Dàzhōng (847 CE) of Emperor Xuānzōng's reign,
when he finally embarked on a Silla ship bound for Japan, returning east.
He shaved his head and donned his monastic robes again,
departing from Chìshān Pǔ.
On the seventeenth day of the ninth month, he arrived at Hakata in Chikuzen,
which was the fourteenth year of Jōwa in Japan.
The Grand Council sent a dispatch to the Dazaifu to welcome Yuánrén to the capital.
Yuánrén then offered silk and cloth to the great deities of Tàishān Sì, Sumiyoshi, Kashiinamyōjin, and others,
giving thanks for heavenly blessings.
The "Pilgrimage Record" concluded its writing on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month of that year.
From its commencement on the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the fifth year of Jōwa (838 CE),
it had taken nine years and seven months to complete.
Examining his itinerary in Táng with current administrative divisions,
he traveled through seven provinces:
Jiāngsū,
Shāndōng,
Héběi,
Shānxī,
Shǎnxī,
Hénán,
and Ānhuī.
The "Rù Táng Xúnlǐ Jì" (Record of a Pilgrimage to Táng) in four scrolls
is Yuánrén's diary of his travels in Táng.
It spans two countries
and a period of ten years.
Although not without interruptions,
the dates and years are arranged
in perfect order.
This book only recently gained widespread recognition.
Yuánrén's original manuscript was formerly preserved at Enryaku-ji in Kyōto,
but is now lost.
The "Cíjué Dàshī Zhuàn" (Biography of Grand Master Cíjué),
written forty-nine years after the Master's nirvana,
clearly recorded the events of his entry into Táng,
entirely based on this original record.
During the Northern Sòng dynasty, the ācārya Chéngxún, who entered Sòng,
was commissioned by Emperor Shénzōng
to present the first three scrolls of this book in the fifth year of Xīníng (1072 CE),
as seen in the fourth scroll of his "Cān Tiāntái Wǔtái Shān Jì" (Record of a Pilgrimage to Mount Tiāntái and Mount Wǔtái).
This indicates that the book had long been in the imperial archives of Sòng.
Ní Chūngrén's "Lìzhèng Ānguólùn",
the "Ruì Yuè Jì",
and the author of "Yuánhēng Shìshū Zhēnggù"
all cited this book,
proving its long circulation.
There are two existing ancient manuscript copies today:
one is the Kanchiin bản from Tōji, Kyōto,
and the other is the Ikeda Nagatanishi collection.
The Tōji Kanchiin bản was written by Hōin Ken'in in the fourth year of Shōō (1291 CE) in Japan.
The fourth scroll has a colophon that reads:
"Finished copying with dim eyes at the Chōrakuji temple quarters on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month, fourth year of Shōō.
Copied from the original.
Later generations can use the attested version for collation."
Recorded by Hōin Daisōjō I Benjōkongō Ken'in.
Also, at the end of the second and third scrolls, it says: "Collated with a written copy,
Ken'in."
The fourth scroll also has a small-print colophon that reads:
"Compared and collated with a written copy.
Unclear matters were noted."
The marginal note on the left reads:
"This is the copy of Nii Sōjō Kakukan."
Hōshi Ken'in's affairs cannot be verified.
Chōrakuji is in Maruyama, Kyōto,
originally a Tendai school temple,
and Ken'in was probably its head.
His collation and referencing used the copy of Sōjō Kan'en,
but the original manuscript he relied upon is unknown.
The "Eiyō Yōki" records that Hōin Kan'en rebuilt
the Daikōdō, Monjudō, Sōjiin, and the Monju Shishi, etc., which were destroyed by fire in the second year of Genkyū (1205 CE), in the first year of Kenryaku (1211 CE).
The Sōjō Kan'en mentioned in Hōin Ken'in's colophon
is likely the one who transmitted this record.
The fourth year of Shōō, when Hōin Ken'in copied it, was over four hundred and thirty years after Yuánrén's death.
This so-called Kamakura ancient manuscript
is designated a national treasure by the Japanese.
In December of the fifteenth year of Taishō (1926 CE), three hundred facsimile copies were printed and circulated by the Tōyō Bunko in Tōkyō.
It included one volume of commentary by Dr. Okada Masayuki, professor at Tōkyō Imperial University,
totaling five volumes.
At the end of the Ikeda Nagatanishi collection, there is a colophon by Daisōzu Chōkai dated the second year of Bunka (1805 CE), which reads:
"Finished copying from the imperial manuscript of Shōzenin in Iimurodani, Hieizan, on the thirteenth day of the second month, second year of Bunka."
Hōin Daisōzu Chōkai, abbot of Keijitsu Kinkaku-ji.
Kinkaku-ji is a Tendai school temple in Kita Saku-gun, Shinano Province.
Thus, the Ikeda copy was transcribed by Daisōzu Chōkai from the Shōzenin copy.
However, the Shōzenin copy from Hieizan is now lost.
Although the Ikeda copy is later in date,
it contains fewer errors and omissions than the Tōji Kanchiin copy.
The Shōzenin original it was based on may have been an ancient manuscript
and is also important for research.
Although the Guānzhìyuàn (觀智院) bản (本) of Dōngsì (東寺) is an ancient transcription,
the manuscript it was based on
seems to have many errors and omissions.
Even after correction with the Kuānyuán (寬圓) Sēngzhèng (僧正) bản,
it still contained no small number of errors and omissions.
Furthermore, due to its transcription in old age,
the handwriting is blurred,
making reading difficult.
It is possible that Yuánrén (圓仁)'s original notes
were already not free from errors and omissions.
In the current book, there are many homophonous characters used interchangeably,
for example, "Nánzhào (南詔)"
is written as "Nánzhào (南照),"
"Lùfǔ (潞府)"
is abbreviated as "Lùfǔ (路府),"
"Liú Cóngjiàn (劉從諫)"
is written as "Liú Cóngjiǎn (劉從簡)"
and so on.
The section "Dēng Wǔtáishān Jìshì (登五台山紀事)" from the 28th day of the 4th month to the 16th day of the 5th month of Kāichéng (開成) 5th year
in the second scroll duplicates that in the third scroll,
and the text varies in detail and brevity.
It is likely that the original manuscript might have undergone deletions,
not that the copyist transmitted variant texts.
It is common for there to be
disordered bamboo slips
due to repeated copying.
For example, in the second scroll, Yuánrén (圓仁)'s petition to the Dēngzhōu (登州) Jiédùshǐ (節度使) for a travel permit on the 5th day of the 3rd month of Kāichéng (開成) 5th year
reappears in the entry for the 17th day of the 2nd month of the same year.
In the second scroll, the record for the 14th day of the 3rd month of Kāichéng (開成) 5th year,
its first half is interspersed with the record for the 16th day.
Following this, records for the 29th day of the 2nd month,
1st day of the 3rd month,
and 2nd day of the 3rd month reappear.
Then, it continues with the latter half of the record for the 14th day of the 3rd month and the events of the 15th
and 16th days.
This is the most severe instance of disordered slips.
The Ikeda Nagada (池田長田)氏 bản has fewer errors.

Judging from the fact that Yuánrén (圓仁)'s petition to the Dēngzhōu (登州) Jiédùshǐ (節度使) for a travel permit on the 5th day of the 3rd month of Kāichéng (開成) 5th year in the second scroll does not reappear,
the Sōngchányuàn (松禪院) bản, Kuānyuán (寬圓) bản, and Dōngsì (東寺) Guānzhìyuàn (觀智院) bản
seem to originate from two different sources.
However, there are identical instances of disordered slips,
which were probably due to oversights by the original transcriber of the manuscript.
The *Xúnlǐ Xíngjì (巡禮行記)* was only published in recent years.
Initially, Kokusho Kankōkai (國書刊行會) included it in the *Zoku Gunsho Ruijū (續羣書類叢)*.
Subsequently, the Tendai-shū Jiumu-chō (天台宗務廳) Documents Section appended it to the *Sì Míng Yú Xiá (四明餘霞)* based on the Ikeda (池田) bản.
Takakusu Junjirō (高楠順次郎) compiled the *Dà Rìběn Fójiào Quán Shū (大日本佛教全書)*,
including it in the *Yóufāng Chuán Cóngshū (遊方傳叢書)*, volume one.
He used the Dōngsì (東寺) Guānzhìyuàn (觀智院) bản as the base text,
and collated it with the Ikeda (池田) bản published in *Sì Míng Yú Xiá (四明餘霞)* and the Kokusho Kankōkai (國書刊行會) bản.
Those who participated in the collation included Tsuji Zennosuke (辻善之助), Wada Hidematsu (和田英松),
Kuroita Katsumi (黑版勝美), and Fujita Yi (藤田易) and other scholars,
all of whom were erudite.
It contains a colophon by Takakusu Junjirō (高楠順次郎) dated June 30th, Taishō (大正) 4th year.
Okada Masayuki (岡田正之) once undertook to write annotations for it,
but died before completing the work.
The *Xúnlǐ Jì (巡禮記)* spans a long period
and covers a wide range of subjects.
From relations between the two countries,
to customs and rituals of the Great Táng (大唐),
government systems,
local administration,
political measures,
religious issues,
diplomacy and international wars,
much is based on direct observation and hearsay,
recorded as casual notes.
Letters and official documents exchanged
are often recorded in full,
serving as an aid for studying the style of public and private correspondence at that time.
Although the recorded facts are not without mis傳訛聞 (errors and misinformation),
they greatly supplement historical records.
Among ancient Japanese diplomats,
study monks,
and students who traveled to China,
though numerous,
those who left important records are Master Zhìchéng (智澄)'s *Xínglì Chāo (行曆鈔)* from the Táng (唐) dynasty,
Āchári (阿闍梨) Chéngxún (成尋)'s *Cān Tiāntái Wǔtái Jì (參天台五台記)* from the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Monk Ruìxīn (瑞訢)'s *Rù Táng Jì (入唐記)* from the Míng (明) dynasty,
Monk Cèyàn (策彥)'s *Chūdù Jí (初渡集)*
and *Zàidù Jí (再渡集)*,
which, along with Yuánrén (圓仁)'s book,
are collectively known as the Five Great Travelogues.
However, in terms of scale and
the abundance of historical facts,
Yuánrén (圓仁)'s book truly stands out.
Many of the facts he recorded
can be used for historical research
and supplement the deficiencies in Chinese records.
For example, in the entry for the 4th month of Huìchāng (會昌) 5th year in scroll 4, it says:
"The Left and Right Shéncè (神策) Armies
are the Emperor's guard armies.
Each army has 100,000 soldiers.
Since ancient times, kings have faced rebellions from their ministers.
However, since the establishment of these armies,
no one has dared to usurp the throne.
Whenever a Zhongwei (中尉) first assumes office, the imperial seal is granted.
According to imperial edict, troops are dispatched to welcome the seal,
and separate public duties are performed,
not belonging to the Southern Bureau.
In the early 4th month of this year (Huìchāng (會昌) 5th year),
an imperial edict was issued to demand the seals of both armies,
but the Zhōngwèi (中尉) refused to surrender the seals.
The edict was issued repeatedly.
The Emperor's intention was to demand the guard army seals and entrust them to the Zhongshu Menxia Ling (中書門下令) for management,
for the Prime Ministers to oversee military affairs,
and all matters were to be handled by the Prime Ministers.
The Left Army Zhōngwèi (中尉) immediately agreed to surrender the seal,
but the Right Army Zhōngwèi (中尉) refused,
and then memorialized, saying:
'On the day the seal is welcomed,
troops welcome it.
On the day the seal is surrendered,
troops must also be mobilized to surrender it.'
The Zhōngwèi (中尉)'s intention was that if the Emperor allowed this,
he would then mobilize troops and cause trouble.
So, he instructed the relevant officials
to secretly arrange troops,
and the Emperor, being fearful, might not demand the seals for now."
This describes the secret struggle between Emperor Wǔzōng (武宗) and the eunuch-led Shéncè (神策) armies.
Wǔzōng (武宗) wanted to reclaim the official seals
and entrust military power to the Prime Ministers,
but Yú Hóngzhì (魚弘志), the Right Army Zhōngwèi (中尉), secretly plotted to resist the order,
and the matter was thus blocked.
Though Wǔzōng (武宗) was heroic,
there were still things he could not control.
This occurred two years after the death of Qiú Shìliáng (仇士良),
when eunuch power was waning.
The biography of Qiú Shìliáng (仇士良) in the *Xīn Táng Shū (新唐書)* records:
"Wǔzōng (武宗) was decisive.
Although Qiú Shìliáng (仇士良) had the merit of assisting him to the throne,
he secretly disliked him,
but outwardly showed him respect."
This was probably out of necessity.
The Huìchāng (會昌) anti-Buddhist movement
saw over 4,600 temples demolished nationwide,
260,500 monks and nuns secularized
and registered as two-tax households,
over 40,000 hermitages and monasteries demolished,
tens of millions of fertile upper-grade fields confiscated,
and 150,000 slaves registered as two-tax households.
Manichaeism, Nestorianism, and other religions
were also implicated and extinguished.
This was a major event in religious history,
yet few Táng (唐) writers recorded it.
This is because Emperor Wǔzōng (武宗) implemented a thorough suppression of Buddhism in Huìchāng (會昌) 5th year,
but died suddenly in the 3rd month of the 6th year after taking Daoist elixirs.
When Emperor Xuānzōng (宣宗) ascended the throne,
he immediately executed Daoist Liú Xuánjìng (劉玄靖) and others,
and revived Buddhist temples.
From then on, both court and commoners avoided discussing the matter.
The *Jiù Táng Shū (舊唐書)* and *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑)*
both record the main points in Huìchāng (會昌) 5th year.
However, the facts actually began at the start of Emperor Wǔzōng (武宗)'s reign.
The *Xúnlǐ Jì (巡禮記)* records them in particular detail,
and these events are compiled below:
On the 11th day of the 6th month of Huìchāng (會昌) 1st year, the Emperor's birthday,
a vegetarian feast was held in the palace.
Monks and Daoists from the two streets were gathered to discuss scriptures.
There were four pairs of debaters.
Two Daoists were granted purple robes,
while Buddhist eminent monks
were not allowed to wear them at all.
The Tripitaka Master Bǎoyuè (寶月) from Southern India entered the palace to meet the Emperor.
He took out a memorial from his bosom, requesting to return to his homeland.
As he did not first consult the Kaifu (開府) (Governor),
he was angrily
detained for five days within the army for exceeding his authority.
Therefore, Bǎoyuè (寶月)'s three disciples each received seven strokes,
the interpreter monk received ten strokes,
but the Tripitaka Master himself was not beaten
or allowed to return home.
On the 3rd day of the 3rd month,
Prime Minister Lǐ (李) heard a memorial regarding monks and nuns.
An imperial edict was issued to send out those without official status,
and unnamed monks were not allowed to keep boy novices.
On the ninth day of the tenth month, an imperial edict was issued:
All monks and nuns in the realm who practice alchemy, incantations, or vital energy techniques, who betray the army,
who bear whip marks on their bodies,
who have tattoos or engage in miscellaneous crafts,
who have committed lewd acts or supported wives,
or who do not cultivate monastic precepts,
are all ordered to return to secular life.
If any monks or nuns possess money, goods, grain, land, or estates,
these shall be confiscated by the government.
If they value their wealth
and willingly return to secular life,
they shall also be allowed to return to secular life by imperial edict,
and be assigned to the two-tax corvée.
The imperial edict is elsewhere.
The Commissioners of Merit for the Two Streets in the capital posted notices in all monasteries,
not allowing monks and nuns to leave,
and keeping the monastery gates closed.
The monk Xuánxuán memorialized that he could create a "sword-wheel" himself,
and personally lead troops to attack the Huíhú Kingdom.
An imperial order instructed that monk to attempt to make the "sword-wheel,"
but he failed.
Furthermore, based on what Prime Minister Lǐ Shēn heard and memorialized,
this clause was initiated.
That monk Xuánxuán was then deceiving and coercing monks and nuns to seize their property.
According to the imperial edict's clause, throughout the realm,
the Grand Secretariat and the Department of the Gate in various prefectures of Dàtóng issued dispatches,
circulating them within the capital's troops and resisting the imperial edict,
unwilling to implement the clause,
because the imperial will did not permit it.
For now, it was permitted to request a temporary suspension for one hundred days, with notices posted in all monasteries,
not allowing monks and nuns to leave the monasteries.
The Commissioner of Merit for the Left Street memorialized:
According to the imperial edict's clause concerning monks and nuns,
excluding those who are already elderly and those with precise monastic discipline,
those who cherished their assets and willingly returned to secular life, including monks and nuns, totaled one thousand two hundred thirty-two persons.
The Commissioner of Merit for the Right Street memorialized:
According to the imperial edict's clause concerning monks and nuns,
excluding those who are already elderly and those with precise monastic discipline,
those who cherished their assets and willingly returned to secular life, including monks and nuns, totaled two thousand two hundred fifty-nine persons.
By imperial order, the Commissioner of Merit for the Right Street memorialized:
According to the imperial edicts of the seventh and
sixteenth days of the tenth month of last year,
monks and nuns ordered to return to secular life
should, if they cherish their assets
and willingly return to secular life,
each be entrusted to their native district to be registered as two-tax households.
Henceforth, any such individuals in other circuits
shall be dealt with according to this precedent.
Regarding their acquired slaves,
monks are allowed to keep one person,
nuns are allowed to keep two female slaves.
The rest shall be managed by their original families.
If they have no family,
the government shall sell them.
Their robes, alms bowls, and other remaining assets shall be collected and stored,
awaiting a later imperial edict for disposition.
Regarding the slaves kept by nuns and monks,
if they possess martial arts skills or understand various medicines or techniques,
they are not to be kept.
They are not to be shaved or privately ordained.
If there is any violation,
the monastic administrators shall record and report it to the authorities.
Regarding other assets, money, and so on,
each Commissioner of Merit shall personally present a memorial,
on the first day of the first month of Huìchāng Three, year Guǐhài.
On the first day of the second month, a dispatch stated:
Monks and nuns who have already returned to secular life
are strictly forbidden to enter or reside in monasteries.
Furthermore, monks and nuns outside the protection [of the capital] are dispatched,
not permitted to live in the capital or enter the garrisons.
The above still pertained to matters arising from specific events and individuals.
Although it involved clearing and purging,
it had not yet fundamentally abolished Buddhism.
But with Wéi Zōngqīng's memorial being criticized and rejected,
Emperor Wǔzōng's intention to destroy Buddhism became clear.
The *Xúnlǐ Jì* states:
In the sixth month of Huìchāng Three, Wéi Zōngqīng, the Grand Master of the Crown Prince, presented twenty scrolls of his commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The current emperor, after examining them,
burned the sūtra commentary.
An imperial edict ordered the Grand Secretariat and the Department of the Gate to pursue and retrieve the drafts from his residence for burning.
The imperial edict reads as follows:
Edict to Wéi Zōngqīng, Grand Master of the Crown Prince, with the title of Silver-Green Guanglu Grandee, Pillar of the State, Founding Male of Guāngyīn County with a fief of three hundred households.
You are listed among the esteemed officials,
and ought to follow Confucian learning.
Yet you are immersed in heterodox theories,
spreading evil winds.
You have opened the door to deceit and delusion,
completely violating the principles of the classics.
Among those wearing caps and sashes,
how profound is such decadence!
Moreover, words not of the Sage
are still prohibited and rejected;
how can foreign doctrines be allowed to spread?
Although we wish to be tolerant,
we fear harming public morals.
You should be demoted,
which is still considered a generous favor.
You may serve as the Administrator of Chéngdū Prefecture,
and be dispatched by post-horse.
Wéi Zōngqīng, Grand Master of the Crown Prince, presented his work on the Buddhist *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, having compiled "Three Virtues" in twenty scrolls.
By imperial edict, the "Great Perfection Mirror Summary" in twenty scrolls [meaning Wéi Zōngqīng's work]
has been fully examined.
The Buddha was originally a person from the Western Barbarians,
whose teachings propagated the doctrine of non-birth.
Confucius was a sage of the Central Land,
whose classics proclaimed beneficial words.
Yet Wéi Zōngqīng, a scholar from a Confucian family,
a prominent figure among the literati,
is unable to expound the teachings of Confucius and Mozi,
but instead blindly believes in Buddhism.
He presumptuously compiles foreign texts
and rashly presents them.
Moreover, the common people of China
have long been infected by this trend.
It is truly appropriate to collectively stop this delusion
and make them return to simplicity.
Yet you gather demonic falsehoods,
further misleading ignorant people.
Holding a position in the imperial court,
how can you not be ashamed?
The sūtra you presented
has already been burned internally.
Its drafts are entrusted to the Grand Secretariat and the Department of the Gate to be pursued, confiscated, and burned.
They are not to be disseminated externally.
Edict issued on the thirteenth day of the sixth month of Huìchāng Three.
The process of the suppression of Buddhism
as recorded is as follows:
In the fourth month of the fifth year of Huìchāng,
a memorial from the gōngdéshǐ concerning the defrocking of monks and nuns was seen.
The order of discussion was
first, to have those under thirty defrocked;
next, to have those under fifty defrocked;
next, to have those over fifty without a cíùbù travel permit defrocked;
thirdly, to have those whose cíùbù travel permits were found to be irregular upon inspection defrocked;
finally, to have all those with cíùbù travel permits that were not irregular defrocked.
This would mean the complete eradication of monks and nuns.
This discussion
was agreed upon throughout the realm.
Because it was carried out in accordance with an imperial edict,
from the first day of the fourth month,
all monks and nuns under thirty were imperially ordered to return to secular life,
and to return to their native places.
Three hundred monks were defrocked daily.
By the fifteenth day, all monks and nuns under forty were finished.
Starting from the sixteenth day,
monks and nuns under fifty were defrocked,
until the tenth day of the fifth month, when it was completed.
Starting from the eleventh day,
those over fifty without cíùbù travel permits were defrocked.
Since last year, memorials concerning monks and nuns
had resulted in the selection of those with crude conduct who did not adhere to their original teachings,
and all were imperially ordered to return to secular life,
and to return to their native places.
This year, there was no distinction made between those with lofty or crude conduct,
nor was it about examining the integrity of eminent monks.
Once their turn came,
they were to be defrocked.
There were frequent imperial inquiries:
How many have been defrocked?
How many have not yet been defrocked?
The numbers were hastened.
Foreign monks were not included in the list of those to be defrocked.
The gōngdéshǐ would report separately and await a decision.
An imperial edict stated:
If foreign monks do not have cíùbù travel permits,
they are also to be imperially ordered to return to secular life,
and to return to their native countries.
Nántuó from Western India and Northern Tiānzhú, residing in Dàxīngshàn Sì,
along with the Tiānzhú Sānzàng Bǎoyuè and his four disciples,
who became accomplished in Central Tiānzhú,
and all understood the Great Dhāranī teachings,
with meticulous adherence to the precepts,
and extensive knowledge of sutras and treatises, were in Qīnglóng Sì, and none had Táng Dynasty cíùbù travel permits.
Many Sīnxīluó monks also had no cíùbù travel permits.
Japanese monks Yuánrén
and Wéizhèng also had no Táng cíùbù travel permits.
The gōngdéshǐ, in accordance with the imperial edict, included them in the category for defrocking.
Another circular to the various monasteries stated:
If there are any monks or nuns who refuse to be defrocked,
they shall be charged with violating the imperial edict,
and immediately executed.
An entry in the eighth month stated:
Recently there was an imperial edict,
that throughout the realm, the monastic robes of defrocked monks and nuns
should all be collected and burned by their respective prefectures and counties,
for fear that if the robes were widely circulated and distributed,
people relying on their power might hide them in private homes,
and secretly wear monastic robes.
It is necessary to strictly collect and inspect them,
and after all are burned, report it.
If after burning,
any monks or nuns are found to be illicitly possessing monastic robes,
during inspections,
if such bundles are found,
they are to be dealt with according to the imperial edict.
The various prefectures and counties, in accordance with the imperial edict, notified all wards and villages
to collect the clothes of monks and nuns,
bring them to the prefectures and counties,
and burn them all.
There was also an imperial edict ordering that all rare treasures, pendants, pearls, jade, gold, and silver from monasteries throughout the realm
be collected and submitted by their respective prefectures and counties.
Another imperial edict stated:
All silver vessels, bells, chimes, cauldrons, and pans used by monks and nuns in monasteries throughout the realm
are to be handed over to the various provincial salt and iron commissioners for collection into the official treasury,
and a record reported.
Although the government decrees were severe,
in Hébĕi, due to the laxity of governance,
they seemed not to be fully implemented.
An entry in the eleventh month stated:
For the past three
or four years, throughout the prefectures and counties, in accordance with imperial edicts, all monks and nuns have been defrocked.
Also, all Buddhist halls and aranya residences throughout the realm have been demolished.
Furthermore, all sutras, images, and monastic robes throughout the realm have been completely burned.
Moreover, the gold from all Buddhist statues throughout the realm has been stripped,
and all copper and iron Buddha statues throughout the realm have been broken into pieces, weighed, and collected.
All money, property, estates, and household slaves of monasteries throughout the realm have been collected by the prefectures and counties.
Only the four military governorships north of the Yellow River, namely Zhèn, Yōu, and Wèi Lù, etc.,
who originally respected Buddhism,
did not demolish monasteries,
did not defrock monks and nuns,
and did not disturb any Buddhist matters.
When imperial envoys frequently came to investigate and punish,
they said, "The Son of Heaven himself comes to demolish and burn,
then it can be done!
We, your subjects, cannot do such things."
Reading this, the specific procedures, scope, and results of Wǔzōng’s suppression and destruction of Buddhism
are clearly known.
It can indeed supplement the omissions in the official histories.
While enduring humiliation, the monastics
also daily created rumors and slanders
to falsely accuse the sovereign and his ministers,
and to destabilize the people's minds.
Many such accounts are recorded in the Xúnlǐ Jì,
for instance, concerning Wǔzōng's relationship with Daoists, it states:
In the second month of the fourth year of Huìchāng,
the Emperor visited the Jīnxiān Guān on the right street.
This was a nunnery,
and among the Daoist nuns in the guān,
one was very beautiful.
The Emperor summoned her and was pleased.
He imperially bestowed one thousand bolts of silk,
and then ordered a eunuch to oversee the renovation of the guān,
which was then connected to the palace,
and a Jīnxiān Lóu was specially constructed.
The guān was originally dilapidated,
but after renovation, it became magnificent,
and the Emperor frequently visited.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of Huìchāng,
there was an imperial edict prohibiting single-wheeled carts throughout the realm.
After the prohibition,
anyone found using a single-wheeled cart
would be executed on the spot.
This was because the Emperor believed the Daoists' teaching that
single-wheeled carts damaged the center of the road,
and feared that this would cause unease in the Daoists' hearts!
There was an imperial edict prohibiting all black pigs, black dogs, black donkeys, and cattle throughout the realm.
This was because Daoists wore yellow,
and perhaps feared that too much black would suppress the yellow and diminish it!
Coastal prefectures and counties were ordered to submit live otters;
the reason for this is unknown.
Recently, there was an imperial edict ordering all Daoists to submit the hearts and gallbladders of male and female children aged fifteen,
which was also due to being deluded by Daoists.
Regarding Wǔzōng's palace crimes, it states:
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Huìchāng,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
Empress Hé of the Guō clan,
because the Empress Dowager was devout and
believed in Buddhism,
always offered remonstrances whenever monks and nuns were defrocked.
The Emperor ordered her to be given medicinal wine,
and she was poisoned to death!
Also, Empress Xiāo of Yìyáng Diàn,
who was the mother of the current emperor,
was very beautiful.
The current emperor summoned her to be his consort,
but the Empress Dowager did not obey the command.
The Emperor demanded a bow and shot her to death;
the arrow pierced her chest,
and she died.
Regarding Wǔzōng's unseemly treatment of his subordinates, it states:
In the fourth year of Huìchāng, an imperial edict ordered the two armies to construct an immortal terrace within the palace,
one hundred fifty chi high.
Starting in the tenth month,
three thousand men from the Left and Right Shéncè Armies were used daily
to carry earth and construct it.
The Emperor eagerly wished for its early completion,
and issued edicts daily to hasten the construction.
The Dūyúhóu of the two armies inspected with sticks.
The Emperor, passing by and seeing this,
asked the inner officer Cháng'ān:
"Who is that man with the stick?"
The officer reported:
"The Hùjūn Dūyúhóu is supervising the construction of the terrace."
The Emperor declared:
"I don't need you to supervise with a stick;
you must carry the earth yourself,"
and immediately made him carry earth.
Later, when he again visited the construction site,
the Emperor personally demanded a bow,
and without reason shot one yúhóu to death.
This was extreme tyranny.
Regarding Wǔzōng's death, it records:
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the sixth year of Huìchāng,
it was heard that the Emperor had died several months prior,
and throughout the various prefectures and counties,
mourning was held and filial attire worn.
He died with his body decaying.
On the first day of the fifth month of that year,
the record of Xuānzōng's (宣宗) enthronement states:
"The new Son of Heaven's surname is Lǐ (李)."
This phrasing is particularly trenchant.
All these records
were probably planned propaganda by the monks of the time,
not the fabrication of Yuánrén (圓仁) alone.
For at that time, Buddhist influence had deeply penetrated people's hearts,
and Wǔzōng (武宗), Lǐ Déyù (李德裕) and others sought to resist it with the strength of a few individuals,
thus ultimately suffering disgrace and ruin.
Upon Xuānzōng's (宣宗) ascension,
policies took a complete turn.
That Lǐ Zànhuáng (李贊皇), with all his wisdom, skill, and accomplishments,
suffered a complete downfall
was likely due to having made too many enemies;
his "burning the city with his red mouth" (incendiary words)
meant that those who condemned him were not only Línghú Táo (令狐綯) and Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) and their ilk.
(Addendum) Regarding Chinese records concerning the Huìchāng (會昌) persecution of Buddhism:
the *Jiù Táng Shū Wǔzōng Jì* (舊唐書武宗紀) in the eighth month of the fifth year of Huìchāng (會昌) contains an edict to abolish Buddhism.
Volume 20 of *Lǐ Wèigōng Huìchāng Yīpǐn Jí* (李衛公會昌一品集) contains a memorial celebrating the abolition and destruction of various temples.
Further references include Dù Mù's (杜牧) *Fánchuān Wénjí* (樊川文集) Volume 10,
*Hángzhōu Xīnzào Nántíngzi Jì* (杭州新造南亭子記) and *Táng Huìyào* (唐會要) Volume 47,
and Sòng (宋) dynasty Zhào Líndé's (趙麟德) *Hóuqíng Lù* (侯鯖錄) Volume 2,
all of which can be consulted.
In summary,
although the *Xúnlǐ Jì* (巡禮記) contains mistaken transmissions and erroneous information,
and rumors and gossip
are everywhere to be found,
yet due to its antiquity
and vast scope,
its appropriate corroboration and cross-referencing,
and critical analysis and explanation,
will certainly be beneficial to those who study Táng (唐) history.
Formerly, Mr. Liáng Rèngōng (梁任公) discussed historical materials
and lamented that the surrounding peoples of our country
were mostly unenlightened,
and that their writings complementing our historical facts were extremely rare.
He considered the "Accounts of India and China" by the Arab Abusaid Hassan
and the travelogue of the Italian Marco Polo to be as rare as phoenix feathers and qilin horns.
Given the nature and content of the *Xúnlǐ Jì* (巡禮記),
it certainly surpasses these two books.
Dr. Gāng Yóuzhèngzhī (岡由正之), in his *Rìběn Hànwénxué Shǐ* (日本漢文學史),
highly praises Yuánrén's (圓仁) literary talent,
stating that his writing is no less skillful than that of Guān Yuándàozhēn (菅原道真) and
Sānshàn Qīngxíng (三善清行),
that his letters have the style of Ōu Sū's (歐蘇) personal correspondence,
and that his travel records are the crown of the five great travelogues.
He further asserts that Yuánrén (圓仁) was skilled in *waka*,
and his works were selected for the *Xù Gǔjīn* (續古今),
*Xīn Gǔjīn* (新古今),
and *Xīn Shíyí* (新拾遺)
three *waka* anthologies.
However, Yuánrén (圓仁) seemed to be deeply focused on Buddhist scriptures
and not on ornate rhetoric.
Staying in Táng (唐) for ten years,
and residing in Cháng'ān (長安) for six,
he was never seen to associate with literati
or to delve into refined literary pursuits.
The *Rù Táng Xīn Qiú Shèngjiào Mùlù* (入唐新求聖教目錄)
records many collections of Táng (唐) poetry and prose among the books Yuánrén (圓仁) brought back,
yet none of Yuánrén's (圓仁) own works
have been transmitted in either Japan or China.
Compared with Cháo Héng (晁衡) and
Kōng Hǎi (空海),
he cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Upon his return to Japan,
the Táng (唐) monk Qī Bái (栖白) presented him with a poem, saying:
The sunset nears your homeland mountain,
The sea-road believes in your returning oar.
Trees vanish, utterly shoreless,
Wind rises, only tides are there.
Year's end, the journey unfinished,
At heaven's edge, your country is still far.
Already you enter the dream of the King of Mǐn (閩),
Inviting fragrant flowers from beyond the border.
(See *Quán Táng Shī*)
At that time, Yuánrén (圓仁) had endured many worldly changes,
experiencing a mix of joy and sorrow,
and countless emotions,
yet no reply poem from him is known.
The prose of the *Xúnlǐ Jì* (巡禮記)
is verbose and rambling,
further marred by errors and omissions,
making it difficult to read through.
Although the book was transmitted,
it remained unpublished for a long time.
It entered the Sòng (宋) imperial library
without any reaction,
which may well be due to this reason.
Occasionally, there are noteworthy passages within it,
such as in Volume 3, describing the scenery of Wǔtái Shān (五台山):
The central peak is the center of the four peaks;
all over the peak, water gushes and the ground is soft,
grass grows more than an inch long,
lush and dense,
covering the ground,
it sinks when stepped on,
and rises again when the foot is lifted.
Every step is wet with water,
cold as ice.
Everywhere there are small hollows,
all filled with water!
Throughout the peak, sand and stones are interspersed,
and countless stone pagodas stand.
Fine, soft grass
grows entwined with moss.
Although the ground is wet with water,
there is no muddy brine,
because the moss and soft grass
have dense roots,
thus preventing travelers from soiling their shoes and feet.
Exotic flowers of strange colors
bloom profusely across the mountain.
Reaching the summit leisurely,
flowers are on all sides,
like embroidered brocade,
exuding a fragrant essence,
perfuming people's clothes.
People say that even now in May it is still cold,
and the flowers are not yet in full bloom.
They say that in June
and July,
the flowers will bloom even more profusely.
The colors of these flowers
are unlike any found in the human world.
It also records the origin of the equal offering of food to monks and laypeople in the mountains:
Those who enter this mountain (Wǔtái Shān (五台山))
naturally develop a sense of equality.
When vegetarian meals are provided in the mountain,
regardless of whether they are monks or laypeople, male or female, old or young,
all are offered food equally,
without regard for their status or age.
In everyone, the thought of Mañjuśrī arises.
Once upon a time, Dà Huáyán Sì (大華嚴寺) held a grand vegetarian feast,
and all ordinary men and women, beggars, and the poor came to receive offerings.
The donor complained:
"We traveled far over mountain slopes
to set up this offering here,
intending only to provide for the many monks in the mountain.
Yet all these worldly beggars
come to receive food.
If we are to provide for these beggars,
we might as well set up the feast locally.
Why come all the way to this mountain?"
The monks persuaded them to give food to all.
Among the beggars was a pregnant woman,
seated and pregnant.
After receiving and finishing her own portion of food,
she asked for a portion for the child in her womb.
The donor cursed her
and refused.
The pregnant woman repeatedly said:
"My child in the womb,
though not yet born,
is also a person.
Why not give it food?"
The donor said:
"You are foolish.
Though the child in your belly is one of a kind,
if it doesn't come out,
who will eat the food if I give it?"
The woman replied:
"If my child in the belly does not get food,
then I also ought not to eat."
She then rose and left the dining hall.
As soon as she exited the hall door,
she transformed into Mañjuśrī (文殊師利),
emitting light that illuminated the entire hall brilliantly.
With a radiant jade-like countenance,
riding a golden-maned lion,
surrounded by ten thousand Buddhas,
she ascended into the air and departed.
The assembly,
thousands of people,
all rushed out at once,
but were bewildered and fell to the ground.
They raised their voices in repentance and apology,
weeping tears like rain,
and all at once chanted the name of the Great Saint Mañjuśrī (文殊師利),
until their voices were hoarse and their throats dry,
but they were not favored with a glance back,
and she vanished as if in a dream.
The food for the great assembly
lost its taste.
Each person made a vow
that from now on,
when offering food and setting up feasts,
regardless of gender, age, status, poverty, or wealth,
all must be provided for equally.
The custom of the mountain
thus established the practice of equality.
These descriptions,
whether the scenery is unusual,
or the stories are strange,
without needing much embellishment,
are already masterpieces.
Rather than saying the writings of a benevolent person are worthy of transmission,
it is better to say that his deep contemplation and hidden virtues,
paying homage to famous mountains,
possess an unattainable profundity within his mind!
Japanese students dispatched to Táng,
and scholarly monks,
all received generous courtesy from the government and people of Zhōngguó,
with thoughtful care and protection,
meticulous in every detail.
Renowned monks and eminent virtuous ones,
with the spirit of treating all people as brothers and all beings as kin,
propagated the ancient teaching that education should be available to all without distinction.
Those who sought instruction or advice,
all departed having obtained what they desired.
Therefore, Zuìchéng,
Kōnghǎi, and others,
remembered their teachers with gratitude,
even until their dying days,
longing for Zhōngtǔ,
as if it were paradise.
Yuánrén achieved fame early in life,
his reputation greatly widespread,
and though past forty,
his disciples filled his gates.
After narrowly escaping death multiple times,
he ventured across the eastern sea,
his fervent quest for Buddhist teachings,
was no different from those who came before him.
He then visited Tiāntái but was denied entry,
remained in Hǎizhōu but was expelled,
hiding on an island coast,
and through connections with powerful figures,
finally managed to fulfill his long-held wish to visit and pay homage to Wǔtái,
and study in Cháng'ān.
Soon after, he encountered the calamity of the Huìchāng Mièfó,
to the point of growing his hair and changing his clothes,
his heart filled with sorrow and frustration.
He witnessed rumors and slanders,
the sovereign and his people estranged,
and bizarre decrees,
which were beyond comprehension.
Before he even left the country,
the policy of destroying Buddhism,
was already heard to be reversed,
with decrees changing from morning to night,
and all authority and credibility lost.
Indeed, ever since Yuánrén and others returned,
Japanese envoys to Táng no longer came,
and Táng also declined from this point on!
When Zhōugōng cultivated virtue, the Yuèchángshì came.
Cultural leadership,
how can it be spoken of lightly!
